But he who is ashamed to do good falls from the state of righteousness and tends toward damnation, as it is said by the Redeemer: Whoever is ashamed of me and my words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in his majesty. And there are some who already conceive good things in their mind, but do not yet openly contradict evils. These indeed, because they are good in mind but have no authority in speech, are not suited for the defense of truth. For he ought to be a defender of truth who neither fears nor is ashamed to speak what he rightly perceives. […]

3:9.t:
But what is a sinner except one who is wounded? And what is a preacher except a physician? If therefore the sinner who lies in his wound is not ashamed, why should the physician be ashamed who provides healing through medicines? Often indeed it happens that a preacher is listened to reverently; but sometimes he is so despised by the perverse as if he were speaking nothing useful to them. Hence it is rightly said now: "I have made your face like adamant and like flint."

Both diamond and flint are hard; but one of them is precious, the other worthless. The diamond is taken for adornment, the flint is trodden underfoot by travelers. And it often happens that when we observe those who receive our correction too humbly, we are ashamed to say certain things to them. But sometimes it happens that when we see those who disregard and hold in contempt our rebuke, we are afraid to bring them the word of preaching. […]

"Fear them not, neither be afraid at their face, for they are a rebellious house."

This has already been said above. But it should be noted how harsh a house is held to be, whose harshness is repeated so frequently. Therefore the sinner must be rebuked and never feared, because it is a provoking house. For a man ought to have been feared if he himself had feared the Author of all things as a man should. For he who did not have the sense of reason for fearing God is to be feared in nothing, inasmuch as he is not what he ought to have been.

3:10.t: Son of man, all my words which I speak to you, take into your heart and hear with your ears. This is the food of the scroll, and these are the words in which, according to the diversity of the hearers, we speak to men either laments or song or woe. And yet it must be noted that the words of God must first be stored in our heart, and heard and understood with great care, and so brought forth to the people.

"And he said to me: Son of man, receive in your heart all my words that I speak to you, and hear with your ears."

We must carefully observe that by the voice of the Lord it is said to the Prophet that he should first hear His words, and afterward speak. For we hear the words of God if we do them. And then we rightly speak them to our neighbors when we ourselves have first done them. This Mark the Evangelist confirms well when he narrates a miracle performed by the Lord, saying: "They bring to Him one deaf and mute, and they besought Him to lay His hand upon him." He indicates the order of the healing, adding: "He put His fingers into his ears, and spitting, He touched his tongue, and looking up to heaven, He sighed and said to him: Ephphetha, that is, be opened. And immediately his ears were opened, and the bond of his tongue was loosed, and he spoke rightly." […]

3:11.t: Go, enter to the exile (or captivity), to the sons of your people. And our Lord came to the people of the Jews, the Father sending him, to preach release to the captives, and that there might be fulfilled in him what is written: Ascending on high he led captivity captive, he gave gifts among men.

"And go, enter in to the captivity of the children of your people."

But as for the fact that the prophet is sent to admonish the people concerning their transmigration, not only should that transmigration be understood which was of that people in body, but also that which had occurred in mind. For they had come from Jerusalem to Babylon. And what is Jerusalem called but "vision of peace," what is Babylon called but "confusion"? But whoever falls from right works into perverse deeds, since he slips from good zeal into vices, comes as it were from Jerusalem to the city of Babylon. For he has abandoned the height of good contemplation and lies in the transmigration of confusion. This often tends to happen to those who, when they do good things, glory in their own virtue in these matters. Hence the Psalmist, lest he should migrate as a captive from the vision of peace, that is, from good deeds, to Babylon, supplicating the Lord, says: "My helper, I shall not migrate." […]

"And you shall speak to them, and you shall say: Thus says the Lord God: if perhaps they may hear and be still."

That the difficulty of hearing is repeated so many times in the divine words, so that it is said, "If perhaps they will hear," what else is designated but the hardness of the exiled people? In these words there is great consolation for us, because if almighty God, sending a prophet, declares that His words are heard with difficulty by a perverse people, why should we wretches be saddened when we are often despised by our brothers in our admonition? For frequently we address those who transgress, often we rebuke them, frequently we deal with them with gentle words, and yet if one hears, another disdains to hear; one partially receives the word of exhortation, and partially refuses to accept it; so that we seem to see daily fulfilled what the Lord narrates through another prophet about what He did in anger, when He says: "I rained upon one city, and upon another I did not rain. […]

3:12.t: And the spirit took me up, and I heard behind me a voice of great commotion: Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place. God, of whom it is written: The Lord taking up the meek, himself took up the prophet too, who was not in the flesh but in the spirit and, walking in the spirit, did not fulfill the works of the flesh, for the Spirit of God was in him; for which reason, despising earthly things, he is also caught up by the spirit and hears behind him a voice of great commotion, forgetting the things that are past and stretching himself toward what is to come, so that he might leave the snares of his enemies behind his back — something of this kind we also read in Exodus, when Pharaoh and all his army were pursuing Israel, and the angel in the pillar of cloud left the front of the camp and came behind their backs and stood all night between Israel and the Egyptians, so that, the adversaries being terrified, Israel might hear: Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place; […]

And concerning the Cherubim it is written that they were yoked unto a chariot, and while their faces looked downwards, the motions of their spiritual natures were directed whither was the Most High, and they likewise were crying out, "Blessed be the honour of the Lord from His country." And spiritual beings stand in this service, and the hosts and ranks of heaven are obedient unto the word of Jesus.
3:12.s: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 9 -- Second Discourse on Poverty

3:12.t:
"And the spirit lifted me up, and I heard behind me the voice of a great commotion: Blessed be the glory of the Lord from His place."

What is this, that after the prophet is sent to the captivity of the sons of the people, he hears behind him a voice of great commotion, saying: "Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place"? For he had been turned toward the sinners of Babylon, and he was hearing the voice of the glory of the Lord from his place behind his back. For the place of God is Jerusalem, that is, the vision of peace, because indeed those hearts see the things that are of God which do not descend to the captivity of Babylon, that is, to the vices of confusion. For God dwells there where true peace is sought, where the glory of interior contemplation is loved. For those who flow down to perversity disdain to be the place of God. Therefore the place of the glory of God is either every holy soul, or each angelic spirit remaining in the heavens. […]

But why do we linger on these matters, we who are able, by the Lord's bounty, to understand these words of the prophet through another and more subtle sense, and to speak more clearly? For he says: "And the spirit took me up." The spirit takes up a preacher when it renders his mind, elevated in love of almighty God, now estranged from earthly desires, so that nothing pleases him to do except those things by which he may gather spiritual gains and carry the fruit of his daily work to the heavenly kingdoms. Hence it is also commanded to us preachers: "Labor not for the food that perishes, but for that which endures unto eternal life."

And it is well added: "And I heard behind me the voice of a great commotion." The prophet, filled with the Holy Spirit, narrates as past events what he foresees will happen, because in predestination those things are already done which still follow in their accomplishment. Hence also in the old translation it is said through Isaiah: "Who has done the things that are to come." […]

But let us hear what the voice itself says: "Blessed be the glory of the Lord from His place." For the hearts of sinners had been the place of the malignant spirit; but when, angry with themselves, they return to life through repentance, they become a place for the glory of the Lord. For now they rise up against themselves, now they pursue with tears of repentance the evils they have committed. Therefore the blessing of glory in praise of the Lord is heard from the very place where previously the injury to the Creator resounded through love of the present age. And the hearts of the penitent, which formerly, set in sins, had been a foreign place, now become the Lord's own place. […]

3:13.t: And the voice of the wings of the living creatures striking one against another, and the voice of the wheels following the living creatures, and the voice of great commotion. (Whereas according to the Hebrew there is understood ἀπὸ κοινοῦ [in common, supplied from the preceding clause]: I heard behind me a voice of great commotion, and 'I heard' the voice of the wings of the living beings, and the voice of the wheels, the Seventy added: And 'I saw' the voice of the wings of the living beings, the voice of them striking one against another, and the rest, in keeping with what is read in Exodus: And all the people saw the voice of God, so that the prophet heard the voice that came behind his back, but saw the one that was before him.) But it is better and truer to have understood the voice as heard rather than seen, both that of the wings striking one another and that of the wheels, of which we spoke above, and that of the great commotion, which showed that the wrath of God was to come upon the people of Israel.

"And the sound of the wings of the living creatures striking one against another."

The prophet hears behind him the sound of a great commotion, because, as has been said, the word of those preaching is followed by the lamentation of the penitent. He hears behind him the sound of the wings of the living creatures, because from that very lamentation of the penitent arise the virtues of the saints, so that they advance all the more in holy action, the more they remember having acted wickedly before their knowledge of life. But there is great uncertainty in these words, because it is not clearly stated by the prophet whether each living creature strikes its wings against itself, or whether these same holy living creatures beat one another in turn with their wings, so that the wing of one touches another, and the wing of another touches this living creature. […]

But if, as we have said, the living creatures in turn strike one another with their wings, and the wing of each strikes against the wing of another, the meaning of this description also lies open, with the Lord's help. What does it mean, then, that these winged creatures in turn strike their wings one against another, except that all the saints mutually touch one another with their virtues, and rouse each other to advancement through the consideration of another's virtue? For all things are not given to one person, lest being lifted up in pride he should fall, but to this one is given what is not given to you, and to you is given what is denied to him, so that while the former considers the good that you have and he does not have, he may set you before himself in his thought; and again, while you observe that he possesses what you yourself do not have, you may place yourself after him in your thought, and so it comes about as it is written: "Considering one another as superiors." […]

Let us see how Paul was touched by the wings of the apostles and stirred to repentance. Considering the evils of his past persecution and the innocent life of the apostles, he said: "For I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God." He considered indeed the innocence of the apostles, and because of his preceding wickedness, all the care he showed in the Church became worthless in his eyes; and he did not consider how many he surpassed by the understanding he had received, because, weighing their innocence, he grieved that he had once been a persecutor. But let us see if any of the apostles marvels at the understanding given to Paul. We must first consult the chief of the apostles himself, who, admonishing his disciples, says: "As also our most beloved brother Paul, according to the wisdom given to him, has written to you; […]

"And the sound of the wheels following the living creatures, and the sound of a great commotion."

We said above that the Testaments are signified by the wheels of sacred Scripture. The voice of the wheels, therefore, is the word of the Testaments. Thus after the voice of the wings of the living creatures, the voice of the wheels is also heard, because when the preaching of the preachers is received, while the virtues of the saints fly upward to accomplish higher things and mutually urge one another toward advancement, the state of the holy Church is raised up, so that throughout the whole world the pages of the sacred Testaments may be read. For everywhere now the holy Gospel resounds, everywhere the words of the apostles, everywhere the law and the prophets. Therefore the voice of the wheels follows after the voice of the wings, because after the miracles of the saints, the words of sacred Scripture are freely and openly heard within the holy Church. […]

3:14.t: The spirit also lifted me and took me up, and I went away bitter in the indignation of my spirit. (LXX: "And the spirit raised and received me, and I went away aloft in the rush of my spirit.") After he was raised by the spirit and taken up by it, then in indignation and in the bitterness of his own spirit he went away whither he was being borne, understanding the indignation of God and turning over in his mind what the vision signified; or else, aloft, he was borne by the very rush of his own spirit, desiring to go where the Lord commanded — but let us understand his spirit not as the Holy Spirit but as the spirit of a man, of which it is spoken in many places, and in Isaiah: By night my spirit rises to you, O God —. And the prophet is carried over, not, as some think, in spirit, but in the body itself, as we also read of Habakkuk according to Theodotion.

For the hand of the Lord was with me, strengthening me. And I came to the exile, to the heap of new grain, to those who dwell by the river Chebar; and I sat where they were sitting, and I remained seven days mourning in the midst of them. (LXX: "And the hand of the Lord came upon me strong. And I entered to the captivity aloft; and I went around those dwelling by the river Chebar who were there, and I sat there seven days dwelling in the midst of them.") Where we translated 'heap of new grain', Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion set down the Hebrew words themselves, 'thel abib', which the Seventy translated 'aloft, and I went around', believing it better to say something than to set down what would raise a question for the reader. But we have learned from the Hebrews that 'thel abib' signifies this: when new wheat or barley is gathered, and after famine and want, before it is threshed on the floor, it promises some hope of food; […]

But it should be known that the more hearers advance in charity and understanding, the greater grace of the Spirit is given to the holy preachers. Hence, when the prophet had first said: "The spirit took me up, and I heard behind me the voice of a great commotion," after the voice of the great commotion of wings and wheels, and again of a great commotion, he immediately adds: "The spirit also lifted me up and took me."

Why does he who had said he was already taken up by the spirit narrate that he was again elevated and taken up? But the mind of preachers advances to higher things when through them the senses of their hearers are moved to desire for almighty God. These holy preachers advance for this reason: that through their ministry the gifts of grace may be multiplied in holy Church, as it is written of this same holy Church: "Making its channels drunk, multiply its generations; in its drops it shall rejoice when it springs forth." […]

But we must ask, since the spirit does not elevate the mind unless it has taken hold of it, why did it first elevate and afterward is said to have taken hold? But in this place "taken hold" means "held firmly." For there are some whom it elevates but does not take hold of, whose understanding indeed flashes forth to spiritual things, yet whose life, remaining in carnal deeds, does not accord with their understanding. For Balaam was elevated by the spirit of prophecy, but was not taken hold of, because he was able to foresee truly things far in the future, and yet was unwilling to separate his mind from earthly desires. But because the holy prophet was elevated in knowledge and likewise taken hold of in his life, let us now hear in what manner he proceeds to preach: "And I went away bitter in the indignation of my spirit."

Ponder, dearest brothers, for whom the gifts of the Holy Spirit had increased, why he departed embittered? […]

So Ahab, that wicked king, when rebuked by the prophet and hearing the divine sentence against himself, was terrified and weighed down with great grief, so that the Lord said to his prophet: "Have you not seen how Ahab has humbled himself before me? Because therefore he has humbled himself for my sake, I will not bring evil in his days." In these words of the Lord we must consider how pleasing to him is the grief of bitterness in his elect who fear to lose the Lord, if repentance so pleased him even in a reprobate who feared to lose the present world? Or how pleasing to him is voluntary affliction for sins in those who please him, if this pleased him even temporarily in one who displeased him? But we must know that no one can do these things from the whole heart out of love for the almighty Lord except one whose soul the Holy Spirit has taken hold of. […]

"For the hand of the Lord was with me, strengthening me."

We cannot perfectly rise to good things unless the Spirit both lifts us up by going before and strengthens us by following after. But we must ask, since it was written above concerning the scroll that he had received: "And it became in my mouth sweet like honey," for what reason is it said afterwards: "I went away bitter in the indignation of my spirit"? For it is indeed very strange if sweetness and bitterness should come together. But according to the sense given above, we must understand that when the word of God has begun to be sweet in the mouth of someone's heart, without doubt his soul becomes bitter against himself. For the more subtly he learns in it how he ought to reproach himself, the more harshly he chastises himself through the bitterness of repentance, since he displeases himself all the more, the more he sees in the sacred volume about almighty God that he should love. […]

3:15.t: Among the other miracles of prophecy, the books of the prophets also have this wonder: that just as in them things are explained by words, so sometimes words are explained by things, so that not only their sayings but also their deeds are prophecy. Hence it is now said: "I came to the captivity, to the heap of new fruits, to those who dwelt by the river Chobar." When the occasion required that he should have indicated that he was coming to the captivity, what necessity of speaking was there to express the place also through fruits, saying "to the heap of new fruits," unless it is that often causes are signified through things and places? For many years of captivity had already passed while Ezekiel was prophesying, and of those who had been led into captivity, many had already died in the death of the flesh, to whose children the prophet was coming to speak. Hence it is also said to him above: "Son of man, I am sending you to the children of Israel, to apostate nations who have departed from me. […]

3:16.t: And when the seven days had passed, the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, I have given you as a watchman to the house of Israel, and you shall hear the word from my mouth, and you shall announce it to them from me. He who is to be a watchman and is to tell the words of God to the people ought to be still for a long time, and to grieve at the things he sees, and to have in his conscience nothing of those things which he is going to rebuke in others.

In that he sat mourning for seven days, and after the seventh day received the words of the Lord's command that he ought to speak, he clearly indicates that during those same days he had been silent while mourning. Now he had been sent to preach, and yet sitting for seven days he was silent. What is it that the holy prophet suggests to us in this silence of his, except that he truly knows how to speak who has first learned how to be silent well? For the discipline of silence is, as it were, a kind of nourishment for speech. And rightly does he receive the gift of speaking through increasing grace, who first keeps silent in an orderly manner through humility. Hence it is said through Solomon: "A time to be silent, and a time to speak." For he did not say, "A time to speak, and a time to be silent," but he puts the time for silence first, and afterwards adds that for speaking, because we ought to learn to speak not by speaking but by being silent. […]

3:17.t: Therefore we are most anxious that you be persuaded not to be misled by such persons, since we know that every one who can speak the truth, and yet speaks it not, shall be judged by God, as God testified by Ezekiel, when He said, "I have made thee a watchman to the house of Judah. If the sinner sin, and thou warn him not, he himself shall die in his sin; but his blood will I require at thine hand. But if thou warn him, thou shalt be innocent." And on this account we are, through fear, very earnest in desiring to converse [with men] according to the Scriptures, but not from love of money, or of glory, or of pleasure.

Be ye not afraid, O penitents, lest the hope which is written in the Scriptures be cut off; for it is fitting for the Spirit of God thus to warn, for a fearful warning is set in Ezekiel the prophet when He said to him: "If all his days a man shall do judgment and righteousness, and at the end of his days he shall do iniquity, in his iniquity he shall die. And if a man shall do iniquity all his days, and he shall repent and do judgment and righteousness, his soul shall live" (Ezek. 33: 18-19). By this one word He has warned the righteous that he should not sin and lose his course; and He gave hope to the wicked that he should turn from his iniquity and live. Again He said to Ezekiel: "Although I cut off the hope of the unrighteous, thou shalt surely warn him; also when I encourage the righteous, set thou fear before him that he may be warned" (abridged thought of Ezek. 33: 7-9). When I say to the sinner: "Thou shalt surely die; […]

It should be noted that He whom the Lord sends to preach, He declares to be a watchman. For he to whom the care of others is committed is called a watchman, so that he may sit in the height of the mind and draw the meaning of his name from the power of his action. For he is not a watchman who is in the lowest place. Indeed, a watchman always stands in a high place, so that he may see from afar whatever is to come. And whoever is appointed as a watchman of the people ought to stand on high through his life, so that he may be able to benefit them through his foresight. Hence another prophet admonishes the watchman, saying: "Get up onto a high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Zion." So that evidently he who has undertaken the office of preaching may ascend to the height of good action; may pass over to lofty things and transcend the works of those who have been committed to him; […]

3:18.t: If, when I say to the wicked: You shall die the death, you do not announce it to him nor speak so that he may turn from his wicked way and live, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity, but his blood I will require from your hand. But if you announce it to the wicked, and he is not converted from his iniquity and from his wicked way, he indeed shall die in his iniquity, but you shall deliver your soul. There are two 'wicked', or 'unjust' as the Seventy translated: one who hears nothing from the watchman and dies in his wickedness, whose blood is sought from the watchman's hands; the other, to whom the watchman announces it, and who, scorning to hear, dies by his own fault, in such a way only that the watchman is free from blame. From this we understand that the Lord threatens the wicked and says: You shall die the death for this reason, that he may turn from his wicked way and live; for the threat is not against men but against sins, nor against those who turn from their vices but against those who remain in sin. […]

In these words, what should we note, what should we carefully consider, except that the subject does not die because of the fault of the superior, nor is the superior without fault when, not hearing the words of life, the subject dies by his own fault? For death is owed to the impious, but the way of life must be announced to him by the watchman, and his impiety must be rebuked. But if the watchman is silent, the impious man himself will die in his iniquity, because it was the merit of his impiety that he was not worthy for the watchman's word to reach him. But the Lord requires his blood from the hand of the watchman, because he himself killed him, because by remaining silent he betrayed him to death. In both of these cases, we must weigh how closely connected are the sins of subjects and superiors, because where the subject dies by his own fault, there the one who is in charge, because he was silent, is held guilty of death. […]

3:19.t: For even though the soil which we cultivate bring forth no fruit, if we have shown all industry, the Lord of it and of us will not suffer us to depart with disappointed hopes, but will give us a recompense; for, says St. Paul, "Every man shall receive his own reward according to his own labor," not according to the event of things. And that it is so, hearken: "And Thou," he saith, "Son of man, testify unto this people, if they will hear, and if they will understand." And Ezekiel says, "If the watchman give warning what it behooves to flee from, and what to choose, he hath delivered his own soul, although there be none that will take heed."
3:19.s: Homily on the Gospel of John 13

3:19.t:
For then your subject dies without you, when in the cause of death he has endured you as one who does not speak against it. For you are joined to the death which you do not oppose. And it should be noted what things ought to be preached by the watchman, namely faith and works. For he says: "But if you have announced to the wicked man, and he has not been converted from his wickedness and from his wicked way." For wickedness pertains to unbelief, but the wicked way pertains to depraved action. And every watchman ought to have this zeal: that he first draw people to the piety of faith, and afterward to the pious way, that is, to good action.

But since the discussion has turned to exhortation, we ought briefly to make known how great should be the order and consideration of speech in the mouth of a pastor. For a teacher ought to weigh what he speaks, to whom he speaks, when he speaks, how he speaks, and how much he speaks. For if one of these is lacking, the speech will not be fitting. […]

3:20.t: Let him who is entrusted with the care of all behave as one who must give account for each individual; knowing that if one of the brethren fall into sin without his having declared to him beforehand the ordinance of God, or if having fallen into sin he abides therein, without having been taught the method of reformation, his blood will be required of the Superior’s hands, as Scripture says. And especially if he has knowingly neglected what pleases God and has weakened the discipline of the community by bearing with the evil ways of individuals in order to win their favour.

But also if the righteous, turning from his righteousness, does iniquity, I will set a stumbling block before him. He shall die because you did not announce it to him: in his sin he shall die, and his righteous deeds which he did shall not be in remembrance; but his blood I will require from your hand. But if you announce it to the righteous man that the righteous man should not sin, and he does not sin, living he shall live because you announced it to him, and you have delivered your soul. Just as we read of two wicked or unjust men: one who did not hear and perished, and the other who heard and persevered in evil, so there are two righteous: one who did not hear and perished, the other who heard and was converted to repentance and saved his soul. And it is to be noted that the righteous can fall and, if he has a teacher toward better things, may draw back his foot; and the wicked or unjust man indeed, if he is not converted, will die in his wickedness and iniquity. […]

Because the preacher remained silent toward the just man who fell into sin, he is held guilty of his blood. And he who did not strive to be diligent in preaching has become a participant in damnation. But when it is said: "He will die in his sin, and his acts of justice which he performed will not be remembered," we must especially consider this: that when we commit evil deeds, we recall our past good deeds to memory in vain, since in the perpetration of evil there should be no confidence in past good deeds. But it can be asked whether preaching should be done to the just man after he has fallen, or also before he falls? The preacher must be vigilant lest he come to a fall—without doubt, even before he falls.

But in all these things which have been said about the just man turned to iniquity, this is difficult to speak of, this is greatly to be feared: that the Lord says, "I will place a stumbling block before him." […]

And by Ezekiel He says: When the wicked turns from his way unto the Lord and do that which is lawful and right, the sins he has committed will not be remembered but he shall live, sayeth the Lord. Thus it is also with the righteous; when he turneth from his righteousness and comitteth sin and iniquity, the righteousness he has done will not be remembered but I will lay a stumbling block before him and by the iniquity he has done he shall die if he remains steadfast in it. Why is this? Because the iniquitous will not stumble on account of his iniquity after he turns unto the Lord. But the righteousness of the righteous will not save him when he sins, if he builds his building on that foundation.

3:21.t:
If, therefore, the preacher freed his soul because he warned the just man not to sin, when the just man has fallen into sin while the preacher remained silent, the preacher is held guilty because he was silent. But who among us, I ask, is sufficient for these things, not only to zealously rebuke sinners, but also to watch over the just lest they fall? For we, conscious of our own weakness, when we behold just men, do not presume to admonish them to hold to the way of justice, which we see they already hold; and yet it is the duty of a preacher to admonish even the just. Hence the distinguished preacher said: I am a debtor both to the wise and to the unwise.

But meanwhile, while I speak, I want to turn my eyes away from myself, and behold, again the divine word drives me back upon myself, that I may see my own negligence and fear that these things I hear are spoken to me. For as I said above, whose heart, scattered among innumerable cares, can gather itself back to itself? […]

3:22.t: And the hand of the Lord was there upon me, and he said to me: Arise, go out into the plain, and there I will speak with you. What we translated from the Hebrew as 'there', which is not found in the Seventy, is set down with significance, and there is no doubt that it signifies the place; for above we read: And I came to the exile, to the heap of new grain, to those who dwell by the river Chebar. And rightly he who had said: I sat, is commanded to rise; and he who had entered to the exile hears: Go out, not into rugged valleys, not onto sheer crags, but into the breadth of the plain, which can contain the glory of the Lord — whence it is also said to the Corinthians: Be enlarged —. When he goes in to the captives, of whom it was said that they rage and persecute him, he needs a strong hand so that he can resist and endure the fury of his persecutors; […]

With the truth of history preserved, the divine utterances sometimes designate causes from time, sometimes from place, which they do not indicate by open speech. From time indeed, as when the Lord was preaching to the Jews it is said through the evangelist: "It was winter." For among those mysteries which the Truth was speaking, what was the reason for adding the name of winter, unless to show through the quality of the time the coldness of heart? Because even when they were receiving the words of truth, the hearts of the Jews remained cold. Sometimes indeed from place, as when to the carnal Israelite people, with Moses descending from the mountain, the law was given in the plains; […]

3:23.t: And I arose and went out into the plain, and behold, there the glory of the Lord was standing, like the glory which I had seen by the river Chebar. At the Lord's command he goes in and at his command he goes out, and he sat with those who were sitting, because the number of the captives could not hear him while he stood. And having gone out into the breadth of the plain, he saw the glory of the Lord standing, which before he had seen walking, and lifting itself up, and at times standing — for it was by the river of the world, 'Chobar' [Chebar], which means 'most heavy', that the glory was seen, which signifies that all the glory of this world flows past and has no stable footing; but the glory of the Lord, standing and abiding, is seen in the plain with the prophet standing, the glory which in the midst of the captives could neither stand nor be seen —.

And I fell on my face. And the spirit entered into me and set me upon my feet, and spoke, and said to me: Go in and be shut up in the midst of your house. Not able to bear the standing glory of the Lord, he fell on his face, so that he might be raised up by the spirit entering into him. This spirit set him upon his feet and spoke, saying: Enter and be shut up in the midst of your house; and the sense is: 'Because you have been strengthened by the sight of the Lord's majesty, fear no one and dread no one, but return into your house — either for the needs of the body, as some think, or as a sign of the siege to come — and, just as Isaiah, barefoot and naked, announced the three years' captivity and nakedness of the people, so you too, shut up in your house, prophesy by the very deed the impending siege of the city of Jerusalem'.

"And rising I went out into the plain, and behold, there the glory of the Lord stood, like the glory which I saw beside the river Chebar."

The prophet saw in the plain the glory of the Lord, which he had seen beside the river Chebar in the midst of the Israelites, because that same majesty appeared to the Gentiles which had first revealed itself to the elect among the Jewish people through the revealing Spirit.

"And I fell upon my face."

Having seen the glory of the Lord, the prophet falls on his face, because although a man may be elevated to understand sublime things, nevertheless from the contemplation of God's majesty he understands the weakness of his own condition; and he who sees himself to be ashes and dust before God's eyes has, as it were, no standing.

3:24.t:
"And the spirit entered into me and set me upon my feet."

When we humble ourselves before God, when we recognize that we are dust and ashes, when, weighing the weakness of our own condition, we do not maintain a state of rigidity and pride, almighty God lifts us up through His Spirit and sets us upon our feet, so that we who have lain and lie humbly within ourselves from the thought of our weakness may stand upright, as it were upon our feet, in good works afterward. Why is this done to the prophet in a plain, unless to specially designate that the Holy Spirit was also to be given to the elect of the Gentiles, who would first cast down from their state of pride those whom He would take up, and afterward establish them upon their feet, that is, upon good works? As it is said through Paul: "Lift up the hands which hang down, and the feeble knees, and make straight paths for your feet."

"And He spoke to me and said to me: Enter and shut yourself in the midst of your house." […]

3:25.t: And you, son of man, behold, bonds have been put upon you, and they shall bind you with them, and you shall not go out from their midst; and I will make your tongue cleave to your palate (or throat), and you shall be dumb and not as a man who rebukes, because it is a provoking house. That he is shut up in his house, that he is tied in bonds, that he does not go out to those among whom he dwells, but amid a multitude of captives suffers the solitude of a prison, is, as I said above, a sign of the siege, which, when Jerusalem is shut up and surrounded by the army of the Chaldeans, permits none of the inhabitants to go out; this is the pot of which Jeremiah speaks, and this prophet himself in what follows, in which the flesh of the people is consumed.

"And you, son of man, behold, chains have been placed upon you, and they shall bind you with them, and you shall not go out into their midst."

If we follow these words through the order of typological exposition, the prophet receives bonds in his house and is bound, because in the last days, when Judea shall have believed, she will experience the most grievous persecutions in the time of Antichrist, so that the ministers of iniquity will not receive his preaching, but by resisting will press it down with the bonds of sorrows. And he does not go out into their midst, because preaching does not reach the hearts of the wicked, while the tongue of the good, bound by tribulations, is silent. For there will be at that time many of the unbelieving Jews who will persecute those very ones from among the Jews who shall have believed. […]

3:26.t: But as for the prophet's tongue cleaving to his palate or throat, and his being made dumb and not having the authority of one who rebukes, the cause is plain: Because it is, he says, a provoking house; and the sense is: So great are their bitternesses and so great their contentions against God that they do not deserve to hear one who rebukes them. From this it is plain that, where there is a multitude of sins, the sinners are unworthy to be corrected by the Lord.

"And I will make your tongue cleave to the roof of your mouth, and you shall be mute, not like a man who rebukes, because it is a rebellious house."

Therefore, the knowledge of the preachers is then compelled to be silent to the reprobate. Hence it is also added here: "And I will make your tongue cleave to the roof of your mouth, and you shall be mute, and not as a man who rebukes, because it is a provoking house." But because, when Enoch and Elijah preach, many of those who then remain from the Jews in unbelief return to the knowledge of truth, just as it is said of the same Elijah: "Elijah will come, and he will restore all things," who are both called through Zechariah two olive trees, and through John two candlesticks, rightly here also it is added: "But when I shall have spoken to you, I will open your mouth, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God." […]

And again, because of the fault of those subject to them, the voice of preachers is forbidden, as the Lord says to Ezekiel: "I will make your tongue cleave to your palate, and you shall be mute, and not as a man who rebukes, because it is a provoking house." As if he were to say openly: Therefore the word of preaching is taken from you, because while the people provoke me in their actions, they are not worthy to receive the exhortation of truth. From whose fault, therefore, the word is withdrawn from the preacher is not easily known. But it is known most certainly that the silence of the Pastor sometimes harms himself, but always harms those subject to him.

3:27.t: But when I have spoken to you, I will open your mouth, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: He who hears, let him hear, and he who refrains, let him refrain, because it is a provoking house. What we read in Ecclesiastes: A time to keep silent and a time to speak, is borne out in the prophetic word as well: that it belongs to the same wisdom both to keep silent and to speak according to the time, and to give fellow servants their rations in due season; whence Isaiah too says to the unbelieving people: 'I have kept silent; shall I keep silent forever? says the Lord'. He, therefore, who on account of the multitude of sins long kept his mouth shut, because he saw that some could be converted, of whom it is said: He who hears, let him hear, and he who from evil refrains, let him refrain and cease, for this reason, with his mouth opened, and not by his own will but by the Lord's command, speaks to the people. […]

"But when I shall have spoken to you, I will open your mouth, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: He who hears, let him hear; and he who is silent, let him be silent, for it is a provoking house."

Then, as it were at the end, the mouth of the prophet is opened, when through the preaching of Enoch and Elijah, as the Jews return to the faith, the prophecy of sacred scripture is recognized to have been about Christ. But since we have spoken these things typologically, let us now discuss the same words to your charity in a moral sense.

Whence it is added here: But when I shall have spoken to you, you shall open your mouth, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God.

Often some desire to hear the word of God, but when they observe others turning away their ear, they themselves also deviate from hearing salvation; […]

4:1.t: And you, son of man, take for yourself a brick, and you shall set it before you, and you shall portray on it the city of Jerusalem. And you shall set in order a siege against it, and you shall build siege-works and heap up a mound, and you shall set camps against it and place battering rams round about. Just as we said before — Go in and be shut up in the midst of your house, and: Behold, bonds have been put upon you, and they will bind you, and you will not go out — that the prophet is a type of the coming siege of the city of Jerusalem, so now he is commanded to portray it on a brick by the geometric art, and the brick itself is to be placed in the prophet's sight, so that, after he has portrayed Jerusalem in the dust, he may draw the whole siege against it, sketching the siege-works and the heaped-up mounds and the ring of the besieging army and the battering rams round about, all the things by which cities are usually taken. […]

"And you, son of man, take a brick for yourself, and place it before you, and draw upon it the city of Jerusalem."

In these words, indeed, what else is designated according to history but the siege and destruction of the city of Jerusalem, and what else is expressed but the affliction of a sinful people? It is called a provoking house.

From this we are instructed that when we know one thing is fulfilled according to history, and we recognize another thing according to history to be empty of reason, we should hold to both in the sacred word, so that we may believe the siege of Jerusalem, which was later accomplished according to the letter, to be prefigured in the words and deeds of the prophet, and yet through that same siege another siege, that is, an interior one, may be designated.

But first we must inquire why the prophet Ezekiel, whenever he beholds sublime things or whenever he is commanded to perform something mystical, is first called "son of man." […]

4:2.t:
"And you shall set the siege against it, and you shall build fortifications, and you shall heap up a mound, and you shall set camps against it, and place battering rams around it."

Therefore the teacher must vigilantly make known to the progressing soul what temptations follow it, so that it may be able to prepare itself cautiously against the snares of the malignant spirit. Hence it is well that now, after the city of Jerusalem has been described on the brick, it is said to the prophet: "And you shall set the siege against it, and you shall build fortifications, and you shall heap up a mound." For when the vision of peace is already being described, it is necessary that the wars of temptations be announced to it. For in order that it may be able to reach those eternal joys of peace, it must without doubt endure here many struggles of tribulations. Of which it is well said: "You shall set the siege against it." […]

4:3.t: And you, take for yourself an iron pan, and you shall set it as an iron wall between you and the city, and you shall set your face firmly toward it, and it shall be in siege, and you shall surround it: it is a sign to the house of Israel. What we said above, that both the prophet himself and the portrayal on the brick — surrounded by siege-works, mound and battering rams — go before as a sign of Jerusalem's coming siege, is now said more clearly, after many things in between: It is a sign to the house of Israel. The iron pan, which is set like a wall between the prophet and the city, shows the great wrath of God, which is worn down by no prayers and is not bent to mercy: for just as iron subdues all metals and nothing is harder than it, so the incredible crimes of Jerusalem by their own fault made God, who is gentle by nature, most hard. The pan is also said to be a wall set in the middle between the people and God, to show that the whole multitude is shortly to be fried and reduced to nothing. […]

"And take to yourself an iron frying pan, and you shall place it as an iron wall between yourself and the city, and you shall set your face firmly against it, and it shall be under siege, and you shall surround it. It is a sign for the house of Israel."

Because iron is a strong metal, and food is fried in a frying pan, what is signified by the iron frying pan except the strong frying of spiritual zeal? For all spiritual zeal fries the soul of a teacher, because he is greatly tormented when he sees any weak persons abandoning eternal things and taking delight in temporal things. How well Paul had taken up the iron frying pan, when, tormented by zeal for souls, he said: "Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burned?" His own heart, which he had set on fire with zeal for souls—what else had he made it but a frying pan, in which he burned with love of virtues against vices? For the fact that he was burned was the frying pan. […]

4:4.t: And you shall sleep on your left side, and you shall place the iniquities of the house of Israel upon it by the number of the days in which you sleep upon it, and you shall take up their iniquity. But I have given you the years of their iniquity by the number of days, three hundred and ninety days, and you shall bear the iniquity of the house of Israel. And when you have completed these, you shall sleep on your right side a second time, and you shall take up the iniquity of the house of Judah for forty days; a day for a year, a day, I say, for a year I have given you. We ask what the three hundred and ninety years are, which are reckoned in place of as many days, during which the prophet slept on his left side, bound and constrained so that he would not move onto his other side, showing the captivity and miseries of the ten tribes, that is, of Israel; and what the other forty years are, during which he lay on his right side for Judah and its iniquities, or, as Holy Scripture relates, slept.

— Just as, therefore, in Israel, that is, in the ten tribes, from Pekah king of Israel, under whom Shalmaneser laid waste much of the Israelite people, to the fortieth year of Ahasuerus, when the persecution of the whole Jewish people was eased, we reckon three hundred and ninety years, so from the first year of Jeconiah, when a great part of Jerusalem was carried over to Babylon, to the first year of Cyrus king of the Persians, which was the thirtieth year of the temple's desolation, forty years are reckoned; under him the captivity of the Jews was relaxed and liberty given back to the people. — Some, joining the three hundred and ninety years of Israel and the forty of Judah, make four hundred and thirty years, and hold that they are fulfilled from the baptism of the Savior to the consummation of the world. […]

But if some contentious interpreter will not accept what we have said, but understands that the harlot named Gomer, daughter of Diblaim, bore the first and the third as males and the second, the middle one, as a female, wanting the Scripture to mean just what is read, let him answer how he explains that passage in Ezekiel where he is commanded by the Lord to bear the iniquities of the house of Israel, that is, of the ten tribes, and for three hundred and ninety days to sleep continually on one side, the left, although in the LXX one hundred and ninety are written, and to sleep so that he never wakes nor changes his side, unless perhaps, sated with sleep, he opened his eyes a little to take the most filthy food of ash-baked bread, made of wheat and barley, and bean and lentil and millet, and baked on human dung. For the nature of things does not allow that any man should sleep always on one side for three hundred and ninety days. […]

4:5.t: — Concerning Israel this must be said: that under King Pekah son of Remaliah, who reigned in Israel twenty years, Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came, and took Ijon, and Abel house of Maacah, and Janoah, and Kedesh, Hazor, and Gilead, the whole land of Naphtali; and he carried them over to the Assyrians. After him Hoshea son of Elah reigned in Israel nine years, and he was taken with all Samaria by Shalmaneser king of the Assyrians, and carried over to Halah and Habor, the rivers of Gozan, in the cities of the Medes. Now Hoshea was taken in the sixth year of King Hezekiah, as the holy history of Kings relates; and from him, if we reckon in order, we shall be able to find in this way for how many years Israel was in distress and pressed by the yoke of captivity. From the sixth year to the twenty-ninth year — for that many years Hezekiah reigned — twenty-four years are reckoned. Manasseh succeeded him and reigned fifty-five years. After him Amon reigned two years. After him Josiah, thirty-two years. […]

— And I greatly wonder why the common copies have 'one hundred and ninety years', and in some it is written 'one hundred and fifty', when plainly both the Hebrews and Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion hold 'three hundred and ninety years', and among the Seventy themselves — and yet they have not been corrupted by the fault of copyists — the same number is found. A most difficult question, and, not to speak proudly, one explained by no one, we believe we have expounded not so much by our own knowledge as by the grace of the Lord, that being fulfilled which he himself promised: Seek and you will find, ask and you will receive, knock and it will be opened to you. […]

4:6.t: — The sleeping on the right side, that is, of the forty years, is easily reckoned. For after Eliakim, who was surnamed Jehoiakim, his son Jehoiachin, surnamed Jeconiah, reigned three months. While he was reigning, the servants of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon went up to Jerusalem, and the city was surrounded with siege-works. And Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to the city, while his servants were attacking it. And Jehoiachin king of Judah went out to the king of Babylon, he and his mother and his servants and his prince and his eunuchs, and the king of Babylon received him in the eighth year of his reign. And he carried out from there all the treasures of the house of the Lord and the treasures of the royal house. And shortly after: And he carried over all Jerusalem and all the princes and all the mighty men of the army, ten thousand, into captivity, and every craftsman and smith; and nothing was left, except the poor of the people of the land. […]

4:7.t: And toward the siege of Jerusalem you shall turn your face, and your arm shall be bared, and you shall prophesy against it. (LXX: "And in the shutting-in of Jerusalem you shall prepare your face, and you shall strengthen your arm, and you shall prophesy upon it.") There is need of a preparing of the face, and of the strength and firmness of an arm bared and stripped, so that the siege of the city may be shown not only by the voice but also by the gesture and bearing of the one prophesying.

4:8.t: Behold, I have surrounded you with bonds, and you shall not turn from your side to the other side, until you complete the days of your siege (or shutting-in). The left parts, because they had been without the temple and the knowledge of God in Samaria, are assigned to Israel; the right, to Judah, in which were the worship and religion of God; and it must be noted that on the one is the punishment of sinners, on the other the exercise of virtue. Nor does he turn from one side to the other, so that no respite from torments is indicated, until the complete conclusion of the aforesaid days is fulfilled. What a day is for the prophet, a year is for those who suffer; and the years Laban counted were to Jacob as a few days. Not only is there variety in punishments according to the difference of merits, but in the recompense of the good as well the lambs stand on the right and the goats on the left; hence also in another place it is written: The heart of the wise is in his right hand, but the heart of the fool in his left. […]

4:9.t: And you, take for yourself wheat and barley and beans and lentils and millet and vetch, and you shall put them in one vessel, and you shall make yourself loaves by the number of the days in which you sleep on your side: for three hundred and ninety days you shall eat it. And your food, which you eat, shall be by weight twenty staters a day; from time to time you shall eat it. And you shall drink water by measure, the sixth part of a 'hin'; from time to time you shall drink it. And you shall eat it like a cake baked under the ashes, and you shall cover it with human dung before their eyes. For what we have translated 'vetch', for which in the Hebrew is said 'chasamim', the Seventy and Theodotion put ὄλυραν, which some think is 'oats' and others 'rye'; but the first edition of Aquila and Symmachus translated 'zeas' or 'zeias', which we call either 'far' [emmer] or, in the native speech of Italy and Pannonia, 'spica' [ear of grain] and 'spelta' [spelt]; to 'in a vessel' the Seventy also added 'of earthenware'.

It must also be noted that, according to the number of the days of the left side, three hundred and ninety loaves baked under the ashes are ordered to be made and eaten one each day, while about loaves for the forty days of the right side there is complete silence, so that Holy Scripture may signify in a hidden way that the punishment is not the same for a sinning people, provided it still has the knowledge of God, and for one that has wholly departed from the religion of the true God. We can also say this, according to the spiritual understanding: that the Jewish people, since its offense against God, eats to this day loaves baked under the ashes, mixed of wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet and oats, of which the one is the food of men, the other of beasts of burden: for in that they seem to believe in one God, they have something of wheat too; […]

Now the prophet is commanded to show by deed the coming famine and want of the people of Israel: for just as in a scarcity of all things no one looks for varieties and delicacies of food, but for how the belly may be filled, so now the prophet puts wheat and barley, beans, lentils and millet and oats into one vessel, and makes three hundred and ninety loaves to eat one each day; and these loaves weigh twenty shekels each — that is, staters; and a shekel, that is, a stater, has four drachmas; and eight drachmas make a Latin ounce —, so that one loaf is said to weigh ten ounces, by which life is dragged out rather than sustained.

4:10.t: The scantiness of the food is increased by the scantiness of the water: for he is commanded to drink each day the sixth part of the Hebrew measure called 'hin' — now a 'hin' makes two Attic 'chois' [choes, an Attic liquid measure], which we can call two Italian 'sextarii', so that the 'hin' is the measure of the Jewish sextarius and of our military one, whose sixth part makes a third of an Italian sextarius —; and this food and drink, in the words of the renowned orator, gives no strength, but keeps off death. As for his saying: From time to time you shall eat (or drink) it, it means from evening to evening, although some wrongly think it is to be understood from year to year.

And the prophet Ezekiel also, when he was about to receive the revelation of the prophecy of the uprooting of the city and the overthrowing of the temple, did the word of God bring into severe tribulations to eat bread by weight, and to drink water by measure, and to sleep upon his side in affliction, and then he arrived at the vision of prophecy. And thus also thou canst shew that all the righteous men and Prophets, either by their own will, or by God's command unto them, endured always tribulations and labours.

4:12.t: And the loaves themselves are made like a barley loaf baked under the ashes; and he is told to cover them with human dung, not with those who are to eat them unaware — for in such a situation ignorance usually tempers miseries — but with them seeing, and before their eyes, so that one may endure the horror of the sight before the nausea of the taste.

And that it is written, according to the Seventy, that Elijah, fleeing Jezebel, found a ὀλυρίτην [made of olyra] loaf, 'baked under the ashes', is a sign of persecution and want; hence he is also fed by ravens, and, because he had found no food in Israel, he was fed with the nourishment of the nations, which were unclean. The Law itself too, which they read and do not understand, is a loaf baked under the ashes, and it is covered with human dung; for which reason Paul the Apostle too says that he counted the gains of the Law and the observance of the former ceremonies as dung, that he might gain Christ.

4:13.t: And the Lord said: Thus shall the sons of Israel eat their bread polluted among the nations to which I will cast them out. And I said: Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, behold, my soul is not polluted, and what died of itself and what was torn by beasts I have not eaten from my infancy until now, and no unclean flesh has entered my mouth. And he said to me: Behold, I have given you the dung of oxen instead of human excrement, and you shall make your bread in it. That the prophets, according to Zechariah, are men of portent, who portend things to come by their deeds, and of whom God says: In the hands of the prophets I have been likened, we read very often in many places. Just as, therefore, Ezekiel eats bread in dung, so the sons of Israel too, or the whole people of the Jews, or, as others think, the ten tribes, will eat polluted bread among the nations; although the threat is not addressed to those who have already been cast out, but to those who were still to be cast out of the land of promise.

4:14.t: I have recalled that the prophet Ezekiel too says something similar, when the Lord had commanded him to cook loaves for himself "in human dung". For he answered the Lord and said: "O Lord, never has my soul been defiled, and carrion or anything unclean has not entered into my mouth. But neither has yesterday's flesh entered into my mouth". Concerning which I often used to inquire within myself, what this exultation of the prophet might be, by which he brought forth before God as something great and said: "I have never eaten yesterday's flesh". But, as I see, taught from this and imbued with these mysteries, the prophet spoke thus to the Lord: I am not so cast down and degenerate a priest as to "feed on yesterday's", that is, on old "flesh". Hear these things, all you priests of the Lord, and understand more attentively what is said. The flesh which from the sacrifices is assigned to the priests is "the word of God" which they teach in the Church. […]

When the prophet had learned this, according to Aquila he expressed his abhorrence three times: 'Ah, ah, ah', but according to Symmachus and the Seventy he answered: Μηδαμῶς, which in Latin is said 'By no means', for which Theodotion translated: 'O Lord God'; lest we should think that he is contradicting the Lord's command, rather than giving reasons, or rather pleading, why he cannot do this; and in the end he obtains what he asked, and the severity of the sentence was tempered by a milder command. It is asked why Ezekiel refused easier things, while Hosea was at once joined to a harlot and did not object, or rather reply, that he had a chaste body and ought not to be stained by union with a prostitute, as the Apostle says: He who cleaves to a prostitute becomes one body with her; from this it is shown that it was a figure of the Synagogue or of the Church, not truly carried out according to the letter, as we discussed more fully when expounding that prophet himself. […]

4:15.t: And that the dung of oxen is granted in place of human dung signifies lighter evils, since he is indeed commanded to eat bread baked in ox dung, but to be far from the uncleanness of human dung; and to this day this sentence is kept among the people of the Jews: they do not eat their bread in human dung — for they neither serve idols nor worship the various monstrous forms of demons — but in ox dung, since they do everything for the sake of the flesh and the belly and the good things of this earth, according to what is said: He who does them shall live in them. But we who despise earthly things not only trample on the foods of human dung and count earthly delights as nothing, but eat the bread which came down from heaven and enjoy that food of which the psalmist sings: Man ate the bread of angels, living not at all on Egyptian meats but on the fineness of manna.

4:16.t: And he said to me: Son of man, behold, I will break the staff of bread in Jerusalem, and they shall eat bread by weight and in anxiety, and they shall drink water by measure and in distress, so that, bread and water failing, each one may collapse upon his brother, and they may waste away in their iniquities. The Hebrew word 'mate' the first edition of Aquila translated 'staff', while the second, and Symmachus and Theodotion, translated στήριγμα, that is, 'support'.

It is written in Jeremiah that the little ones, that is, the common people of the Church, asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them; but Paul, who was a man and knew that Christ had broken the loaves of the Law and given them to the disciples to be distributed, speaks confidently. And those who need the milk of infancy and are not able to take solid food cannot eat the staff or strength of bread; and nothing so strengthens the mind of the one who eats as the bread of life, of which it is written: And bread strengthens the heart of man.

What he had shown by deed was to come, he also declares by word; and the whole sleeping on the left and the right side, and the bread baked under the ashes and mixed from a variety of six kinds, signifying the evils of the world, tends to this: to proclaim the want of food in Jerusalem and an incredible scarcity of water, so that each one collapses upon his brother, hoping from another for the help that he does not see to be in himself — for it is the nature of men that, when evils press and the weight of distress, they put their confidence in their neighbor rather than in themselves —, and they waste away in their iniquities, while they suffer all things for their iniquities. And I fear that this breaking of bread may be found in our Jerusalem too, in which the vision of peace is discerned: bread which the Lord breaks when he is angry and judges us unworthy of his bread; […]

5:1.t: Moreover, just as in the hair of the head and the beard there is a token of beauty and manhood, and if they are shaved off a shameful nakedness appears, and the outermost and, so to speak, dead part of the whole body is in the hair of the head and the hairs of the beard, so Jerusalem and its people, dead and separated from the living body of God, is handed over to famine and pestilence, to slaughter and the sword, to captivity and dispersion. From this dispersion, under the figure of the hairs, some part is bound in the height of the cloak, so that a small amount is again handed over to burning, from which an infinite flame and the whole devastation of punishment goes forth into all the house of Israel.

5:2.t: And you, son of man, take for yourself a sharp sword like a barbers' razor (or shaving the hairs), and draw it across your head and your beard, and you shall take for yourself a balance of weight and divide them. A third part you shall burn with fire in the midst of the city, according to the completion of the days of the enclosure; and a third part you shall cut down with the sword round about it; but the other third you shall scatter into the wind, and I will bare the sword after them. And you shall take from there a small number, and you shall bind them in the top of the cloak; and from them again you shall take, and cast them into the midst of the fire, and burn them; from it a fire shall go forth into all the house of Israel. […]

5:4.t: But as to his saying: From it (that is, from the people of the Jews, or according to the Seventy: From her, so that the city of Jerusalem is understood) a fire shall go forth into all the house of Israel, the history of the Maccabees relates it: that a certain part of the Jews gave themselves over to Antiochus Epiphanes and stirred him up to the persecution of the people, and many other things which are written in the same history and in the volumes of Josephus, and especially the dissension of Hyrcanus and Alexander, through the occasion of which Gnaeus Pompey took Jerusalem and subjected it to Roman dominion; and afterwards, under Titus and Vespasian, the city was taken and the temple overthrown, and, after fifty years, under Aelius Hadrian the city was burned down to the ground and destroyed, so that it lost even its former name.

5:5.t: Thus says the Lord God: This is Jerusalem; in the midst of the nations I have set her, and round about her lands; and she despised my judgments, so as to be more impious than the nations, and my precepts more than the lands which are round about her: for they have cast away my judgments, and in my precepts they have not walked. That Jerusalem is situated in the middle of the world this same prophet testifies, showing that she is the navel of the earth; and the psalmist, expressing the nativity of the Lord: Truth, he says, has sprung from the earth; and then, the passion: He has wrought, he says, salvation in the midst of the earth. For on the side of the east she is girded by the region which is called Asia; on the side of the west, by that which is called Europe; on the south and the south wind, by Libya and Africa; on the north, by the Scythians, Armenia and Persia and all the nations of Pontus.

She was set, therefore, in the midst of the nations so that, since God was known in Judea, and in Israel his name was great, all the nations round about might follow her examples; but she, following the impiety of the nations placed around her, surpassed even them in her wickedness. Symmachus translated this beautifully: This Jerusalem, which I set in the midst of the nations, and the regions around her, has exchanged my judgments for impieties which she learned from the nations, and my justifications from the regions which are round about her, because they have rejected my ordinances, and in my judgments they have not walked. But that what the Seventy said: My justifications unjustly from the nations, and my ordinances from the regions which are round about her, has no coherence is clear even if I keep silent.

5:7.t: Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because you have surpassed the nations that are round about you, you have not walked in my precepts, and have not done my judgments, and have not acted according to the judgments of the nations that are round about you, therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, and I myself will execute judgments in the midst of you in the eyes of the nations. And I will do in you what I have not done, and the like of which I will not do again, because of all your abominations. (In place of what we translated: Because you have surpassed the nations that are round about you, Symmachus translated: Because your multitude was from the nations that are round about you. Aquila's second edition: Because you have been numbered among the nations that are round about you; and further, LXX: "Because your occasion is from the nations that are round about you".) […]

'Why,' he says, 'should I complain that you have not walked in my precepts and have not done my judgments, when you have even surpassed all the nations round about in your wickedness, and have not done what they often did by the natural law written in their hearts? Therefore not through angels nor through any ministers, but I myself will execute judgments in you, with all looking on, such as I have not done in you before and will not do again'. And by saying 'judgments' he shows the truth of the sentence, lest his wrath should seem to exceed the measure of the punishments.

5:9.t: Nor did he do in any nation such things as he did in Jerusalem; and the mighty shall suffer torments mightily; and: The like, he says, I will not do again. He said well: I will not do the like, for after the killing of Christ he was going to do much harsher things: for it is one thing to have worshiped idols at times, for which they had been punished before, and another to have slaughtered the Son of God.

5:10.t: Therefore fathers shall eat sons in the midst of you, and sons shall eat their fathers, and I will execute judgments in you, and I will winnow all your remnants into every wind. To what he had said above: Because you have surpassed the nations that are round about you (or Because your occasion is from the nations that are round about you), you have not walked in my precepts, and have not done my judgments, he has referred 'therefore' three times. First thus: Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, and I myself will execute judgments in the midst of you; secondly: Therefore fathers shall eat sons in the midst of you; thirdly: Therefore, as I live, says the Lord God, unless because you have violated my holy place with all your offenses, and the rest. Yet it must be noted that where things are seemly and honorable, and in accordance with the merit of those who undergo them, God professes that he does them himself; […]

5:11.t: Therefore, as I live, says the Lord God, unless because you have violated my holy place with all your offenses and with all your abominations, I too will break (or according to the Seventy I will cast you off), and my eye shall not spare, and I will not have pity. This is said properly to Jerusalem: 'Because you have violated my holy things by deserting me, and have worshiped idols in my temple, I too will break all your idols and crush and cut them down, or I will cast you off because you first cast me off, and my eye will not spare when I see you submitting your neck to famine, the sword and slavery, nor will I have pity, because you do not deserve mercy', for it is written: Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy. […]

5:12.t: A third part of you shall die by pestilence and be consumed by famine in the midst of you, and a third part of you shall fall by the sword round about you, but the third part of you I will scatter into every wind, and I will unsheathe the sword after them. And I will fulfill my fury and make my indignation rest upon them, and I will be consoled; and they shall know that I the Lord have spoken in my zeal, when I have fulfilled my indignation upon them. (The Seventy, because above they had set down four parts, whereas the prophetic word proved that there are only three, in the ravaging by burning and by sword and by dispersion, so that superfluously the one part of burning was divided into two parts, in this place too divided that same first part into two, so as to say: A fourth part of you shall be worn away by death, and a fourth part of you shall be consumed by famine in the midst of you, and a fourth part of you shall fall round about you, and a fourth part of you I will scatter into every wind; […]

5:13.t: This only I will add, which is necessary, regarding what he says: And I will fulfill my fury and make my indignation rest upon them, and I will be consoled; and they shall know that I the Lord have spoken in my zeal, when I have fulfilled my indignation upon them: how the fury and indignation and zeal of God are to be understood, we have often explained, namely that God speaks with human affections, not that he himself is angry, but that we, through punishments and torments, may feel God to be angry. Zeal, moreover, is to be taken under the μετάφορᾳ [metaphor] of a husband and wife: a husband, as long as he loves his wife, is jealous; if he has neglected her, he says what we shall say in what follows: My zeal shall depart from you; and I will no longer be angry with you. […]

5:14.t: And I will give you into a desert, (and what follows:) and into a reproach to the nations which are round about you (is not found in the Seventy, in place of which they added of their own: and your daughters round about you; and again according to both editions:) in the sight of everyone passing by. Now it profits Jerusalem that all the vices in her should be made desolate and reduced to a desert, and that she should recognize her own sins, so that she who ought to have been an example of virtues to the other nations may be an example of miseries. Her daughters, moreover, we can understand as cities or villages, or as the churches scattered throughout the whole world, so that whoever is a pilgrim of this age, and says with the psalmist: I am a sojourner and a pilgrim, as all my fathers, and of whom it is said: Those who passed by did not say: The blessing of the Lord be upon you, may see her reproach and grieve.

5:15.t: And you shall be a reproach and a blasphemy, an example and an astonishment among the nations which are round about you (in place of which in the Seventy is read: And she shall be στενακτὴ — that is, 'worthy of groaning'; and from Theodotion there has been added: — καὶ δηλαϊστὴ, a word of which we have no knowledge; in place of which the three other translators rendered 'blasphemy', which in the Hebrew is called 'geddupha'. And there follows:), when I have executed judgments in you in fury and indignation and in rebukes of wrath, which I the Lord have spoken. That Jerusalem is worthy of groaning when she has offended God, and he has executed judgments in her in fury and indignation, Paul too testifies, who says: We were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest, and again: We who are in this tabernacle groan, being burdened; and we speak with Jerusalem: I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him. […]

5:16.t: When I send the most evil arrows of famine, which will be deadly, and which I will send to destroy you, and I will gather famine upon you, and I will crush the support (or staff) of bread. That famine and pestilence and most evil beasts and whatever other evils we endure in this world come because of our sins is manifest. Hence also that famine which is recorded to have happened in Ruth, and in the volume of Kings under Elijah, when the heaven was shut for three years and six months, and under Elisha, whose incredible want a sudden abundance made good, was sent by the judgment of God. And this was not only done then in Jerusalem, but is done also in our Jerusalem, in which, because of the greatness of our sins, first a famine of hearing the word of God is sent; then death follows the famine, so that we who did not hear: Taste and see that the Lord is sweet, may afterwards experience: The death of sinners is most evil. Of the support and staff of bread we have spoken above.

5:17.t: And I will send upon you famine and most evil beasts, even to utter destruction, and pestilence and blood shall pass through you, and I will bring the sword upon you; I the Lord have spoken. That most evil beasts are brought upon a land of desolation which has been laid waste by famine, sword and pestilence, the present times also show, when dogs, domestic animals, are roused to madness against the flesh of their masters, and the land is filled with bears and wolves and all other kinds of beasts; and by pestilence and blood passing through it he signifies disease and the sword. But into our Jerusalem too most evil beasts are sent, when we are given over to passions of ignominy and to a reprobate mind and to the consciousness of sins, which torment and tear apart our soul. Dissensions, heresies, schisms, rivalries, envies, sorrows, detractions, many desires, avarice — which is the root of all evils —, these are most evil beasts; […]

6:2.t: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set your face toward the mountains of Israel, and you shall prophesy to them, and you shall say: Mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord God. Thus says the Lord God to the mountains and the hills, to the crags and the valleys.
