Since 'Adonai' the Lord is often said in this prophet, it seems that it should be briefly explained for the sake of the Greeks and Latins who have no knowledge of the Hebrew language: 'Adonai' is one name among the ten names of God, and it means 'lord', which we often use of men as well — indeed Sarah too, calling Abraham her 'lord', called him by this name; and where it is said: My lord king, 'Adonai' is written — ; when therefore two names, 'lord' and 'Lord', are joined, the first name is common, the second is properly God's, the one which is called ἄρρητον, that is, 'ineffable', and which was written on the golden plate that was on the forehead of the high priest. […]

6:3.t: But otherwise, upon those also who are lifted up into pride, and of whom the Apostle speaks: Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up, a sword is brought, so that all their images, which they have fashioned from their own mind, may be crushed, and they may lie slain and perceive that they are dead, seeing that their images and fictions profit them nothing.

Behold, I will bring a sword upon you, and I will destroy your high places; and I will demolish your altars, and your images shall be broken, and I will cast down your slain before your idols. And I will lay the corpses of the sons of Israel before the face of your images, and I will scatter your bones around your altars, in all your dwellings. It is said to the mountains of Israel that God will destroy their high places, on which men worshiped fashioned gods, and will break the altars and images, and will cause their worshipers to be slain in the sight of the shrines, so that the corpses of the dead may lie where the victims formerly lay, and the bones may be scattered — not of the mountains, but of those who lay on the mountains — round about the altars and in all the cities and villages of Israel. This according to the letter.

6:5.t: And as for his saying that he scatters the bones of the mountains around the altars, he indicates that all the strongest of them are to be separated from one another — for it profits perverse knowledge that the wicked be divided from the wicked — ; and as those who, with a most wicked consensus, were building a tower were, for their own benefit, scattered and their tongues divided, lest the most wicked consensus make them worse, so the bones of the mountains are scattered, that they may understand their vain endeavors. (This which we have put: And I will lay the corpses of the sons of Israel before the face of your images, is not found in the Seventy.)

6:6.t: Through these words an occasion is given us rather to follow the spiritual understanding, so that the cities of the heretics, which are interpreted as churches, and the high places of their pride and the altars of their perverse doctrines may be broken, and the idols may perish which they had feigned for themselves out of their own heart, and the shrines may be crushed — for these are the temples which had risen up against the temple of the Lord, and which in the Greek tongue are called τεμένη, that is, 'fanes' and 'shrines' — , and all the works of the mountains may be crushed which are not works of God but of the masters of false knowledge.

The cities shall be deserted, and the high places shall be demolished, and your altars shall be scattered and shall perish, and your idols shall be broken and shall cease, and your shrines shall be crushed, and your works shall be blotted out; and the slain shall fall in your midst, and you shall know that I am the Lord. The reason is plain why the cities of the mountains are to be deserted: namely, that the high places and altars may be demolished, and the idols destroyed, and the shrines perish, and all worship of images cease; that the slain may fall in the midst of the mountains, and they may know that he himself is the Lord.

6:7.t: And when the slain have fallen in the midst of the mountains — either those whom the mountains themselves had slain, or the men of the Church who had slain them, living wickedly as they were, unto their salvation — then there will be an end of the proud mountains, so that they may know that he himself is the Lord. It may also happen that, out of the one people of the mountains of Israel, when some have been slain, the others come to know: for when the pestilent man is scourged, the fool will be wiser.

6:8.t:
[Passage quoted, Ezek. vi. 7.]

This also seems to me to agree with the passages from the other prophets. For whom could you call the "saved" but those called by the others "a remnant, and the drop, and the dew of that people," by which was signified the band of the Apostles of our Saviour? They truly being saved from the destruction of all their race, even in their scattering remembered God, so that it must be agreed that what was written referred to them.
6:8.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 2, Chapter 3

6:8.t: And I will leave among you those who escape the sword among the nations, when I have scattered you into the lands; and your freed ones shall remember me among the nations to which they have been led captive. That which the Lord says to Elijah: I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal, and which the apostle Paul writes: And now in this time a remnant according to the election of grace has been saved, can fit this passage. For the apostles too, who were of the seed of Israel and had escaped the sword, were preserved for this reason: that they might be scattered among the nations, and preach the Gospel in the lands, and remember God among the nations in which they were dwelling in the time of captivity. This can also be said: that some from the Jewish captivity were preserved for this reason, that among the nations they might remember his name and proclaim his power. […]

6:9.t: Because I have crushed their heart, fornicating and departing from me, and their eyes fornicating after their idols; and they shall be displeased with themselves over the evils which they had done in all their abominations, and they shall know that I the Lord have not spoken in vain, that I would do this evil to them. (Much of this passage has been passed over by the Seventy, and this has been changed: I swore to their fornicating heart, in place of which we have put: I have crushed their heart, fornicating.) Now he swore and decreed that he would do what he showed in deed; or else, he crushed the heart fornicating and departing from God — the heart of those to whom he speaks through Hosea: They have been led astray by a spirit of fornication — , and the eyes fornicating after idols — through whose windows death is said to have entered: for which reason in Daniel too the two elders ordered Susanna to be unveiled, that they might enjoy the beauty of her bared body — .

It profits the heretics too that their heart be crushed, that most evil treasury of perverse doctrines, because it has departed from the Lord, and their eyes, fornicating after their own inventions; and they, when they have remembered the Lord, will be displeased with themselves in all their abominations, and, understanding the truth of the true faith, will know that he himself is the Lord. And for this reason he often brings on tribulation, which seems ruinous and most grievous to those who suffer it: that they may be turned to penance.

6:10.t: Nor has the Lord spoken in vain, that he would do evil or evils, when at his threat those who lay under the sentence do penance; but if the heart is hard and untamable, not perceiving, even through punishments, the benefits of the one who corrects, it is said to them: In vain have I struck your sons; you have not received discipline.

6:11.t: Scripture has taught us to sing with gravity, to sing psalms spiritually; it has taught us also to dance wisely, when the Lord says to Ezekiel: clap with your hand and stamp with your foot; for God, the censor of morals, would not demand the actor's movements of a loose body, nor would he command of men unseemly clatterings and womanish clappings, so as to bring so great a prophet down to the mockeries of the stage and the softness of women. The revealed mysteries of the resurrection do not agree with the disgraces of dancing exacted. There is indeed, there is a clapping proper to good deeds and acts, whose sound may go out into the world and the glory of things well done may resound; there is an honorable dancing, in which the mind leaps for joy and the body is lifted up by good works, when we hang our instruments upon the willows. […]

Thus says the Lord God: Strike with your hand and stamp your foot, and say: Alas, for all the abominations of the evils of the house of Israel. The prophet is commanded to show the magnitude of the sins with hands and feet and speech, so that, by the gesture of his body and the lowering of his voice, he may display the bearing of one stunned and amazed and weeping. For just as, whenever we behold something new and astonishing, we shudder in body as much as in mind, so that we clap our hands and strike our feet on the ground and lower our voice to weeping, so now the prophet, discerning with the eyes of the mind the punishments to come, speaks concerning all the abominations of the evils of the house of Israel which follow. Spiritually, we strike with the hand when we separate ourselves from evil works; we stamp the foot when we do not walk in the way of sinners; […]

Who are to fall by sword, famine, pestilence. This is the cause of mourning: that the inhabitants of the mountains and the worshipers of the altars of the idols are to fall by sword, famine, pestilence. Those who are led about by various errors and change their faith daily and are carried about by every wind of doctrine, these are cut down by the sword and divided into parts, abandoning the unity of the Church's faith. But he who does not have spiritual food dies of famine, not knowing him who said: I am the life. Further, he who, given over either to single vices or to several, cannot be separated from them, falls by pestilence, as if by a kind of lethargy.

6:12.t: He who is far off shall die by pestilence, but he who is near shall fall by the sword, and he who is left and besieged shall die by famine, and I will fulfill my indignation upon them. He who escapes the siege of the city and moves away to the deserts will die by pestilence; he who is near will fall by the sword of the enemy; but he whom the hostile army surrounds will perish by famine and want; and in all these the indignation of God will be fulfilled, so that those who remain may know that he himself is the Lord. Whoever also withdraws from the Church will at once die by pestilence; he who seems to himself a man of some learning and diligent will, unless he takes care, be struck by the sword of the enemy; he who is content with simple faith — like the brute animals he does indeed spend his time in the Church, yet he brings nothing to completion in any good work, nor is he an imitator of the ant, which in harvest prepares food for itself and carries it in — , he will die of famine; […]

6:13.t: And you shall know that I am the Lord, when your slain are in the midst of your idols, round about your altars, on every lofty hill and on all the summits of the mountains, and under every shady tree, and under every leafy oak, the place where they burned sweet-smelling incense to all their idols. It is plain according to the letter and needs no interpretation, that on the mountains of Israel and on the lofty hills, among the very altars of the idols and the groves, which are called shady trees, the army of Israel was cut down, so that where they had sinned, there they would be punished. According to ἀναγωγὴν [anagogy, the higher sense] let us follow the order set forth. […]

6:14.t: I will stretch out my hand over them, and I will make the land desolate and forsaken from the desert of Deblatha in all their dwellings; and they shall know that I am the Lord. O mountains of Israel, when your slain have fallen in the midst of the altars of your idols, on every lofty hill, on all the summits of the mountains, and I have filled with the corpses of the dead your groves, in which they once burned sweet-smelling incense to their idols, then I will stretch out my hand for vengeance, which until now had been held back, and I will reduce the whole land of Israel to a wilderness, from the desert of Deblatha — which is in the land of Hamath, which today is called Ἐπιφάνεια [Epiphania] of Syria — in all their dwellings, so that it may be plain to all that there is nothing between the wilderness and the Great Sea which the enemy's blade has not consumed — many think that it is the same place of which it is written in Jeremiah: And they seized Zedekiah in the desert which is near Jericho, and all his retinue […]

7:2.t: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: And you, son of man, thus says the Lord God to the land of Israel: The end has come, the end upon the four 'wings of the earth'. These we have translated 'regions of the world': namely the east and the west, the south and the north; of which wings Isaiah also speaks: Lord, from the wings (or ends) of the earth we have heard wonders, which were being wrought throughout the whole world by the apostles; and of the saints it is written: If you sleep in the midst of the lots, wings of a dove silvered over, and its hinder parts in the greenness of gold; whence the Lord too, when he had drawn near and seen Jerusalem, wept and said: How often I would have gathered your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not?; he it is who, in the song of Deuteronomy, spread out his wings, took them up and bore them on his shoulders. […]

7:3.t: Now the end is upon you, and I will send my fury against you, and I will judge you according to your ways, and I will set against you all your abominations. And my eye will not spare you, and I will not have mercy, but I will set your ways upon you, and your abominations will be in your midst, and you shall know that I am the Lord. (In this chapter, in the Seventy translators, the order has been changed and confused, so that the first things are last and the last either first or in the middle, and the middle things themselves are moved now to the end, now to the beginning; wherefore we, following both the Hebrew itself and the other translators, have set down the order of the truth.) […]

7:4.t: And as for his saying: My eye will not spare you, and I will not have mercy, like a most merciful physician who wishes to cut away rotten flesh and to burn out decayed wounds with the cautery, he does not spare so that he may spare, he does not have mercy so that he may have mercy the more, lest anything rotten remain in the body that would corrupt the living flesh by its nearness. But the Lord strikes the one whom he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives; to this understanding belongs that saying: I will strike and I will heal, for every medicine has bitterness for a time, but afterwards the fruit of the pain is shown in health; something of this kind God speaks through Amos: Since I have known you out of all the tribes of the earth, therefore I will avenge upon you all your sins; for the Lord knows those who are his. […]

7:5.t: Thus says the Lord God: One affliction, an affliction, behold, comes. The end comes, the end comes; it has awakened against you, behold, it comes. Crushing comes upon you who dwell in the land. (These words are not found in the Seventy, but in their edition they were added under asterisks from the translation of Theodotion; let us, however, follow the Hebrew.) In place of 'affliction', which we have put for the sake of clarity following Symmachus, who translated κάκωσιν [ill-treatment], both in the Hebrew and in the Greek κακία or πονηρία is written, that is, 'malice'. And it is said that the time of the final sin of the land of Israel has arrived, so that it no longer escapes the sentence of God which it had long been deserving. And because it had not yet filled up its sins, the punishment was for that reason being deferred, according to that which is written: For the sins of the Amorites are not yet complete; whence the Lord too says to the Jews: You also, he says, fill up the measure of your fathers. […]

7:6.t: We can also interpret this place spiritually against the people of the Jews, upon whom came the end and consummation from the blood of Abel the righteous to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom they slew between the temple and the altar. For as long as they did not lay hands on the Son of God, the Lord's sentence dozed for them and was put off; but when they killed the heir so that the inheritance might perish, then it awoke against them, and the whole order and tangle of miseries rose up, because they did not seek heavenly things but desired to cling to the earth.

7:7.t: 'Crushing' has come — which in the Hebrew is called 'sephphira', and which Aquila translated προσκόπησιν, that is, 'contemplation' and 'looking forward' — which you, ever fearful, dreaded would come upon you — and which Theodotion translated πλοκὴν, that is, the 'order and connected web' of all evils —. Further, what is said: Upon you who dwell in the land, we ought to take according to that saying of the Ἀποκαλύψεως [Revelation] of John: Woe upon all who dwell on the earth — for the saint is not a dweller on the earth but a stranger and sojourner, and he says: I am a stranger and a sojourner, as all my fathers were. For this reason Abraham too is called 'a Hebrew', that is, περάτης, and 'sojourner' and 'passer-through' and 'wayfarer', hastening to pass from the present age to the things to come —.

The time has come, the day of slaughter is near, and not of the glory of the mountains. The Hebrew word 'adarim', which we, dividing it into two words, the first 'ad', the second 'arim', have translated following Theodotion as 'glory of the mountains', Symmachus turned into 'postponement' and said: And the time is near, a day of haste and not of postponement. (But the Seventy translated thus: The time has come, the day has drawn near, not with disturbance nor with pains.) Theodotion: The time has come, the day of famine is near, and not of the glory of the mountains. And the time of slaughter and of famine is proven even now in the Jewish people, which has neither prophets nor the word of God by which the soul of believers is fed. By the mountains understand the teachers and those who have knowledge of the Scriptures, of whom it is said in another place too: You give light wonderfully from the everlasting mountains. […]

7:8.t: Now from near at hand I will pour out my wrath upon you, and I will unfold my fury upon you, and I will judge you according to your ways, and I will lay (or give) upon you all your abominations. If we wish to reckon from the fifth year of the exile of King Jeconiah to the ninth year of the reign of Zedekiah, when Nebuchadnezzar came and besieged Jerusalem, there will be three years in between. Hence it is rightly said: 'Now from near at hand I will pour out my wrath upon you; I will by no means foretell things to come to you nor threaten things that will happen long afterwards; now I will fulfil my fury upon you: and this fury and wrath is not without judgment, but is so that it may repay your ways upon your head and make you feel all your abominations'. We can also speak of the final captivity: that after the killing of Christ, when the end came upon them and sin awoke against them, there was fulfilled that which the apostle Paul writes: Now the wrath of God has come upon them to the end; […]

7:9.t: And my eye will not spare, nor will I have mercy, but your ways I will lay (or give) upon you, and your abominations will be in your midst, and you shall know that I am the Lord who strikes. The causes of the severity and harshness, or, as the heretics think, of the cruelty of God, in that 'my eye will not spare, nor have mercy', he adds, saying: 'I will give you your ways, and your abominations will be in your midst, so that you may feel what you have done and, seeing your abominations set either before your eyes or in the midst of all, may correct your error by repentance, and, withdrawing from your former works, when you hate what you have done, then you will know that he himself is the Lord who strikes for this reason: to correct, and: He chastises every son whom he receives'.

7:10.t: But the Seventy, according to that sense in which it is written: For you do not know what the coming day may bring forth, said: 'Behold, the day gives birth to what it had conceived long before, and the end comes, and the encompassing has gone forth, which is to encompass and hold all your evils (or, as Symmachus translated, inspection, so that the Lord may see all that you have done and consider your works and render to each what he deserves)'. And on what they likewise translated: The rod has blossomed, we can use that testimony: Do not take the rod away from your son, and that of the apostle: What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?; and God too resounds through the mouth of the psalmist: I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with scourges; but my mercy I will not take away from them.

Behold the day, behold, it comes, contraction has gone forth; the rod has blossomed, pride has budded; iniquity has risen up in the rod of impiety: not from them, and not from the people, nor from their noise; and there will be no rest for them. (LXX: "Behold, the day gives birth, behold, the end comes, the encompassing has gone forth, and the rod has blossomed, pride has budded, injury has been roused, and it will crush the strength of the wicked, and not with disturbance nor with haste, and they are not of them, nor is there beauty in them.") 'The day', he says, 'has been contracted and shortened, and the captivity presses close at hand; the rod which for a long time threatened you has blossomed, and from the blossom it is bringing forth the fruit of blows; […]

For this reason, then, the Lord visits and strikes: that all the pride which long lay hidden, shut in, may spring up and lie open, and injury may be roused against the pride that has sprung up and is budding, and the strength of the wicked may be crushed, not with disturbance nor with haste; for the end of the blossoming rod is health and correction, which comes not by the merit of those who are corrected, nor by a beauty which they do not have in themselves, but by the mercy of the Lord. A difficult place, and one in which the Hebrew and the Seventy differ greatly; many things have been added to the Seventy from the edition of Theodotion, so that they might seem to have some coherence.

7:12.t: The time has come, the day has drawn near. It is not only to Jerusalem that it is said that the time of its captivity has come and the day has drawn near on which it is to be walled in by the Babylonian army; but to him too who exulted over his barns built and enlarged, the Lord speaks: Fool, this night your soul will be taken from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?; whence the apostle too: The time, he says, has been shortened; and in another place: For the figure of this world is passing away; and it must be noted that he did not defer it to the future but spoke of the present, 'is passing away', and that daily 'the figure of the world' slips by: for it never remains in the same state, but the figure of things growing and diminishing ever flies past and is changed; whence the Lord too: Heaven, he says, and earth will pass away. But if these things, by which all that is in the world is contained, pass away and go by, what in human affairs can be everlasting?

Let him who buys not rejoice, and let him who sells not mourn. It is natural to rejoice in the purchase of possessions and to mourn in their sale. But when slavery and captivity are pressing, both joy and sorrow are vain in either case. Hence the apostle too: The time has been shortened; for the rest, let those who have wives be as though they had none, and those who weep as though they did not weep, and those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice, and those who buy as though they did not possess, and those who use this world as though they did not make full use of it; for the flood too overwhelmed those buying and selling, as the Lord says in the Gospel.

For wrath is upon all its people. (This is not found in the Seventy.) For 'people' one may also take 'multitude' and 'crowd' according to the Hebrew: for this is what 'amona' signifies. And the reason is clear why he who buys ought not to rejoice and he who sells should cease to weep: because the wrath of God is shortly to come upon the whole multitude of the land of Judea, or of Jerusalem; for this is understood from the preceding words, in which it is written: Thus says the Lord God to the land of Israel, and the rest.

7:13.t: For he who sells will not return to what he has sold. He speaks according to the Hebrew custom: for every purchase used to return to the seller in the fiftieth year, the year of release, which among them was called the jubilee; before the year of release comes, then, when possessions return to their former owners, captivity will burst in, which will take away the whole accustomed life of the city. But what the Seventy translated: For he who buys will not return to the seller, though according to the history it does not hang together at all, according to anagogy can have this sense, so that we may say that he who had been deceived by heretical error, when he has understood the fraudulence of his teacher, by no means returns to the seller, that is, to the teacher, but despises and scorns him.

And still their life is among the living: for the vision to all its multitude will not go back. Just as the possession will not return to its former owner, since the overthrow of the city is impending, so the vision and prophetic threat, which is directed to the whole multitude of the city, will by no means go back and become void, but will be fulfilled in fact, while those to whom the prophetic word is directed are still living. And he says this to show the captivity is imminent, lest according to their custom they should say: 'This vision is for many days hence and will be fulfilled after long times'. We can also say this: that after the prophetic vision withdrew from the Jews — The law, indeed, and the prophets until John the Baptist —, after the killing of the Savior it by no means goes back to them, nor do they any longer deserve to have prophets. And significantly: 'To all', he says, 'the multitude the vision will not go back'; […]

And a man in the iniquity of his life will not be strengthened. (LXX: "And a man in the eyes of his life will not obtain.") And the sense according to the Hebrew is: his iniquity will not profit a man, nor will it furnish him any strength; according to the Seventy: even the man who desired what he thought precious in the world will not obtain it, but, as liberty perishes, all that is beautiful will be lost. Now the ambiguity of the Hebrew letters 'iod' and 'uau', which are distinguished only by size, caused some to translate 'iniquity' and others 'eyes'.

7:14.t: Sound the trumpet, let all be made ready. (LXX: "Blow the trumpet and judge all things.") Of the blast and sound of trumpets we read in many places, as there: Lift up your voice like a trumpet, and elsewhere: Blow the trumpet at the new moon, on the notable day of our solemnity, and in the apostle: For the Lord himself, at the command and at the voice of the archangel and at the trumpet of God, will descend from heaven, and in the Gospel: Do not blow a trumpet before you; and the history of Numbers tells of beaten and silver trumpets, which are compared to the prophetic word and to the apostolic teaching. And now it is commanded that all be made ready for wars at the signal of the blast of the horn. But as for what the Seventy said: And judge all things, no one doubts that it befits the power of the apostles, who, after the trumpet of the angels has sounded, are to judge the twelve tribes of Israel on twelve thrones; one of whom, Paul, said: We shall judge angels, and elsewhere: In you the world will be judged. […]

And there is no one who goes to battle; for my wrath is upon all its multitude. (These words too are not found in the Seventy.) God had commanded that they sound the trumpet to make ready an army which could resist the strength of the Babylonians, but it did no good to have commanded it, since there is no one among the people who dares to go forth to wars. And the people has been unnerved and lacks the strength to fight for this reason: because the whole wrath of God is upon all its multitude, that is, understood, of the city of Jerusalem or of the land of Judea; but also of the Jerusalem of our land: when either public persecution or the incitements of various vices strive to overcome us, in vain do the teachers sound the trumpet and hasten to make us ready for wars, since there is no strength in the people, which has been withdrawn for this reason, that present sins have deserved the wrath of the Lord.

7:15.t: The sword without, pestilence and famine within; he who is in the field will die by the sword, and those who are in the city will be devoured by pestilence and famine. And those of them who flee will be saved, and they will be on the mountains like doves of the valleys, all trembling, each in his iniquity. (The Seventy were entirely silent about 'doves of the valleys', or, as Theodotion translated, 'meditating'.) And what we have translated: All trembling, each in his iniquity, Theodotion translated thus: All murmuring, each one in her iniquity, so that under the metaphor of meditating doves he signifies that each one of the people weeps for his own sin and understands and perceives why he suffers these things. Now the three parts — of some who are to die in the city by pestilence and famine, and of others whom the sword will kill outside, and of those who have escaped captivity by flight — we read of above; […]

For the God of all spoke by the voice of Ezechiel: "As I live, says the Lord, surely inasmuch as you have defiled My holy things with all your impurities, I will also reject you; My eye shall not spare, nor will I pity." "They that are in the plain shall die by the sword: and them that are in the city famine and pestilence shall consume. And those of them that are saved shall be delivered, and shall be upon the mountains as meditative doves." For Israel did not perish from the very roots, nor, so to speak, stock and branch: but a remnant was delivered, of which the foremost and the first-fruits were the blessed disciples, of whom it is that he says, that they were upon the mountains as meditative doves. For they were as heralds throughout the whole world, forth-telling the mystery of Christ, and their office is praise and song, and, so to speak, to cry aloud in psalms, "My tongue shall meditate on Your righteousness: and all the day on Your praise."
7:15.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

7:17.t: All hands will be weakened and all knees will flow with waters. And they will gird themselves with sackcloth, and dread will cover them. (For 'knees flowing with waters' the Seventy translated: Thighs will be defiled with moisture.) When all have trembled and fled to the mountains, the hands of all will be weakened, and no one will be able to resist the enemy, and through the greatness of their fear urine will defile their knees, nor will the bladder be able to hold back the waters flowing forth; they will gird themselves with sackcloth, and trembling will possess all things; granted that this was done in that people not only under the Babylonians but also under the Romans, when the wrath of God came upon them to the end. […]

7:18.t: On every face shame, and on all heads baldness. The blush of the face is a sign of shame, and the consciousness of sins shines out in the face, and there is hope of salvation when shamefacedness follows wrongdoing; hence to her who with hard heart gloried in her sins it was said: The face of a harlot has become yours, you do not know how to blush. Baldness of the head too signifies mourning, when the hair loses its comeliness and we lose the beauty of our locks; accordingly it is said to Jerusalem: For the ornament of your head you have baldness, because of your works, and another prophet: All heads, he says, in every place will be shorn, and every beard will be shaved; Micah also to the same Jerusalem: Make yourself bald, he says, and be shorn for the children of your delights; enlarge your baldness like the eagle; […]

7:19.t: Their silver will be cast outside, and their gold will be in the dunghill. (LXX: "Their silver will be cast into the streets, and their gold will be for contempt.") As flight and captivity compel them, they will cast their riches, the weights of gold and silver, into the streets, desiring only to save their lives, so that what were formerly their luxuries may not be a burden. Otherwise, according to anagogy, all the silver of the captives and of those fleeing from Jerusalem will be cast into the streets, onto the broad and spacious way that leads to death, because they have abandoned the narrow path of salvation; but all the gold will be for contempt and will be reckoned as a dunghill and uncleanness: for what is outside the Church of the Lord cannot have cleanness.

Their silver and their gold will not be able to deliver them on the day of the fury of the Lord. (And this is not found in the Seventy.) No one doubts that in the time of siege and famine gold and silver do not deliver the hungry, and that teeth dashed against the most precious metal are blunted as on the hardest stone. Accordingly there follows:

They will not satisfy their soul, and their bellies will not be filled. By present evils we have learned that many rich men, amid silk, gems and weights of gold and silver, worn out by want, have had the end of beggars. But that the silver and gold of those who are outside the Church do not deliver the souls of their possessors on the day of the fury of the Lord, but that they have everlasting hunger and are tormented with an empty belly, is shown by that testimony in which it is said: The ransom of a man's soul is his own riches. His own riches are those which the truth of Christ has taught us, who commanded us to make for ourselves friends of the mammon of iniquity, who may receive us into the eternal tabernacles.

For it has become the stumbling block of their iniquity. 'Therefore', he says, 'neither will the soul of those who possess gold and silver be satisfied nor their belly be filled: because this very gold and silver has become the stumbling block of their crimes'. And he signifies the idols which, fashioned of gold and silver, condemn their own makers. (But the Seventy translated: For torment was their iniquity, so that the wicked may be tormented in their own error and understand that they have wickedly turned the gifts of God into blasphemy).

7:20.t: And the ornament of their necklaces they set for pride, and they made of it the images of their abominations and idols. (LXX: "The choice things of the world they set for pride, and the images of their abominations and their stumbling blocks they made of them.") 'What I', he says, 'had given as an ornament and as riches to those who possessed them, they turned to pride, so that from the very things by which they could have freed their soul through almsgiving and good works they took material for arrogance; then from the gold and silver they made idols and turned my gifts into images of demons'. But as for what the Seventy said: The choice things of the world they set for pride, it is to be referred to gold and silver, than which nothing in the world is thought more precious; and as for what follows: Their stumbling blocks, let us know that it was added from the edition of Theodotion. […]

For this reason I have given it to them for uncleanness. And I will give it into the hands of strangers to be plundered, and to the impious of the earth for a prey, and they will defile it. (LXX: "For this reason I have given them to them for uncleanness. And I will hand them over into the hands of strangers that they may plunder them; and to the pestilent of the earth for a prey, and they will pollute them.") 'Because from the gold and silver, that is, from the ornaments of the necklaces which I had given them, they made for themselves images of their abominations and idols, for this reason I have given those things to them for uncleanness and for dung', for which Symmachus translated nausea, wishing to express the filth of idols. 'And I will hand them over', he says, 'into the hands of enemies that they may plunder everything, and so that I may not so much defile them as show to have been defiled the things which earlier seemed most holy'. […]

7:22.t: And I will turn away my face from them, and they will violate my secret place; and there will enter into it emissaries (or, as the Seventy translated, rashly, or, as Symmachus and Theodotion, 'those bursting in' and 'the pestilent') and they will defile it. 'When', he says, 'for the causes given above, the abominations of the people, I turn my face away from them and by no means judge them worthy of my eyes, then they will violate my secret place (which signifies 'the Holy of Holies', for which the Seventy translated vision, to show that the presence of God had been in the holy places), and the impious and pestilent of the earth will burst into those places which, apart from the priests and the high priest alone, no one else dared to enter'. This we know was done both by the Babylonians, and by King Antiochus and Gnaeus Pompey, and, finally, under Vespasian and Titus, when the temple was taken and overthrown, and all things were perpetrated which the prophet's following discourse embraces. […]

7:23.t: Make a conclusion, for the land is full of the judgment of bloods, and the city is full of iniquity. (LXX: "And I will bring disturbance, for the land full of the judgment of bloods, and the city full of iniquities.") The Hebrew word 'arethic' Aquila translated 'conclusion', Symmachus and Theodotion καθήλωσιν, that is, 'nailing fast', for which the Seventy put φυρμόν, which we have rendered as 'disturbance'. 'Therefore, O prophet, conclude my wrath upon the land of Judea and upon the city of Jerusalem in a brief word: so that, as the land is full of the judgment of bloods — for all are judged in blood, shedding innocent blood, as Scripture records the Jews also did in the person of Naboth —, so their own gore too may be shed and the city shown to be full of iniquity — for under Manasseh too the city of Jerusalem was filled from gate to gate with the blood of the prophets —. And conclusion and disturbance and nailing fast will come upon them, so that no one can escape the impending miseries'.

7:24.t: And I will bring the worst of the nations, and they will possess their houses. (And this is not found in the Seventy.) 'In place of priests and prophets I will bring the Babylonians, the worst of all the nations, that they may possess your houses and subject you to slavery'. But our houses too, that is, our souls — for we are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in us —, the worst demons will possess, if our land is full of bloods and our dwelling full of iniquity.

And I will make the pride of the mighty cease, and they will possess their sanctuaries. (LXX: "And I will turn away the roaring of their strength, and their holy things will be polluted.") All pride offends God. Therefore the worst of the nations will possess the houses of the mighty and the proud and will take hold of their sanctuaries, because the unclean man enters the place of holiness and defiles it with his uncleanness. And significantly, because the holy things of God had been polluted and the secret place violated, he did not say: 'They will possess my sanctuaries', but: 'their' sanctuaries, which after their defilement ceased to be 'mine'.

7:25.t: Anguish is at hand. (LXX: "Propitiation will come.") — According to the preceding order Aquila and Theodotion rightly translated that 'anguish' is at hand, and Symmachus 'grief'; but the Seventy, in the midst of all the sorrowful things, put a word of gladness, so that the mind of the mourner may be sustained and may hope for better things amid adversities, and for the Lord propitious, of whom it is written: The Lord raises up those who are dashed down. — We, however, following Symmachus, have joined the former sentence to the latter, so as to say: As anguish comes upon them, they will seek peace and there will be none, which according to the Seventy cannot stand at all: for if 'propitiation will come', how 'will they seek peace and not find it'? And he will seek peace and not find it who heard from the apostles: Peace to this house, and did not keep it nor make it rest in his mind; but, put to flight by evil works, it cannot be found. […]

7:26.t: Trouble upon trouble will come, and report upon report. (LXX: "Woe upon woe will be, and messenger upon messenger.") Just as it is said to the saints: Rejoice, again I say: rejoice, and of them it is written: They will go from strength to strength, so that they may heap future goods upon present goods, so also to these, upon whom anguish has come and who have sought peace and not found it, there will come trouble upon trouble, or woe upon woe — according to what is written in Revelation too: One woe has passed, and another woe will come —, and report will come upon report, and messenger upon messenger — according to that saying of blessed Job: While one was still speaking, another messenger came, adding evils to evils, and describing the roaring and the throng of the approaching Babylonian —.

And they will seek a vision from the prophet, and the law will perish from the priest, and counsel from the elders. Properly, each thing is sought from each: the prophecy of things to come is sought from the prophet; the interpretation of the law is the priest's office; prudent counsel is what mature age searches out, according to that which is written: In the counsel of the saints and in the congregation, great are the works of the Lord. And these things were sought from the prophets and elders and priests not only at that time, when the Babylonian army was coming against Jerusalem, but they are required daily in the churches, which, if they have lost vision, law and counsel, boast in vain that they have prophets and priests and elders.

7:27.t: The king will mourn and the prince will be clothed with grief (or, according to the Seventy, with destruction; who, intending I know not what, were entirely silent about what we have expressed from the Hebrew speech: The king will mourn.) That Zedekiah mourned, and that all the princes of the people of the Jews were covered with grief, Holy Scripture records. But we can — although at first sight this may seem blasphemous — say that the king who mourns our vices and sins is Christ, who speaks in the Psalms: What profit is there in my blood, while I go down into corruption? and who, drawing near to Jerusalem, wept over it and said: Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you, how often I would have gathered your children as a hen gathers her chicks under wings, and you would not? The princes too will be either, in a good sense, the apostles who mourn sinners, or, in the contrary sense, those to whom it is said: Hear the word of the Lord, princes of Sodom. […]

And the hands of the people of the land will be troubled. (Or, according to the Seventy, will be weakened.) When there is no vision in the prophet and no knowledge of the law in the priest and no counsel in the elders, and the king has mourned and the prince is in grief or in destruction, consequently the hands of the people too will be troubled, losing their order, or will be weakened, no longer having their ancient strength. And beautifully the people whose hands will be troubled, and whose citizenship is not in heaven, is called not the people of God but the people of the land, of whom it is written: Let those who depart be written upon the earth.

According to their way I will do to them, and according to their judgments I will judge them. (Or, as the Seventy translated, I will avenge myself on them.) To sinners God renders according to their ways, so as to keep the truth of judgment; but toward the saints he exceeds the measure of mercy: The sufferings of this time, indeed, are not worthy of the future glory which will be revealed in us. For the wages of sin is death, which the sinner receives according to his ways and his works; but the virtue of the righteous enjoys the Lord's bounty, of which Paul speaks: The gift of God is eternal life. And what he added: And according to their judgments I will judge them, sounds that Gospel saying: With what judgment you judge, it will be judged of you, and that apostolic one: In that in which you judge another, you condemn yourself; for you do the same things that you judge.

And they shall know that I am the Lord. This little verse is often set down in this prophet, because the knowledge of God follows punishments and torments, so that him whom they do not understand through benefits they may come to know through torments.

8:1.t: And it came to pass in the sixth year, in the sixth month, on the fifth of the month: I was sitting in my house, and the elders of Judah were sitting before me. We read that the preceding vision came to the prophet in the fifth year of the exile of Jeconiah, in the fourth month, on the fifth of the month. But this one, which we now wish to expound, is recorded to have taken place in the sixth year of the same king, in the sixth month, on the fifth of the month. From this it is clear that these things which are written took place a year and two months later, and that either the prophecy was interrupted for a year and two months, or the things which the preceding discourse wove together were carried out over the whole fourteen months. […]

And the hand of the Lord God fell upon me there, and I saw: and behold, a likeness as the appearance of fire; from the appearance of his loins and downward, fire, and from his loins and upward as the appearance of brightness, as the vision of electrum. (LXX: "And the hand of Adonai the Lord came upon me there, and I saw, and behold, a likeness as the form of a man; from his loins and downward, fire; from his loins and upward ※ as the vision of a breeze: as the vision of electrum.") The Hebrew text does not contain 'man'; and the 'vision' 'of a breeze', which is not found in the Seventy, we have added from Theodotion; and where we said: The hand of the Lord fell upon me, Symmachus translated: The hand of the Lord befell me, which in the Hebrew is said 'thephphol' [it fell]; and the hand signifies ἐνέργειαν, that is, 'working', so that he might be able to know the mysteries of the vision.

8:2.t: And this must be considered: that he does not see the truth itself but the likeness of fire, since from the loins downward fire appeared, and from the loins upward as the appearance of brightness, as the vision of electrum. For 'brightness', which in the Hebrew is called 'zor', Theodotion translated 'breeze', so as to show the refreshments of God in the upper parts. Indeed, in the volume of Kings too, blessed Elijah beholds the coming of the Lord not in the storm and the whirlwind, not in the blazing of fire, but in the appearance of a breeze, thin and most gentle, so as to prove the mildness of almighty God. Now the works of intercourse, which are signified by the loins, downward, are purged by fire, and the works of the virtues, which rise from the loins to the higher parts, have brightness and splendor; […]

8:3.t: And the likeness of a hand, sent forth, took hold of me by a lock of my head (LXX: "And he stretched out the likeness of a hand and took me up by the fringe of my crown.") Here too it is the likeness of a hand, not the hand itself, that is stretched out: for there is nothing bodily in God; and a hand is seen, as a member of the human body, so that by its familiarity it may in no way terrify him who is taken up and seized: for if it had touched the prophet in the likeness of a snake or of any other of the beasts, the very unlikeness of the members would have terrified the one taken up. And a part of the hair is seized, because human nature cannot bear the grasping of the whole head. For 'lock' the Seventy translated κράσπεδον, that is, 'fringe', of which the one is usually taken of hair, the other of garments.

And the spirit lifted me up between earth and heaven. First he is seized by the likeness of a hand; afterwards he is lifted up by the spirit, and the spirit does not raise him at once to heaven, but between earth and heaven, so that, leaving earthly things behind for the time being, he may hasten toward heaven. We can also say this: that the prophet was seized by the likeness of God's hand on account of good works, and is lifted up by the spirit on account of the knowledge of spiritual things.

And he brought me to Jerusalem, in the vision of God, near the inner door that looked toward the north, where the idol of jealousy had been set up to provoke rivalry. And behold, there was the glory of the God of Israel, according to the vision that I had seen in the plain. (LXX: "And he brought me into Jerusalem, in the vision of God, to the vestibule of the gate that looks toward the north, where was the statue of the possessor." But this, which is found in certain codices, ※ And in the statue the image of jealousy: has been added from Theodotion. The rest likewise.) When he says: He brought me to Jerusalem in the vision of God, he shows that he was carried over not in the body, but in the spirit. According to this kind of vision we too can behold both the heavens and the depths of the sea and the lower regions, while we embrace in thought the principles of each. […]

8:4.t: And the glory of the God of Israel was there, not because it took delight in such a neighbor, but so that by its presence it might destroy the idol of jealousy and the temple; hence the overthrow of the city and of the temple also follows after a short time; and it is written in Isaiah that a narrow bed can by no means hold two, and a short cloak cannot cover both, Scripture signifying that saying of the Apostle: What agreement has Christ with Belial? The temple of God with an idol?

8:5.t: And he said to me: Son of man, lift up your eyes toward the way of the north. And I lifted up my eyes toward the way of the north, and behold, to the north of the gate of the altar, the idol of jealousy in the very entrance. (Where we have put: To the north of the gate of the altar, the idol of jealousy in the very entrance, the Seventy translated: From the north toward the eastern gate, which is not found in the Hebrew, leaving out the other things which are written there.) 'He said to me,' he says, '(either the glory of God which I had seen in the plain, or the spirit which lifted me up between heaven and earth), and he spoke to me after he had carried me over into Jerusalem and made me see either the city or the temple, and he commanded me to lift up my eyes toward the way of the north; for there the statue of Baal had been set, which he calls the idol of jealousy, in the very entrance of the gate'. […]

8:6.t: And he said to me: Son of man, do you think you see what these are doing, the great abominations which the house of Israel is doing here, so that I should withdraw far from my sanctuary? And turning again you will see greater abominations. 'Lest you think,' he says, 'that I abandon the temple unjustly and leave the city to be overthrown, look at what they do in the temple; and when you have beheld those things, do not think that this is the end of their crimes: you will behold still greater things'. This can indeed also be understood of our Jerusalem and our temple, when, after the example of Hophni and Phinehas, we work the crimes of idols in the tabernacle of God, and commit fornication with those women who have vowed themselves to the warfare and ministry of God, and pluck off the first portions of his sacrifices, giving them for the use of clients and servants, and do everything for the sake of gain. […]

8:7.t: And he brought me in to the door of the court, and I saw, and behold, one hole in the wall; and he said to me: Son of man, dig through the wall; and when I had dug through the wall, one door appeared. And he said to me: Go in, and see the most wicked abominations which these are doing here. (This which I translated: And I saw, and behold, one hole in the wall, is not found in the Seventy.) And because everything is shown as if in an image and a painting, he says that he saw one hole in the wall, and that he was ordered to dig it through and make it larger, so that, the hole having been opened, he might enter more widely and see what he could not see while placed outside. By this it is shown that, in the churches as well as in each of us individually, greater vices are revealed through small ones, and that through certain holes, as it were, one arrives at the greatest abominations: for by the fruits the tree is known, and out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. […]

8:10.t: And I went in and saw, and behold, every likeness of creeping things and of animals, an abomination, and all the idols of the house of Israel were painted on the wall round about, throughout. Not only did the idol of jealousy stand at the entrance of the north gate, but all the walls of the temple too were painted with various images of idols, so that there was no beast which the painting on the wall did not show. This we see to this day in the shrines of idols and the temples of the Gentiles: that a foolish religion worships every kind of beast; whence Vergil too: And of every sort, he says, of gods the monsters and barking Anubis — as if those which he praises were not monsters too —, against Neptune and Venus and against Minerva. […]

8:11.t: And seventy men of the elders of the house of Israel, and Jaazaniah son of Shaphan was standing in the midst of them, who were standing before the paintings, and each one had a censer in his hand, and a vapor of cloud was rising up from the incense. When he says that there were seventy men of the elders of the house of Israel who held censers in their hands, he shows that there were many other presbyters too who were not doing this, but were perhaps held fast by other sins, and that one, Jaazaniah son of Shaphan by name, stood in their midst, as the prince of the crime and sacrilege of those who, having abandoned the worship of God, were worshiping idols, and in the temple were adoring not God, whose temple it was, but the paintings on the walls. […]

8:12.t: And he said to me: Surely you see, son of man, what the elders of the house of Israel are doing in the darkness, each one in the secret of his bedchamber; for they say: The Lord does not see us, the Lord has forsaken the earth. 'From what they do in the temple when gathered together,' he says, 'it is shown what each one does in his own chamber'. But according to the ἀναγωγὴν [anagogy, the higher sense] it can better be understood that some princes of the churches do in darkness things which are shameful even to speak of. This is the hidden man of the heart, of whom it is said: Enter into your chamber, and again: He who sees in secret will repay you. […]

8:14.t: And he said to me: Turning again you will see greater abominations which these are doing. And he brought me in through the door of the gate of the house of the Lord which looked toward the north, and behold, women were sitting lamenting Adonis. What we have translated 'Adonis', both the Hebrew and the Syriac language call 'thamuz'; hence, because according to the pagan fable the lover of Venus, a most beautiful youth, is said to have been slain in the month of July and afterwards to have come back to life, they call that same month of July by the same name and celebrate an annual festival for him, in which he is lamented by women as though dead, and afterwards, coming back to life, he is sung of and praised. And consistently, after it has been shown what the princes and elders of the house of Israel did in the temple and in darkness and in their chambers, the vices of the women too are described, who lament when deprived of the company of their lovers, and exult if they have been able to obtain them. […]

8:15.t: And since we read above, after the idol of jealousy which appeared at the north gate: Turning again you will see greater abominations, and, after the paintings of all the beasts had been shown along the wall, which the seventy presbyters and Jaazaniah son of Shaphan were adoring, holding censers in their hands, it is said a second time: Turning again you will see greater abominations which these are doing, because women were sitting lamenting Adonis, so after the third sin too it is said: Turning again you will see abominations greater than these. But what abomination is greater than the three preceding crimes? Clearly the fourth, which follows: And behold, at the door of the temple of the Lord, between the vestibule and the altar, about twenty-five men with their backs toward the temple of the Lord and their faces toward the east, and they were worshiping the rising of the sun, because, despising the Lord, that is, the Creator, they were adoring the sun, that is, the Lord's creature, although the Lord himself had […]

8:16.t: And he said to me: Surely you have seen, son of man; turning again you will see abominations greater than these. And he brought me into the inner court of the house of the Lord, and behold, at the door of the temple of the Lord, between the vestibule and the altar, about twenty-five men with their backs toward the temple of the Lord and their faces toward the east, and they were worshiping toward the rising of the sun. What we have translated 'vestibule' following Symmachus, who put πρόπυλον [gateway], where the Seventy and Theodotion translated the Hebrew word itself, 'aelam', Aquila's first edition translated προστάδα [porch] and the second the 'aelam' of the temple; this we can express as the 'portico' of the temple, or the unroofed 'court' which was between the temple and the altar.

8:17.t: And he said to me: Surely you have seen, son of man; is it a light thing to the house of Judah that they should do these abominations which they have done here, because, filling the earth with iniquity, they have turned to provoke me? And behold, they put the branch to their nostrils. (Where we said: And behold, they put the branch to their nostrils, the Seventy translated: And behold, they themselves like men sneering, to which there was added from Theodotion: They stretch out the branch, so that the whole together reads: And behold, they themselves stretch out the branch as if sneering, for which Symmachus translated: As if sending out a sound in the likeness of a song through his nostrils.) […]

8:18.t: Therefore I too will act in fury: my eye will not spare, nor will I have mercy, (and what follows:) and when they cry to my ears with a loud voice, I will not hear them (is not found in the Seventy). 'For all these things,' he says, 'which they have done, I too will act in fury and my eye will not spare, nor will I have mercy'. Hearing this, the heretics of old slander the Creator as cruel and bloodthirsty, and do not consider that the apostle Paul, who is surely the apostle of the good God — as they themselves would have it —, writes to the Corinthians: If I come again I will not spare, so as to chastise offenders with the rod and draw back the erring to salvation; for those who do not understand what is profitable for them, and often pray for contrary things, it is expedient that they not be heard by the Lord. Hence in the prayer too we say: Your will be done; not our will, which is accustomed to err, but your will, which knows the things to come; […]

9:1.t: And he cried in my ears with a loud voice, saying: The visitations of the city have drawn near. For 'visitations' the Seventy translated 'vengeance': for Mine indeed is vengeance, and I will repay, says the Lord, and every vengeance is a visitation, as of one who is sick, as of one who has wounds, as of one who awaits the hands of physicians, according to what is written elsewhere: I will visit their iniquities with the rod, and their sins with scourges; but my mercy I will not take away from them. And rightly, as we said above, visitation or vengeance is said to draw near, with the captivity close at hand.

And each one has a vessel of slaughter in his hand. He did not say 'had', as the Seventy translated, for he is not narrating things past, but shows things present and future. Whoever, therefore, strikes the wicked in that they are wicked, and has vessels of slaughter to kill the worst, is a minister of the Lord.

9:2.t: And behold, six men were coming from the way of the upper gate which looks toward the north, and each one a vessel of destruction in his hand; and one man in their midst clothed in linen, and a writer's inkhorn at his reins; and they went in and stood beside the bronze altar. And the glory of the Lord of Israel was taken up from the Cherub over whom it was, to the threshold of the house; and he called the man who was clothed in linen and had a writer's inkhorn at his loins. For 'linen', which we translated following Symmachus, the Seventy translated ποδήρη [a robe reaching to the feet], Theodotion the Hebrew word itself, 'baddim', Aquila 'choice things'; again, where we said: And a writer's inkhorn at his reins, the Seventy put: And a sapphire girdle upon his reins, Theodotion: Κάστυ [inkhorn] of the scribe in his hand, Aquila: Μελανοδοχεῖον (that is, Inkhorn) of the scribe at his loins, Symmachus: He had a writer's tablets at his reins; […]

Some interpret the six men as six angels who obey the will of God, and understand that one, who had the high priest's garments, as the Savior, according to the fact that the angel of great counsel is a priest, and to what is said: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. Now ποδήρη, which the Seventy translated, is one of the eight garments of the high priest, which in Latin is called 'talaris' [ankle-length]; and from the fact that it comes down to the feet, it was allotted this name — I know that many years ago I published a book on the vesture of the high priest, to whose explanation I send the reader, for I cannot say everything in every place —. And as to what Aquila's first edition and Theodotion called κάστυ, for which in the Hebrew one reads 'cesath': when I asked a Hebrew what it meant, he answered me 'that in the Greek tongue it is called καλαμάριον [pen-case], from the fact that pens are stored in it'; we say 'atramentarium' [inkhorn], from the fact that it holds atramentum [ink]; […]

9:3.t: The glory of the Lord of Israel also went up, or was taken up, from the one Cherub, and went to the threshold, or to the open-air part of the court of the house and of the vestibule, which is in no way pressed down by a roof but enjoys the freedom of the air. This very glory of the Lord called the man who was in the attire of a high priest and had the inkhorn at his loins, and said what Scripture attests.

9:4.t: God says that only those can escape who have been reborn and signed with the sign of Christ; when sending his angels to lay waste the world and to destroy the human race he threatens more seriously than the last time.… This sign pertains to the passion and blood of Christ and that he is kept safe and unharmed whoever is found in this sign.
9:4.s: Treatise V. An Address to Demetrianus 22

9:4.t: Thus he suffers and is dishonoured; and although he still ventures with shameless confidence to disguise himself, yet now, wretched spirit, he is detected the rather by them that bear the Sign on their foreheads; yea, more, he is rejected of them, and is humbled, and put to shame. For even if, now that he is a creeping serpent, he shall transform himself into an angel of light, yet his deception will not profit him; for we have been taught that `though an angel from heaven preach unto us any other gospel than that we have received, he is anathema.'
9:4.s: LETTER TO THE BISHOPS OF EGYPT 1:2

9:4.t: And I have heard many, after such experience, blame themselves, and say, What advantage is it that I have grieved? I have not recovered my money, and I have injured myself. But if thou hast grieved on account of sin, thou hast blotted it out, and hast reaped the greatest pleasure. If thou hast grieved for thy brethren who have fallen, thou hast both encouraged and comforted thyself, and hast also restored them; and even if thou wert not to profit them, thou hast an abundant recompense. And that thou mayest learn that this grieving for those who have fallen, though we should not at all benefit them, still brings us a large reward, hear what Ezekiel says; or rather, what God Himself speaks through him. For when He had sent certain messengers to overturn the city, and to consume all the dwellings with sword and fire, along with their inhabitants, He thus charges one of them: "Set a mark upon the forehead of the men that groan, and are in anguish." […]

And the Lord said to him: Pass through the midst of the city, in the midst of Jerusalem, and mark a tau upon the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve over all the abominations that are done in its midst. And to those he said, in my hearing: Pass through the city following him, strike; let your eye not spare, nor have pity: old man, youth and virgin, little child and women, kill to utter destruction; anyone upon whom you see the tau, do not kill, and begin from my sanctuary. He who was clothed in an ankle-length garment, or a linen one, and displayed priestly attire, is commanded to put a sign upon the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve over all the abominations that are done in the midst of Jerusalem. For 'sign', which the Seventy, Aquila and Symmachus translated, Theodotion put the Hebrew itself, 'tau', which among the Hebrews is the last of the twenty-two letters, so as to show perfect knowledge in the men who groan and grieve; […]

9:5.t: And the six men are commanded, apart from those who can say: The light of your countenance has been signed upon us, O Lord, to kill all: to spare not the old man, not the young man, not the virgin, not the little child, not the woman — according to the mystical senses, the old men are those in the Church of whom it is said: A man's gray hairs are his prudence; the young men, those who are most ready for the battles of faith; the virgins, those who keep chastity with their whole mind; the little children, those who are given the milk of infancy to drink and do not yet take solid food; the women, those who attest the frailty of their sex by the weakness of their soul — ; none of whom is spared if they believe themselves to be anything apart from the seal of Christ.

9:6.t: And what follows: And begin from my sanctuary (or, as the Seventy translated: And begin from my holy ones) signifies either the priests who busied themselves in the temple and worshiped idols, or those who, by the merit of their priesthood, were called holy among the people and who had been the cause of sin among the peoples, and these were the first to deserve punishment: for it is time for judgment to begin from the house of God.

You who are first in riches will be the first to bear the yoke of captivity, according to what is written in Ezekiel: Begin from my sanctuary. Not from the saints, as most people think, but from the overthrow of the temple, which was holy.

They began, therefore, with the elder men who were before the face of the house. And he said to them: Defile the house and fill the courts with the slain. For 'courts', which in Hebrew are called 'aseroth', the Seventy put 'ways'. Now the elder men are slain, of whom we read above that they had censers and burned incense to idols. Nor is there any sanctity of the temple left, because, the God of religion having been offended, all things have been defiled, so that whence came the sin, thence may come the judgment. And the courts in the temple are filled with corpses, and not the ways, which surely were outside, unless perhaps we can understand the ways as the streets of the city. Nor could the angels have dared to defile with the blood of the dead the temple in which the glory of God had formerly dwelt, had not the Lord of the departing glory commanded this. Everyone who is dead through sin defiles the courts of the temple and the ways of the city of the Lord in which he lives; […]

I return to what I was saying before: Why then did distress and destruction hit the house of Eli the priest, the righteous old man, a priest and a judge of Israel during forty years? Was it not because of Pinehas and Hophni his sons who treated the women scornfully that came to pray in the tabernacle, though he himself did not sin, at any rate not wilfully, but only in so far as he was silent and reprehended with words only, without showing fervour against the fornication of his sons, so that the judgment of the Lord took revenge on them? And lest any one should think that the Lord shows His zeal only against those who are sinners in their lifetime, He also displays it against this audacious sin hated of Him, in the case of those who are near to Him, His priests and judges and the heads of the people and against those men who were holy unto Him and by whose hands He had done wonderful things, yet whom, when they violated the laws He had laid down, He did not spare. […]

9:7.t: And they went out, and struck those who were in the city. (Or, as others translated: They struck the city, naming the city itself in place of those who were in the city.)

9:8.t: And when the slaughter was complete, I remained, and I fell upon my face and, crying out, I say: Alas, Lord God; will you then destroy all the remnant of Israel, pouring out your fury upon Jerusalem? When all who did not have the seal had been laid low in the slaughter, the prophet fell on his face, thinking, because of the multitude of the slain, that no one but himself had remained. Because this seemed to be contrary to the sentence by which the Lord had ordered that the men with signed foreheads were not to be slain, it was for that reason removed in the common edition; but we, following the Hebrew truth, have put: I remained; […]

9:9.t: And he said to me: The iniquity of the house of Israel and of Judah is great, exceedingly, very much; and the land is filled with bloods, and the city is filled with turning away. For they said: The Lord has forsaken the land, and: The Lord does not see; therefore my eye too will not spare, nor will I have pity: I will repay their ways upon their head. The Lord, seeing his prophet weep for the people and marvel at the greatness of the indignation, gives the reasons, not, as he thought, of a punishment unjust or exceeding measure, but of a deserved and just sentence: 'The iniquity,' he says, 'of the ten tribes of Israel and of the two tribes of Judah is great, and not only great but exceedingly great'; nor was it enough to have said this, but he added 'very much', so that the greatness of the punishment might match the greatness of the iniquity. […]

9:10.t: Since, therefore, they thought either that there was no providence, or that the providence which had formerly been among the peoples had at this time abandoned its own people, for that reason God's eye too will not spare, nor will he have pity: so that, raging against vices, he may be placable to virtues, and may repay their ways and sins upon their heads, either upon the ruling part of the heart or upon the princes of the people, according to the book of Numbers, in which the heads of the peoples are said to be princes.

9:11.t: And behold, the man who was clothed in linen, who had the inkhorn at his loins, answered, saying: I have done as you commanded me. (LXX: "And behold, the man who was clothed in a podere — that is, an ankle-length garment —, and girded as to his loins with a girdle, and he answered a word, saying: I have done as you charged me.") He is the man who was ordered to pass through the midst of Jerusalem and to put a sign on the foreheads of the men groaning and grieving over all their iniquities. He says, therefore, that he has fulfilled the Lord's commands and has armed the foreheads of those who mourn with the seal of the letter 'tau'. But the six men, whom the Lord had commanded, saying: Pass through the midst of the city following him, and strike; and have pity on no one, to utter destruction, report nothing of the kind; for to carry out a sentence that is proved not by word but by deed is a matter not of gladness but of grief. […]

10:1.t: And I looked, and behold, in the firmament that was above the head of the Cherubim, as it were a sapphire stone, as it were the appearance of the likeness of a throne appeared above it. And he spoke to the man who was clothed in linen, and said: Go in into the midst of the wheels that are beneath the Cherub, and fill your hands with coals of fire that are between the Cherubim, and pour them out upon the city. Concerning the firmament that was above the Cherub, and the sapphire stone that had the likeness of a throne, and the wheels that followed the living creatures, let it suffice to have spoken above, and let the reader be content with the explanation of those things.

10:2.t: But now, as for the command given to the man who was clothed in linen — for which the Seventy in this place translated 'robe' — that he should take coals of fire from the midst of the Cherubim and pour them out, or scatter them, upon the city, it seems to me to show this: that after the slaying and slaughter of many, and the corpses of the dead in the streets, coals of fire are taken up to purge, or cleanse, Jerusalem, according to what is written in Isaiah: He will sanctify him in burning fire, and will devour the material like hay. These are the coals which, as a remedy for the tongue and for lying, laying waste vices and sins, the prophet, when questioned, longs for: What shall be given to you, and what shall be added to you against a deceitful tongue? The sharp arrows of the mighty, with desolating coals; and we shall be able to find many things of this kind in the holy Scriptures, of which we have often spoken. […]

And he went in in my sight. Now the Cherubim were standing on the right side of the house when the man went in, and a cloud filled the inner court. And the glory of the Lord was lifted up from above the Cherub to the threshold of the house, and the house was filled with the cloud, and the court was filled with the brightness of the glory of the Lord. And the sound of the wings of the Cherubim was heard as far as the outer court, like the voice of God almighty speaking. And when he had commanded the man who was clothed in linen, saying: Take fire from the midst of the wheels that are between the Cherubim, he went in and stood beside the wheel; and a Cherub stretched out his hand from the midst of the Cherubim to the fire that was between the Cherubim, and took it, and gave it into the hand of him who was clothed in linen; who, receiving it, went out. And there appeared in the Cherubim the likeness of a man's hand beneath their wings. […]

10:3.t: Now as the man who was clothed in linen garments went in, the Cherubim were standing on the right side of the house, so that the holy powers on high might be seen to hold the right-hand part of the house of God, and those that are sent for punishments — of whom it is written: A sending through most evil angels — may be believed to occupy the left-hand parts. And when the glory of the Lord had been lifted up from the Cherub who was about to hand the coals of fire to the man, and had passed over to the threshold of the house, at once the inner court is filled with cloud, darkness and gloom; for punishments are not carried out while the majesty of the Lord is present, and the glory of the Lord is seen in the court, of which it is written: The sound of the wings of the Cherubim was heard as far as the outer court. […]

10:5.t: The prophet Ezekiel clearly declares that "cherubim" is the name of the angelic powers that he describes as having appeared to him with wings, according to the pattern in which they are ordered to be deployed here.

10:6.t: And he goes in, as is said a second time, into the midst of the wheels that are beneath the Cherubim, to fill his hands with coals of fire. When he had gone in, he only stood beside the wheel and, stunned either by sorrow for Jerusalem that was to be punished or by the greatness of the glory, did not himself put his hand to the fire; but one of the Cherubim, that is, a Cherub, put out his hand and took the fire that was in the midst of the Cherubim and gave it into the hand of him who was clothed in linen garments; who, receiving it, went out; and yet Scripture does not say what he did when he had gone out, so as to leave the narration of a sad event to our understanding rather than set it before our eyes.

10:8.t: Note, reader, in what points the former vision and this one agree or disagree, so that from the comparison of the two, without any prompting from us, you may understand the divine mysteries; note also what I pointed out before: how in the firmament, and in the throne, and in the hand of a man, not the reality but the likeness is spoken of; for we do not contemplate the glory of the Lord face to face with unveiled countenance, but we see all things in likeness and image, as long as we are encompassed by a frail and corruptible body.

10:9.t: And I looked, and behold, four wheels beside the Cherubim; one wheel beside one Cherub, and another wheel beside one Cherub, and the appearance of the wheels was like the sight of a chrysolite stone, and their aspect was one likeness for the four, as if a wheel were in the midst of a wheel. And when they went in four directions, they went and did not turn back as they went, but to the place to which the first one turned to go, the others also followed and did not turn about. And their whole body and necks and hands and wings and rims were full of eyes round about the four wheels; and these wheels he called whirling, in my hearing. Now one had four faces: the one face the face of a Cherub, and the second face the face of a man, and in the third the face of a lion, and in the fourth the face of an eagle. And the Cherubim were lifted up. […]

10:12.t: And again, where we rendered: And their whole 'body', with 'of the wheels' understood, in the Hebrew it is written: And all their 'fleshes', and necks and hands and wings and rims; note that flesh is spoken of in the heavenly powers, so that, when we read: Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God, nor corruption incorruption, we may know that not the substance of the flesh but its works are condemned: for 'basar', which is written in this place, signifies not 'body' but 'flesh'. Now by the rims of the wheels he meant the iron tires by which the roundness of the wood is bound and held tight.
