'Because I spread my cloak, or my wings, over you and covered your confusion, therefore I swore to you and entered into a pact, or covenant, with you, so that you might be joined to me rather than to the others who wished to turn aside to you' — according to that: The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek; for an oath is the end of every dispute, and: As I live, says the Lord, 'I would rather have the repentance of the sinner than his death' —. At the time of the nuptials, then, Israel received the oath of God in place of every dowry gift — and because David had said of himself: Remember, O Lord, David and all his meekness, who swore to the Lord, vowed a vow to the God of Jacob, the Lord himself also swears to him, as Scripture says: The Lord has sworn truth to David, and will not frustrate him.

And you became mine. And I washed you with water, and cleansed your blood from you, and anointed you with oil. 'Because I spread my wings and covered your disgrace and swore to you and entered into a pact with you, therefore you have become my possession, so that you, who were another's when you were seen unclean, began to be mine when I confirmed my pact with you by an oath', or, according to the custom of the prophets: 'You became mine', he says, 'stands for: you were joined to me in marriage; and I washed you', he says, 'with the water of saving baptism': Unless, indeed, one is reborn of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God; and elsewhere we read: He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire, of which baptism Isaiah too speaks, saying: The Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and will cleanse the blood from their midst, by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning. […]

16:10.t: And I clothed you in parti-colored garments. (LXX: "And I dressed you in varied garments.") In the ceremonies of the Law, so that, occupied in the study of them, you would forsake idols. These are the varied garments with which Joseph was clothed, and his brothers could not sell him until they had first stripped him of the variety of his tunic; and of the bride it is said in Psalm 44 (45): The queen stood at your right hand in gilded clothing, surrounded with variety; this is the garment of which the Apostle too speaks: Having put on the new man, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of the Creator. Do we want to know what the varied garments are? Let the same Apostle teach us, writing to believers: Put on therefore the bowels of mercy, of goodness, of humility, of meekness, of patience — what is more beautiful than this variety? […]

And I shod you with violet. (LXX: "And I shod you with hyacinth.") Aquila and Symmachus translated 'violet', the Seventy and Theodotion 'hyacinthine', for which in the Hebrew is written 'thas'. And beautifully, because the discourse is directed to Jerusalem and, under the person of a woman, all her adornment is set out, ὑακίνθινα [hyacinth-colored] or ἰάνθινα [violet] shoes are spoken of, which do not suit the person of men — indeed, those who are to keep the Passover are commanded, without any variety of color, to have their loins girded and their feet shod; these are the shoes of which the Apostle writes: Feet shod in the preparation of the Gospel of peace; Philo, the most eloquent man among the Jews, compares the ὑάκινθον [hyacinth] in the vestments of the high priest to the air, by which he thinks the higher and heavenly things are signified —. […]

And I girded you with fine linen. Jerusalem is not only clothed in parti-colored garments and shod with ὑακίνθινις, but is also girded with fine linen, from which the finest threads are woven in the vestment of the high priest; and the wife in Proverbs, who wove two cloaks for her husband, of the present age and of the future, is said to have made garments for herself of fine linen and purple. With this fine linen the reins are girded whenever the rich incitements of lust are to be thinned, and nothing of gross moisture is left in them, and we fulfill the precept of the Apostle, who says: Stand therefore with your loins girded in truth — as though he said in other words 'with fine linen' —. And the Lord says to the apostles: Let your loins be girded, and lamps in your hands: for unless we bind up the flowing humors of the loins, we cannot have lamps in our hands; whence God also says to Job: Gird up your loins like a man. […]

And I clothed you with fine stuffs. (LXX: "And I surrounded you with trichaptum.") For which Aquila put 'flowery' or 'palpable', Symmachus 'garment', Theodotion the Hebrew word itself, 'messe'; and when I was diligently inquiring what the word 'trichaptum', which the Seventy translated, meant, and could find from none of the Greeks either the usage or the ἐτυμολογίαν [etymology] of the word, at last I learned that it was coined by the Seventy — for new names must be fixed to new things —, because the garment was of such fineness that it was believed to have the thinness of hairs and of the hair of the head; whence I too, wishing to express the thinness of the garment, translated 'subtilibus' [fine stuffs] for 'trichapto', because it was woven with fine warp and weft. And fittingly, to those whom he had rebuked, saying: The heart of this people has grown fat, and Jacob ate and drank and was filled and grew fat, and the beloved kicked and forsook God his maker, fineness of garments is now granted; […]

16:11.t: It is true that a festival such as the birthday of Peter should be seasoned with more gladness than usual; still our merriment must not forget the limit set by Scripture, and we must not stray too far from the boundary of our wrestling ground. Your presents, indeed, remind me of the sacred volume, for in it Ezekiel decks Jerusalem with bracelets.

And I adorned you with adornment. Here he sets down the adornments in general, which in what follows he enumerates one by one: bracelets and torque, earrings and crown, and the rest, which adornments he bestowed on Jerusalem, and in Isaiah it is said that by her own fault she lost them all: for it is written: Because the daughters of Jerusalem were lifted up (that is, were proud) and walked with lofty neck, and the rest: instead of a girdle they were girded with ropes, and instead of the adornment of the head disfigured with baldness, and instead of beautiful and soft clothes surrounded with the roughness of sackcloth.

And I put bracelets on your hands. (LXX: "And I surrounded your hands with bracelets.") When God gives us good works, he puts bracelets around our hands. Whence also he says that he was likened in the hands of the prophets, and we frequently read that the word came in the hand of Haggai or Jeremiah and the others; in Job too the lip of the dragon is pierced with a bracelet, and all his venomous hissings, which are understood in perverse dogmas, are pierced by the ring of good works.

And a torque around your neck. For 'torque', which we translated following the second edition of Aquila and Symmachus, the Seventy and Theodotion translated κάθεμα [pendant] — which is written not only here but also in Isaiah: The Lord will take away the glory of their garment, and the little lamprey-chains and the clusters and the rings, and the κάθεμα —; and I think that by κάθεμα they meant a necklace of various gems descending onto the breast of women, which itself too is a most beautiful adornment of women.

16:12.t: And I gave an earring over the mouth (or your nostrils). The Hebrew word 'nezem', except for Symmachus, who translated ἐπιρρίνιον [nose-ring], all translated 'earring', not that earrings are put in the nostrils — they are called 'inaures' [earrings] from the fact that they hang from the ears [aures] —, but that a ring, made in the likeness of earrings, is called by the same word; and to this day, among the other adornments of women, golden rings are wont to hang from the forehead over the mouth and to overhang the nostrils. These we receive according to mystical understanding when with the Apostle we can say: We are the good odor of Christ in those who are being saved, and in those who perish: to some an odor of death unto death, to others an odor of life unto life; when we live and it can be said of us: The dead shall not praise you, O Lord, but we the living, then God smells the odor of our sacrifice of good fragrance, and we have the golden ring of divine senses and dogmas in our nostrils; […]

And rings for your ears. (LXX: "And little wheels upon your ears.") He who stops his ears so as not to hear the judgment of blood, and hedges them with thorns so as not to become a partaker with the envious and the detractors — of whom it is written: Do not mingle with detractors; for their destruction will come suddenly, and who knows the ruin of both? —, namely both of him who detracts and of him who gladly listens, this man has rings and little wheels in his ears — not the wheels which follow the Cherubim: for that belongs to the evangelical powers, but little wheels, in the diminutive —, which befit human frailty. Therefore it is also said to God: The voice of your thunder in the wheel: for in those who pass over earthly things and touch the earth with scarcely the slightest footprints — of whom it is written: Holy stones are rolled upon the earth —, the voice of the Lord's thunder and of lofty dogmas resounds; […]

And a crown of beauty on your head. (LXX: "And a crown of boasting upon your head.") We translated 'beauty' following Symmachus, for the elegance of the sense; otherwise both in the Hebrew, 'thopherth', and in the other translators, καύχησις, it is called 'boasting'. The other adornments belong to individual members; the adornment of the head is the dignity of the whole body; and he calls crown the diadem of women, by which the abundance of the hair is bound and adorned. Do we want to know what the crown of beauty on the head of Jerusalem is? Let us unroll Exodus, in which it is written: And he made a plate of gold, and wrote on it letters formed with the seal of the sanctification of the Lord, and put it upon the head of Aaron; […]

16:13.t: And you were adorned with gold and silver. We have often said that gold pertains to the mind, silver to speech. And may the Lord grant us that we may deserve to receive the divine sense and wisdom, and to bring forth with grace of eloquence what we conceive in the mind, and by no means to make idols of these, as the heretics do, of whom it is written: I gave them silver and gold; but they made Baal of the silver and gold. And this, according to the spiritual understanding, is the more fitting for the adornment of women; otherwise silver, the cheaper material, is the adornment of country women and of poor women and maidservants, which does not befit Jerusalem, who is said to have advanced to be queen.

And you were clothed with fine linen and many-threaded stuff and many colors. (LXX: "And your cloaks of fine linen and trichapta and variegated things.") The Hebrew word 'mesi' Theodotion here too set down as it stands, as above, Aquila ἄνθινον [flowered], Symmachus 'polymitum' [many-threaded], and we, what above we called 'subtile' [fine], here, following Symmachus, called 'polymitum'; the Seventy translated 'trichapta', keeping their former interpretation, so as to show garments fine like hairs. Now the whole adornment of women is described: that she is washed, that she is cleansed, that she is anointed with oil, and is clothed in parti-colored garments, is shod with ὑακίνθινις, is girded with fine linen, is clothed with trichapta or fine stuffs, receives bracelets, and the golden torque, rings hanging over the mouth, and little wheels in the ears, a diadem on the head, is decorated with gold and silver — although silver is the cheaper material —, and after all this there is added: You were clothed with fine linen […]

Fine flour and honey and oil you ate, and you became beautiful greatly, exceedingly. After the clothing he takes care of food, that Jerusalem may eat fine flour and honey and oil, either separately, as many reckon, or, by a mixture of the three, a sweeter bread, the bread which came down from heaven; and under three names, as some think, it indicates the mystery of the Trinity, not that there is one substance and another, but that by the diverse names of fine flour and honey and oil the one sweetness of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit is shown. And this is to be noted, that in many sacrifices fine flour is offered, the marrow of the wheat and the purest, of which it is written: And he satisfied them with the fat of wheat, not of barley nor of meal, which is offered only when a husband is moved by a spirit of jealousy. […]

And you advanced to a kingdom. — This is not found in the Seventy, who perhaps, translating the Scriptures at Alexandria from the Hebrew truth into the Greek language, feared to publish it, lest they seem to offend the king of Egypt by recording that a kingdom was owed to Jerusalem by God; although the learned prove that only the five books of Moses were translated by them. — After manifold adornment, then, after the crown, after the abundance of gold and silver, after the most beautiful garments and mantles, after incredible beauty, she advances to be queen, because she is the city of the great king, of whom it is written: O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king's son; and in the Revelation of John Jerusalem is described as a bride adorned and arrayed for her husband; in the Psalms also it is said of her: The queen stood at your right hand in gilded clothing, surrounded with variety. […]

16:14.t: In Ezekiel, God speaks to Jerusalem: "You were perfect through my beauty." And this is the meaning of the text: "You were not perfect through your own works or through your own knowledge and the boasting of your heart but through my beauty, which I had put on you freely through my mercy."

And your name went forth among the nations because of your fairness; for you were perfect in my beauty, which I set upon you, says the Lord God. (LXX: "And your name went out among the nations in your fairness; which was made complete in loveliness, which I set upon you, says the Lord God.") Symmachus translated this passage more clearly: And your name went forth among the nations; which was perfect because of my dignity, which I had set upon you, says the Lord God. And the sense is: 'By my benefits and my incredible bounty you came to the title of queen, so that the talk of all the nations spoke of you, and you were perfect, not by your own merits and virtues but by my liberality': Unless, indeed, the Lord builds the house, they have labored in vain who build it. Unless the Lord guards the city, he has watched in vain who guards it; […]

But since often, when preaching is abundantly poured forth in fitting ways, the mind of the speaker is elevated in itself by a hidden delight in self-display, great care is needed that he may gnaw himself with the laceration of fear, lest he who recalls the diseases of others to health by remedies should himself swell through neglect of his own health; lest in helping others he desert himself, lest in lifting up others he fall. For to some the greatness of their virtue has often been the occasion of their perdition; causing them, while inordinately secure in confidence of strength, to die unexpectedly through negligence. For virtue strives with vices; the mind flatters itself with a certain delight in it; and it comes to pass that the soul of a well-doer casts aside the fear of its circumspection, and rests secure in self-confidence; and to it, now torpid, the cunning seducer enumerates all things that it has done well, and exalts it in swelling thoughts as though superexcellent beyond all beside. […]

16:15.t: And having confidence in your loveliness you fornicated in your name, and you laid out your fornication to everyone passing by, to become his. Great is the peril of trusting not in the clemency of God but in one's own beauty; and the more exalted anyone has been, the more he ought to fear lest he fall and fornicate in his own name. For the adverse powers despise ordinary foods and desire foreign nourishment; whence it is said of the devil: His foods are choice; he does not want to deceive just anyone: it is King Saul, who was chosen by the Lord, and Judas the apostle that he hastens to trip up. Let us not, therefore, trust in our own loveliness, nor think the liberality of God to be our own virtue, but rather let us hear: Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what the coming day may bring forth, and in another place: Brothers, if a man is overtaken in any sin, you who are spiritual, perfect such a one in a spirit of meekness, considering yourself, lest you too be tempted; […]

16:16.t: And taking some of your garments you made for yourself high places sewn together here and there; and you fornicated upon them, as has not been done nor will be. (LXX: "And you took some of your garments and made yourself idols sewn together; and you fornicated upon them, and you will not enter nor shall it be.") Symmachus translated this passage thus: And when you had taken some of your clothes, you made yourself many-colored high places; and you fornicated in them, things not done nor to be. For 'sewn together' and 'variegated' and 'high places' or 'idols', Aquila and Theodotion translated ἐμβολίσματα, which signifies 'diverse rags sewn together here and there' and 'an idol made like a plaster', as it were 'a πολύρραφον [much-stitched] garment'. 'I clothed you', he says, 'in variegated garments, and you were dressed in fine linen and many-threaded stuff and the variety of many forms; […]

16:17.t: And you took the vessels of your beauty, from my gold and from my silver which I gave you, and you made yourself male images, and you fornicated with them. According to the letter, the Lord commanded in the Law that there be made censers, bowls, a lampstand, the ark of the Covenant: all either of gold or gilded, and others of silver, all of which Jerusalem melted down and turned into idols of Bel or Baal, Chemosh, Ashtaroth and Milcom. According to the spiritual understanding, we make idols of the gold and silver of the holy Scriptures when we corrupt the grace of sense and eloquence by heretical depravity, and set our mouth in heaven, and our tongue passes through the earth; and male images is the name given to those in which every heresy fornicates, from the fact that each one thinks that what he worships and holds, which he has fashioned, is most robust and cannot be overthrown by any assault; […]

16:18.t: And you took your many-colored garments, and covered them. 'The male images' is understood, so that she turned all the finery she had received for use into blasphemy. And we do this whenever we surround heretical depravity with prudence, temperance, fortitude, righteousness and all the virtues and, under their pretext, deceive all the simple, so that, seeing the honey of the virtues, they do not beware of the poisons of the vices.

And my oil and my perfume you set before them. And my bread (or, as the Seventy translated, my loaves which I gave you), fine flour, honey and oil with which I nourished you, you set in their sight for an odor of sweetness. The oil of which we spoke above, and the perfume or incense of which the psalmist cries out: Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight, and the loaves of proposition which we are commanded to offer to God, the fine flour too, the purest sense of the Scriptures, and the honey which Jonathan tasted, and his eyes were opened and he was strengthened, wretched Jerusalem set in the sight of the idols — or before the male images —, that they might be for an odor of sweetness to them, things which by their nature are sweet and most delightful but, when they are offered to idols and false doctrines, are turned into bitterness.

16:20.t: And it came to pass, says the Lord God. And you took your sons and your daughters whom you bore to me, and you sacrificed them to them to be devoured — is your fornication a small thing, that you sacrificed my sons? —, you gave them up, consecrating them to them. And after all your abominations and fornications, you did not remember the days of your youth, when you were naked and full of shame, trampled in your blood. (LXX: "And it came to pass, says Adonai the Lord. And you took your sons and your daughters whom you bore, and you sacrificed them to them for consumption, as though you had committed little fornication, and you killed your sons and gave them up when you offered them to them. This over and above all your fornication and your abominations; and you did not remember the day of your infancy, when you were naked and disgraced, you lived mingled in your blood.") […]

16:23.t: For what saith He? "An evil and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign." Now what He saith is to this effect: What marvel if ye behave so to me who have been hitherto unknown to you when even to the Father, of whom ye have had so much experience, ye have done the very same? forsaking Him, ye have run unto the devils, drawing to yourselves wicked lovers. With this Ezekiel too was continually upbraiding them.
16:23.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 43:1

16:23.t: To our Jerusalem too, whether the Church or the souls of believers, if they have been negligent and have lain open to all vices, a twofold word of cursing is addressed, so that they hear: Woe, woe to you, says the Lord God, according to what is written in the Revelation of John: Woe upon all the inhabitants of the earth. For if a holy man says: I am a stranger and a sojourner, as all my fathers were, why should not the sinner be said to be an inhabitant of the earth?

And it happened after all your wickedness, woe, woe to you, says the Lord God, and you built yourself a brothel, and you made yourself a place of prostitution in all the streets; at every head of the way you built the sign of your prostitution, and you made your beauty abominable, and you parted your feet to every passer-by, and you multiplied your fornications. And you committed fornication with the sons of Egypt, your neighbors, of great flesh, and you multiplied your fornication to provoke me. (LXX: "And it came to pass after all your wickednesses, ※ woe, woe to you, ⁚ says Adonai the Lord, and you built yourself a dwelling of fornication, and you made yourself prostitution in every street, and at the beginning of every way you built your fornications, and you corrupted your beauty, and you spread your legs to every passer-by, and you multiplied your fornication. […]

16:24.t: Now he builds himself a brothel who sins with complete brazenness of brow, according to what is written: The sinner, when he has come into the depth of impiety, despises. And he raises a very high place in all the streets: For wide and spacious is the way that leads to death.

What we have said once, and again and again, let it suffice to have said for good: that under the person of a woman who commits fornication after her husband's many benefits, the fornication of Jerusalem is described: how she withdrew from God and was joined to idols and was not content with hidden fornication, but built herself a brothel and in every way set up a sign for passers-by — that they might come to the harlot and sate their lust, not so much their own as hers who spread her legs to every passer-by —, and disfigured the greatness of her beauty by the greatness of her fornication; and among other things she prostrated herself to the Egyptians too, her neighbors, out of love for great flesh, and, to display every kind of foulness, was disfigured by a manifold kind of filth.

16:25.t: And he builds at every head of the way, so as to leave no kind of sin untried, but, imitating the harlot of Proverbs, openly in the streets and at the corners of the streets he invites the foolish young men passing by to his embraces, and defiles the beauty of the soul which he received as a gift from God the creator.

And all his ways are full of foulness, and to all the thoughts that supply the incitements of vices he opens his heart and spreads his legs, and he commits fornication with the Egyptians his neighbors, whose examples he follows, namely the heathens, who glory in their foulnesses, and he is so wicked as to surpass even them in foulness. And all this he does to provoke God to anger. Now the Egyptians are said to be of great flesh, either because of the greatness of their foulness or because of the deformity of their sins: hence the holy man is said to be of little flesh, which in him decreases daily and is thinned away by the virtues, so that it is no longer called flesh but spirit; and he says in the psalm: My soul has thirsted for you, O God, how manifoldly my flesh for you (or, as some copies have, how my flesh has been consumed), in a desert land, pathless and waterless, so in the holy place I have appeared to you; […]

16:26.t: Now no one doubts that Palestine is a neighbor of Egypt, since the Lord says to Abraham: I will give you all the land, from the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates, so that on one side it has the Egyptians, on the other the Assyrians, with whom too she is said further on to have committed fornication; and the fornication of Jerusalem with the Egyptians is the imitation of their idolatry.

16:27.t: Behold, I will stretch out my hand over you, and I will take away your justification, and I will give you up in the souls of those who hate you, of the Palestinian daughters, who blush at your wicked way. (LXX: "But if I stretch out my hand over you, and I will take away your ordinances, and I will give you into the souls of those who hate you, of the daughters of the foreigners, who made you turn aside from your way." And what follows: Ἠσέβησας, that is: You acted impiously, is fitted according to the Seventy to the following section, according to the others it is the end of the preceding one.) Now the Lord stretches out his hand over Jerusalem, to correct her in her sinning and to take away her ordinances, which, as long as she kept the precepts of God, were called the ordinances of the Lord, but when she worshiped idols and exchanged religion for impiety, are called her ordinances — which is to be understood not only of the law and the ceremonies, but also of the sabbaths and the feast days and the new moons: for […]

16:28.t: And you committed fornication with the sons of the Assyrians, because you had not yet been filled; and after you committed fornication, not even so were you satisfied. And you multiplied your fornication in the land of Canaan with the Chaldeans, and not even so were you satisfied. (LXX: "And you acted impiously, and you committed fornication with the sons of Assyria, and not even so were you satisfied; and you committed fornication, and you were not filled. And you multiplied your covenants toward the land of Canaan of the Chaldeans, and not even in these were you filled.") Above it was written that Jerusalem committed fornication with the sons of Egypt her neighbors, who are of great flesh; here the other neighborhood, that of the Assyrians, is indicated; and therefore they are handed over to both nations: because they venerated the images of both, and, entering Chaldea, which is the land of Canaan, they took on in exchange the errors of those to whose rule they were subject. […]

16:30.t: In what shall I cleanse your heart, says the Lord God, when you do all these works of a harlot and wanton woman? For you have built your brothel at the head of every way, and you have made your high place in every street; nor have you become like a harlot who increases her price by disdain. (LXX: "What shall I do to your heart, says Adonai the Lord, when you have done all these works of a fornicating and shameless woman? ÷ and you committed fornication threefold in your daughters ⁚ when you built your brothel at the beginning of every way, and made your base in every street; and you were not like a harlot gathering wages.") And what the Seventy said: And you committed fornication threefold in your daughters, is not found in the Hebrew, nor did any of the other translators put it. […]

And this which, as we said above, is not found in the Hebrew: You committed fornication threefold in your daughters, is said either to Jerusalem according to the letter: that she committed fornication in every way in her towns and villages, and no corner or street remained where she did not set up the signs of idolatry; or to the Church and to the believers who were deceived: who did not heed that word of the Apostle: May the God of peace himself sanctify you in all things, and may your spirit and soul and body be kept whole without complaint at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but committed fornication in every way, both in body and in spirit and in soul. We read in Proverbs: But you, describe them threefold, that you may answer words of truth which are proposed to you, and we are commanded to understand the utterances of truth, that is, the holy Scriptures, threefold: first, according to the letter; second, in a middle way, through tropology; third, more loftily, so that we may know all mystical things. […]

16:31.t: 'For your idolatry was committed not in secret but with full license, so that at all the beginnings of the ways and at the crossroads you set up altars, and made your base, or your high place, of which we spoke above, in every street; nor did you imitate the cunning harlots, who are accustomed to increase the price of lust by difficulty and thereby provoke their lovers the more to madness — according to the Seventy: You were not like a harlot gathering wages —, but you gave what you ought to have received, so that not even in this, that you committed fornication and followed demons, were you protected by their help, but, oppressed by various captivities, you felt your calamities'. […]

16:32.t: Your cruelty is a false faith. An heretical congregation is an adulteress woman; for the Catholic hath never from the beginning left the couch and the chamber of her Spouse, nor gone after other and strange lovers. Ye have painted a divorced form in new colours, ye have withdrawn your couch from the old wedlock, ye have left the body of a mother, the wife of One Husband, decking yourselves out with new arts of pleasing, new allurements of corruption.
16:32.s: Letter 3: Against the Treatise of the Novatians

16:32.t: But as an adulterous woman who brings in strangers over her husband. To all harlots wages are given, but you have given wages to all your lovers, and you made gifts to them that they might come in to you from every side to commit fornication with you. And it has happened in you contrary to the custom of women in your fornications, and after you there will be no fornication; for in that you gave wages and did not receive wages, the contrary has happened in you. (LXX: "An adulterous woman ÷ like you ⁚ receiving wages from her husband. To all who committed fornication with her she gave wages, and you gave wages to all your lovers, and you loaded them that they might come to you round about in your fornication. And there happened in you a perverse thing against women in your fornication, and after you they have not committed fornication; in that you gave wages and wages were not given to you, there also happened in you a perverse thing.") This which is written in the Seventy: Like you, is not found in the Hebrew; […]

Whatever we have said of Jerusalem, refer also to the Church and to the souls of believers, who give their marriage gifts — namely gold in understanding and silver in speech and the garments by which our foulness and disgrace are veiled — to their lovers, either to the contrary powers or to the teachers of perverse doctrines, when they assert that luxury does no harm, and that indiscriminate lust, according to the genitals of the body, demands intercourse by natural law, that all foods are to be used without distinction, since they were made for this, to be eaten, that prudence is necessary only in so far as it profits oneself, and that righteousness has no place, for if it prevailed one would have to beg, and other things of this kind; receiving which, wretched Jerusalem, in whom there ought to have been a vision of peace, turned the sharpness of her intellect and the charm of her eloquence to foulness; […]

16:33.t: And whereas all fornicating women are accustomed to receive wages from their lovers, Jerusalem did the contrary, giving rather than receiving; and to show the lavishness of her wages: She loaded them, he says, that they might come to her round about, lest there be any neighbor who was not mingled in her disgrace.

16:34.t: And indeed Jerusalem surpassed the other harlots in this too, that she not only gave her own things, which she had acquired by labor in the practice of foulness, but also bestowed her marriage gifts on her lovers and debauchers. And so great was the adulteress's exposure to every magnitude of foulness that she is ranked above not only present but also future harlots; hence we too translated according to Symmachus: 'And after you there will be no fornication; for in comparison with you every fornication from now on will be reckoned lighter'.

16:35.t: Therefore, harlot, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God: Because your bronze has been poured out, and your disgrace has been uncovered in your fornication over your lovers, and over the idols of your abominations in the blood of your sons whom you gave to them, behold, I will gather all your lovers with whom you mingled, and all whom you loved, together with all whom you hated; and I will gather them against you from every side, and I will lay bare your disgrace before them, and they will see all your foulness. And I will judge you with the judgments of adulteresses and of those who shed blood, and I will give you into the blood of fury and jealousy. And I will give you into their hands, and they will destroy your brothel, and they will demolish your place of prostitution, and they will strip you of your garments, and they will take away the vessels of your beauty; and they will leave you naked, and full of disgrace. […]

16:36.t: According to tropology, every soul has received spiritual money from God, according to that passage of the Gospel which is told in the parables of the five, the two and the one talents, and of the ten servants receiving a mina each, who, when they have acted negligently, will become debtors of fifty denarii and of five hundred; and for this reason, in the presence of the lovers, whom we understand to be the demons and the contrary powers, the disgrace of Jerusalem is uncovered, either on the day of judgment or in the time of penance, when they are rebuked; and at first, indeed, God almighty alone discerns hidden things, as the word of the Gospel says: And the Father who sees in secret, and in another place: God searching hearts and reins, and in the volume of Kings: You alone know the hearts of all men; […]

16:42.t: But if, chastised, you do not come to your senses, if, rebuked, you are not amended, if, scourged, you despise it, know that, if you have so far advanced in sinning, his jealousy will depart from you, and that will be said to you which through the prophet Ezekiel is said to Jerusalem: "therefore my jealousy shall depart from you, and I will be angry over you no more".

It is a great wrath of the Lord, when here he is not angry with us: for he reserves us like a calf for the slaughter. For to Jerusalem he says: 'Many are your sins and many your iniquities, therefore I will not be angry with you.' That is, when you were only an adulteress, I was jealous over you as one who loves you; but when you had many lovers, I despised you, and I will not be angry with you. Just as a man is jealous over his wife when he loves her; but if he is not jealous, he hates her, and does not attain to the words of him who says: 'I will visit their iniquities with a rod.' And again: 'And I will not visit their daughters when they have committed fornication.'

16:43.t: 'And all these things', he says, 'you have done, forgetful of former benefits, and you have provoked me to anger, or grieved me, whom you ought to have provoked to joy by good works. Therefore I too have rendered your works upon your head. And although I overthrew you, O adulteress, yet I will exercise less of my anger on you than you deserved'; so that in this too the divine clemency may be shown, that the sins are greater than the punishments.

16:44.t: Behold, everyone who speaks a common proverb will take it up against you, saying: As the mother, so also her daughter. You are the daughter of your mother, who cast off her husband and her sons; and you are the sister of your sisters, who cast off their husbands and their sons. (LXX: "These are all the things which they said against you in a parable, saying: As the mother, also the daughter. You are the daughter of your mother, who leaves her husband and her sons, and sisters of your sisters, who left their husbands and their sons.") After the κατάλογον [catalogue] of the vices and of the chastisement of Jerusalem, by which she is drawn back to salvation, there is also applied a proverb worn by the common speech of the people, or, as the Seventy translated, a 'parable': Such as the mother, such also the daughter.

16:45.t: Now the mother of Jerusalem, as is written both above and in what follows, is called 'chethaea' [Hittite], and it means 'raving' or 'turning into madness', by which are shown the incitements of this world, which lead the captive soul to destruction and separate her from her husband — there is no doubt that by him the word of God and doctrine are meant —; and she is the sister of her sisters, who, as we shall read a little later, are called Sodom and Samaria, of whom the one signifies the life and luxury of the Gentiles, the other the snares of the heretics. Furthermore, what is read in the Seventy: Sisters of your sisters, who repulsed their husbands and their sons, makes no sense — for what other sisters did Sodom and Samaria have, who are the sisters of Jerusalem? […]

Your mother a Hittite, and your father an Amorite. And your greater sister is Samaria, she — and her daughters — who dwells at your left hand; but your sister lesser than you, who dwells at your right hand, is Sodom and her daughters. But you have not walked in their ways, nor done a little less according to their crimes; you have done things almost more wicked than they in all your ways. (LXX: "Your mother a Hittite, and your father an Amorite. Your elder sister is Samaria, she — and her daughters — who dwells on your left; and your sister younger than you, who dwells on your right, is Sodom and her daughters. And not even so did you walk in their ways, nor did you act a little less according to her iniquities; and you surpassed them in all your ways.") Above he had said: Your father an Amorite and your mother a Hittite; here, with the order and the number changed: Your mother a Hittite and your father an Amorite. […]

The heretics who nevertheless accept the Old Testament are accustomed to understand three natures from this passage: spiritual, animal and earthly, and they refer the spiritual to Jerusalem, the animal to Samaria, the earthly to Sodom; let us briefly ask them how three natures, spiritual, animal and earthly, which are certainly different from one another, are said to have one mother and one father — which does not agree with their fiction —, and how the animal and the earthly nature, according to this same prophet, are restored to their ancient state, that is, to the spiritual — which is itself also contrary to their reasonings —. Now that Samaria is to be understood of the heresies is proved both in the prophet Hosea and in many other places, and especially by that testimony: Woe to those who despise Zion and who trust in the mountain of Samaria; they have gathered as a vintage the chiefs of the nations; […]

16:46.t: Now that Samaria and Sodom are the sisters of Jerusalem, of whom one is on the left and the other on the right, you will confirm even according to the bodily understanding, if you look toward the east from the temple of Jerusalem; and Samaria is called greater because she sinned first and was led into captivity by the Assyrians, and Sodom lesser and younger, which is referred to the crowd of the Gentiles; otherwise, at that time Sodom did not exist, for before we read of Jerusalem in the Scriptures, it had been destroyed by divine fire together with Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim.

16:47.t: And Jerusalem, in the middle between the two sisters, which by another name is called Judah, was led by the Chaldeans into Babylon, and Jerusalem sinned far more wickedly than Samaria and Sodom, worshiping in the temple the idol of Jealousy and afterwards killing the Son of God. Furthermore, according to tropology, Samaria and Sodom, that is, the heretics and the heathens, often commit lighter things than those who are reckoned to be Jerusalem, that is, the churchmen; hence it is said to the Corinthians, who believed indeed in Christ but were weighed down by evil works: Fornication is actually heard of among you; and such fornication as is not even among the Gentiles, so that someone has his father's wife, and the rest.

16:48.t: As I live, says the Lord God, Sodom your sister, she and her daughters, has not done as you and your daughters have done. Behold, this was the iniquity of Sodom your sister: pride, fullness of bread and abundance, and the idleness of her and of her daughters, and they did not stretch out a hand to the needy and the poor; and they were lifted up and committed abominations before me, and I took them away as you saw. And Samaria did not commit half of your sins; but you have surpassed her by your crimes, and you have justified your sisters in all your abominations which you have wrought. (LXX: "As I live, says Adonai the Lord, if Sodom your sister has done, she and her daughters, as you and your daughters have done. Nevertheless the iniquity of Sodom your sister was pride in fullness of breads and in abundance. She abounded in delights, she and her daughters ÷ this she had, she and her daughters ⁚ and she did not take hold of the hand of the poor and needy; […]

16:49.t: But for all this, some are of so senseless a disposition, as even after these words to say, "Nay, far be it from me to weep at any time, but may God grant me to laugh and to play all my days." And what can be more childish than this mind? For it is not God that grants to play, but the devil. At least hear, what was the portion of them that played. "The people," it is said, "sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play." Such were they at Sodom, such were they at the time of the deluge. For touching them of Sodom likewise it is said, that "in pride, and in plenty, and in fullness of bread, they waxed wanton." And they who were in Noah's time, seeing the ark a preparing for so many years, lived on in senseless mirth, foreseeing nought of what was coming. For this cause also the flood came and swept them all away, and wrought in that instant the common shipwreck of the world. Ask not then of God these things, which thou receivest of the devil. […]
16:49.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 6:9

16:49.t: He therefore who swears and says: As I live, says the Lord, in describing the crimes of Sodom and her daughters, set first pride, which is properly the devil's, and the first sin; hence the same Apostle: Lest, puffed up, he says, with pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil, on account of which he fell from heaven: For he had said: I will make strength and wisdom of understanding, I will take away the boundaries of the nations and lay waste their strength and shake the inhabited cities, and I will seize the whole world with my hand like a nest, and like broken eggs I will carry it off, and: God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble; we read also in another place: Why is earth and ashes proud?; and the Gospel relates the pride of the Pharisee overcome by the humility of the publican; whose seedbed is fullness of bread and abundance of all things and idleness, or, as the Seventy translated, an opulence of delights and luxury; […]

Furthermore, as to the fact that for 'delights' the Hebrew contains 'idleness', it should be known that it belongs to this sense: every soul of the idle man is in desires; that is, something must always be being done, lest the field of our breast, when the hand ceases, be overrun by the brambles of evil thoughts.

The belly when filled with all kinds of food gives birth to seeds of wantonness, nor can the mind, when choked with the weight of food, keep the guidance and government of the thoughts. For not only is drunkennesswith wine wont to intoxicate the mind, but excess of all kinds of food makes it weak and uncertain, and robs it of all its power of pure and clear contemplation. The cause of the overthrow and wantonness of Sodom was not drunkenness through wine, but fulness of bread. Hear the Lord rebuking Jerusalem through the prophet. "For how did thy sister Sodom sin, except in that she ate her bread in fulness and abundance?" And because through fulness of bread they were inflamed with uncontrollable lust of the flesh, they were burnt up by the judgment of God with fire and brimstone from heaven. […]
16:49.s: The Twelve Books on the Institutes of the Coenobia, Book 5, Chapter 6

16:49.t: And again, through meat and luxuries the Sodomites also were polluted with an unclean matter, and pleasures and the love of the belly brought them unto that limitless wickedness, even as the prophet of God maketh known concerning them, "This was the iniquity of thy luxurious sister Sodom, who was satisfied with bread, and dwelt at ease;" for by reason of being filled with bread, and delicacies they polluted themselves with unnatural lust. Let these things and others which are like unto them be in thy remembrance, O thou that wishest to travel in the path of heaven, and cut off and cast away from thee the fettering weight of the belly, which sinketh the soul into the depths of wickedness like a millstone in the sea.

16:51.t: And what follows: And you have justified your sisters in all your abominations which you have wrought, does not declare Sodom and Samaria simply righteous, but by comparison with those who are worse, just as the publican too, of whom we spoke above, is called righteous not absolutely but by comparison with one worse. And yet, though Sodom and Samaria are such, they have not sinned even half, in comparison with Jerusalem: The servant, for, who knows the will of his master and does not do it will be beaten with many stripes, and: The mighty will mightily suffer torments.

16:52.t: And they are no longer named the people of God, and a holy nation, but rulers of Sodom, and people of Gomorrah; having exceeded in this even the iniquity of the Sodomites, as the prophet also saith, ‘Sodom is justified before thee.’ For the Sodomites raved against angels, but these against the Lord and God and King of all, and these dared to slay the Lord of angels, not knowing that Christ, who was slain by them, liveth.

Therefore you too, bear your shame, you who have surpassed your sisters by your sins, acting more wickedly than they; for they have been justified by you. (LXX: "And you, endure your torment, in that you corrupted your sisters in your sins, by which you acted iniquitously beyond them, and you justified them beyond yourself.") The second plank after shipwreck is, when you have sinned, to blush, and not to fall under that reproach which is spoken against Jerusalem: The face of a harlot has become yours; you do not know how to blush. Now he bears his torment who is tortured by his own conscience, and in this world endures torture of his own will, so that he may not endure eternal torments; and we corrupt our brothers or sisters by our sins when through our sins they are provoked to greater crimes — let what I say be made clearer thus: imagine someone set on the summit of the priesthood not living well and disfiguring his dignity by his works: is not the lay brother corrupted by the imitation of his vices? —; […]

Therefore you too, be ashamed and bear your disgrace, you who have justified your sisters. (LXX: "And you, be ashamed and take up your disgrace, because you have justified your sisters.") Shame is followed by disgrace, disgrace by chastisement, chastisement by consolation, consolation by salvation, according to that word of the Apostle: Tribulation works patience, patience proof, proof hope. And hope does not put to shame — no doubt with respect to the future, since in the present it has blotted out its sins through shame —; something of the same kind is sounded by that word of the Gospel too: There is a shame that leads to death, and there is a shame that leads to life; the Holy Spirit too exhorts sinners in the Psalms: Let all my enemies be put to shame and be afraid; let them be turned back, and be put to shame very swiftly; it is written also in another place: Tell your sins first, that you may be justified, and again: The righteous man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech. […]

It is one thing to have an action set forth as praiseworthy in itself and another to have it extolled in comparison with something worse than itself. We rejoice in one way when a sick person is cured and in another when he improves a little. Even in the sacred Scriptures, Sodom is spoken of as justified in comparison with the crimes of the people of Israel.

And Scripture keeps up this comparison on the other side also, i.e., in weighing the merits of sinners, so that in comparison with the wicked it justifies those who have sinned less, saying: "Sodom is justified above thee;" and again: "For what hath thy sister Sodom sinned?" and: "The rebellious Israel hath justified her soul in comparison of the treacherous Judah."
16:52.s: The Third Conference of Abbot Theonas, Chapter 4

16:53.t: And I will turn them, restoring them, with the turning of Sodom with her daughters, and with the turning of Samaria and of her daughters; and I will turn your return in the midst of them, that you may bear your disgrace, and you will be ashamed in all that you have done, consoling them. (LXX: "And I will turn their turnings with the turning of Sodom and of her daughters, and I will turn the turning of Samaria and of her daughters; and I will turn your turning in the midst of them, that you may bear your torment, and have disgrace from all that you have done to provoke me to anger.") Great is the progress of Jerusalem, that, after the shame and disgrace brought upon her by the judgment of God, which she willingly accepted and bore, saying: I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, restoration to her ancient state should be promised her. […]

16:55.t: Furthermore I questioned him about another saying that is written in Ezekiel; namely, that he said to Jerusalem:—Sodom and her daughters shall be built up as of old, and thou and thy daughters shall become as of old. So he explained this saying to me, and began to make a defence, and said to me “As to this that God said to Jerusalem by the Prophet, Sodom and her daughters shall be built up as of old, and thou and thy daughters shall become as of old; this is the force of the passage, that Sodom and her daughters shall be in their place as of old, and shall be made subject to Israel; and Jerusalem and her daughters shall be in the splendour of royalty as of old.” When I heard this defence from him, it was very contemptible in my eyes, and I said to him:—“Inasmuch as the words of the Prophet were said in wrath, is the whole passage wrathful, or is part of it wrathful and part of it gracious?” He answered:—“A wrathful passage is altogether wrath, and there is no peace in it.” […]

And your sister Sodom and her daughters will return to their antiquity, and Samaria and her daughters will return to their antiquity, and you and your daughters, return to your antiquity. (LXX: "And your sister Sodom and her daughters will be restored as they had been from the beginning, and Samaria and her daughters will be restored as they were from the beginning, and you and your daughters will be restored as you were from the start.") The Jews, among the other fables and endless genealogies and ravings which they invent, dream this too: that at the coming of their Christ, whom we know to be Antichrist, and in the kingdom of a thousand years, Sodom is to be restored to its ancient state, so that it will be like the paradise of God and like the land of Egypt, and that Samaria will receive its former happiness, so that they will return from the Assyrians to the land of Judea — for we read that the ten tribes were taken captive by Pul and Shalmaneser and Tiglath-pileser, kings of the Assyrians, and are captives […]

16:56.t: But Sodom your sister was not heard in your mouth in the day of your pride, before your wickedness was uncovered, as at this time, to the reproach of the daughters of Syria, and of all the Palestinian daughters round about you, who surround you on every side. Your crime and your disgrace you have borne, says the Lord God. (LXX: "If Sodom your sister had not been for hearing in your mouth in the days of your pride, before your wickednesses were uncovered, as now is the case with the daughters of Syria, and if this had not been, what would have been done to you, and to all round about you, the daughters of the foreigners who surround you on every side? Your impieties and your iniquities, you, bear them.") Symmachus translated this passage thus: Because Sodom your sister was not in hearing through your mouth in the day of your pride, before your disgrace was uncovered, as in the time of the reproach of the daughters of Syria, and of all the Palestinian daughters who are round about you, who surround you on every side. […]

16:57.t: 'Syria' in the Hebrew tongue is called 'aram', which means 'loftiness'; and according to the explanation of that passage of the prophet Isaiah in which Aram and Ephraim conspire against Judah and Jerusalem, the subtle wisdom of the heathens, which promises itself the loftiness of knowledge, in all the wickedness of the heretics, attacks Judah, in which is the true confession, and cannot prevail; here too the same arrogance of Syria, that is, of the philosophers, together with the daughters of the foreigners, in whom is shown the manifold error of the diverse doctrines among the nations, mocks Jerusalem and holds in reproach her by whose vices it has been surpassed.

16:59.t: For thus says the Lord God: And I will do to you as you despised the oath, so as to make void the covenant. And I will remember my covenant with you in the days of your youth, and I will raise up for you an everlasting covenant. And you will remember your ways, and you will be ashamed when you receive your sisters with you, the greater with your lesser ones; and I will give them to you as daughters, but not by your covenant. And I will raise up for you my covenant with you, and you will know that I am the Lord, that you may remember and be ashamed, and that it may no longer be yours to open your mouth because of your shame, when I have been appeased toward you in all that you have done, says the Lord God. (LXX: "Thus says Adonai the Lord: And I will do in you as you have done, as you despised these things, so as to transgress my testament. And I will remember my testament which I made with you in the days of your youth, and I will raise up for you an everlasting testament. […]

16:63.t: And that it may no longer be yours to open your mouth because of your shame: for it belongs to the saints to open the mouth — according to the Apostle, who says: My mouth is open to you, O Corinthians —, and to the Lord Savior — who, opening his mouth, taught them, and who says in the psalm too: I will open my mouth in parables —; but to the sinner it is said: You have sinned, be still, and: Why do you take up my testament through your mouth?, and: Praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner; and the holy man deserves to hear: Open your mouth and I will fill it. From this we understand that even when, through the mercy of the Lord, we have received back our former glory, nay rather have received the everlasting covenant of the Gospel, after the Lord has been appeased toward us in all that we have done, we keep the memory of past sin and always close our mouth, because we have been saved not by our works but by the grace of God.

17:2.t: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, propound a riddle and tell a parable to the house of Israel, and you shall say: Thus says the Lord God: A great eagle with great wings, long in the extent of its limbs, full of feathers and of variety, came to Lebanon and took the marrow of the cedar; it plucked off the top of its foliage and carried it over into the land of Canaan; in a city of merchants it set it. And it took of the seed of the land and set it in the ground for seed, that it might make firm its root upon many waters; on the surface it set it. And when it had sprouted, it grew into a broader vine of low stature, its branches looking toward it, and its roots were under it; so it became a vine, and bore fruit in vine-shoots and sent out offshoots. […]

17:3.t: And Ezekiel actually calls Jerusalem Libanus when he says, "The great eagle, with great wings, that hath the dominion, cometh to Libanus, and tore off the tender boughs of the cedar." And he goes on to explain this himself, as happening when Nebuchadnezzar shall come to Jerusalem and take her rulers, and that which follows. But Ezekiel's prophecy is about the first siege, and Zechariah's about the second.
17:3.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 8, Chapter 4

17:3.t: Now in the present prophecy of Ezekiel two eagles are set forth; of the first we must speak now, of the other we shall treat in what follows. And meanwhile let us gather the simple history. A great eagle with great wings, long in the extent of its limbs, full of feathers and of variety (or, as the Seventy rendered, full of talons) is Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Chaldeans, of whom Hosea also speaks: As an eagle over the house of the Lord. He, ruling over many nations and hedged about by a countless army, came upon the house of God — no doubt it means the temple — or, as Scripture now says, to Lebanon, of which Zechariah speaks: Open your gates, O Lebanon; and let fire devour your cedars. Howl, fir tree, for the cedar has fallen, since the magnificent have been laid waste; and often the temple, which was renowned and lofty, is called Lebanon in the holy Scriptures. And it took the marrow of the cedar, and plucked off the top of its foliage and carried it over into the land of Canaan; […]

According to anagogy — although the interpretation may seem forced — this must be known: that, just as the other living creatures are customarily referred both to a good and to a bad sense, so also is the eagle. Of the lion it is said in a good sense: A lion's whelp is Judah; in the contrary sense: Our adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion, and that in the psalm: He lies in wait in secret, like a lion in his den. He lies in wait to seize the poor. In a good sense it is said of the eagle that the righteous man, having become rich, may make himself wings like an eagle, that he may be able to return to the house of his superior, and in Isaiah it is written that the righteous may put forth feathers like eagles, may run and not grow weary, may walk and not hunger; […]

17:5.t: In his place he took of the seed of the same land, that is, of the royal stock, Mattaniah, the paternal uncle of Jeconiah, whose name he changed, and he called him Zedekiah and set him as king in Jerusalem, and put him over many peoples. And yet he set him on the surface, and did not make his power firm with a deep root of rule, but set him so that he might be looked upon and be under Babylonian power, or: Of low stature, its branches looking toward it, so that he would indeed rule over the peoples of the Jews, but would look to the authority of the Babylonian who gave the orders: for this is what Scripture says: Of low stature, its branches looking toward it — understand: toward the eagle — which the Seventy rendered more plainly: And it sprang up — what had been planted — and became a weak and small vine, so that only its branches appeared, and he would seem indeed to have a kingdom, but his kingdom itself, low and weak, would be ruled by the will of the Babylonian prince. So much for the present passage for now; […]

17:6.t: Afterwards, intending to speak of the oaths and treaties, "He took," saith he, "of the seed of the land, and planted it in a fruitful field, that it might take root by great waters. He placed it to be looked upon; and it grew, and became a weak vine, and of small stature, and it stretched out its branches towards him, and its roots were under him." Here he calls the city of Jerusalem a vine; but in saying that it stretched out its branches towards the eagle, and that its roots were under him, he refers to the treaties and alliances made with him; and that it cast itself upon him.

17:7.t: And there was another great eagle with great wings and many feathers; and behold, this vine, as if sending its roots to it, stretched out its vine-shoots to it, that it might water it from the beds of its growth. In good land upon many waters he planted it, that it may make foliage and bear fruit, and become a great vine. Say: Thus says the Lord God: Shall it then prosper? Will he not pull up its roots and strip off its fruit, and dry up all the vine-shoots of its growth, and it will wither? And not with a great arm nor with many peoples, so as to pull it up by the roots. Behold, it is planted; shall it then prosper? Will it not, when the burning wind touches it, be dried up, and wither in the beds of its growth? (LXX: "And there was another great eagle with great wings, with very many talons; and behold, this vine was entwined toward it, and its roots toward it, and it stretched out its branches toward it, that it might water it with the clod of its planting. […]

17:8.t: It had been planted in good land by Nebuchadnezzar, that it might make foliage and bring forth fruit and grow into a broader vine; therefore the prophet is commanded to speak to the vine which had been planted by Nebuchadnezzar and had sent its branches to the Egyptian eagle: 'Shall it prosper because it has attempted to do this, and will not all its offshoots and vine-shoots at once be dried up? And not,' it says, 'with a great arm nor with a numerous people'; for Zedekiah, fleeing and left destitute of the help of the Egyptian king, was caught by the leaders of Nebuchadnezzar in the deserts of Jericho, and all his companions were scattered here and there, as is written in the volume of Kings and in Παραλιπομήνῳ [Chronicles] and in Jeremiah.

17:12.t: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Say to the provoking house: Do you not know what these things signify? Say: Behold, the king of Babylon comes to Jerusalem, and he will take its king and its princes, and lead them to himself into Babylon; and he will take of the seed of the kingdom, and strike a covenant with him, and receive an oath from him; but he will also take away the mighty of the land, that the kingdom may be lowly and not lift itself up, but keep his compact and observe it. But he, withdrawing from him, sent messengers to Egypt, that it might give him horses and a numerous people; shall he prosper or obtain safety who has done these things? And shall he who has broken the compact escape? As I live, says the Lord God, surely in the place of the king who made him king, whose oath he made void and whose compact, which he had with him, he broke, in the midst of Babylon he shall die. […]

17:16.t: Surely, it says, in the place of the king who made him king, whose oath he made void and whose compact, which he had with him, he broke, in the midst of Babylon he shall die; for we read that Zedekiah was captured, led to Riblah, and there, after his sons had been killed, blinded, and, shut in a cage like a wild beast, carried over to Babylon — whence also Scripture, though it seems to be contrary to itself, is nevertheless most true in both: it had been said to Zedekiah: And you shall enter Babylon and: You shall not see it: for he entered, because he was led to Babylon, and he did not see it, because he had been blinded —.

17:17.t: But what follows: And not with a great army nor with a numerous people will Pharaoh make war against him, in the casting up of a mound and the building of ramparts, to kill many souls, is understood in two ways: either the Egyptian king, coming against Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, will not be able to give battle nor with a small army resist so great a multitude; or Zedekiah himself will be conquered by Pharaoh, from whom he hoped for help, not that Pharaoh conquered him — or that Scripture anywhere attests this —, but that Nebuchadnezzar's conquest was brought about on the occasion given by the king of Egypt; and that not he who was besieging seemed to conquer Jerusalem, but he in whom Zedekiah had hoped in vain.

17:18.t: Behold, it says, he gave his hand to the king of Egypt, and handed himself over, and committed the sacrilege of perjury against God: 'Will it,' it says, 'profit him?'. And when he has done all these things, he shall not escape.

17:19.t: Therefore thus says the Lord God: As I live, surely the oath that he despised and the covenant that he transgressed I will lay upon his head, and I will spread my net over him and he shall be caught in my dragnet, and I will bring him into Babylon, and I will judge him there in the transgression by which he despised me. And all his fugitives with the whole column shall fall by the sword; and the rest shall be scattered to every wind, and you shall know that I the Lord have spoken. It is a worldly maxim: Deceit or valor, who would ask, in an enemy?, which those who say that enemies are to be deceived by fraud are wont to set against us; yet even if we were to assent to it, Zedekiah did much worse: for he did not deceive an enemy, but a friend to whom he had been bound by a covenant of the Lord. Therefore, so long as you do not swear and do not enter into a compact under the name of God, it belongs to prudence and courage either to deceive or to overcome the adversary in whatever way you can; […]

17:22.t: Thus says the Lord: And I myself will take of the marrow of the lofty cedar, and will set it; from the top of its branches I will strip off a tender shoot, and I will plant it upon a high and eminent mountain. On the lofty mountain of Israel I will plant it, and it will break forth into a sprout and bear fruit, and it will become a great cedar, and all birds will dwell under it, every winged creature nesting under the shade of its foliage. And all the trees of the region shall know that I the Lord have brought low the lofty tree and raised up the low tree, and dried up the green tree and made the dry tree flourish: I the Lord have spoken and have done it. (LXX: "For thus says Adonai the Lord: And I will take away of the choice parts of the cedar from the top ※ and I will give from the head of its branches ⁚, from their heart I will take away, and I will plant upon a high mountain; […]

17:23.t: He broke forth into a sprout and bore fruit, and surpassed all the cedars by his loftiness, so that all the birds of heaven dwell under him, and all winged creatures are protected by his shade — he of whom Habakkuk says: Horns in his hands: there his strength is hidden, and who desires to gather, like a hen, the chicks under his wings —, so that all the trees of the region may know that he himself is the Lord; τροπικῶς [figuratively] speaking of believers: he who brought low Israel, once a lofty tree, and exalted the lowly people of the Gentiles; who dried up the green tree of the Jews, flowering and sprouting in the Law and the Prophets, and made the dry tree of the nations flourish, so that what he had always spoken he might fulfill in deed; the same thing is signified also by the words of Simeon in the Gospel, saying: Behold, this one is set for the ruin and for the resurrection of many, and by the grain of mustard seed which, though it is the smallest of all seeds, once it has grown is a dwelling place for birds.

17:24.t: Some interpret it otherwise, referring the lofty tree brought low and the low tree exalted to the passion of the Lord Savior: Who, though he was in the form of God, did not count it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; and after the resurrection the very tree was afterward raised on high which, at first green, was dried up in death and afterward, reviving, recovered its former greenness. Others, in Jewish fashion, refer both to Israel: that at the first coming it was brought low and dried up, and at the second it will be restored to its former state, when that is fulfilled which the apostle Paul says: When the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel will be saved.

18:1.t: For both this man hath sinned and his parents, but his blindness proceedeth not from that. And this He said, not signifying that though this man indeed was not in such case, yet that others had been made blind from such a cause, the sins of their parents, since it cannot be that when one sinneth another should be punished. For if we allow this, we must also allow that he sinned before his birth. As therefore when He declared, "neither hath this man sinned," He said not that it is possible to sin from one's very birth, and be punished for it; so when He said, "nor his parents," He said not that one may be punished for his parents' sake. This supposition He removeth by the mouth of Ezekiel; "As I live saith the Lord, this proverb shall not be, that is used, The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge." And Moses saith, "The father shall not die for the child, neither shall the child die for the father."
18:1.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 56

18:2.t: WHAT DOES IT MEAN THAT GOD, WHO IS PROCLAIMED AS JUST, HAS PROMISED TO REPAY THE SINS OF THE FATHERS UPON THE CHILDREN TO THE THIRD AND FOURTH GENERATION? — Anyone who doubts that God does nothing and says nothing unjust is out of his mind. Therefore, if the words of the Lord are not suppressed, but everything that relates to this same question is set forth, what seems obscure will come to light, and what is thought hardly just will be recognized as devout. For whoever suppresses the words of a question is either ignorant or shifty, preferring accusation to teaching. Further, the Lord indeed promised that He would repay the sins of the fathers upon the children, but upon those who hate Him, that is, those who, involved in their fathers’ evils, have served idols just as their fathers did. For he is an enemy of God who transfers the honor of His name to a creature. […]
18:2.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 14: ON REPAYING THE FATHERS' SINS UPON THE CHILDREN

18:2.t: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: What is it that you turn a parable into this proverb among you in the land of Israel, saying: The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the teeth of the sons have been set on edge? (LXX: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ÷ Son of man, ⁚ what is the parable among the sons of Israel, of those who say: The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the teeth of the sons have been set on edge?") What the Seventy said, Son of man, is not found in the Hebrew. Now divine Scripture warns that what was said in Exodus, I am the Lord your God; a jealous God, who render the sins of the fathers upon the sons to the third and fourth generation for those who hate me, and show mercy to thousands for those who love me and keep my precepts, and again, The Lord descended in a cloud and stood beside Moses, and Moses called on the name of the Lord, and the Lord passed before his face, and he called on him, saying: Lord God, compassionate and merciful, patient and of much mercy and true, […]

It was this new covenant that was prophesied about when it was said by Ezekiel that the children should not bear the iniquity of the parents, and that it should no longer be a proverb in Israel, "The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge." Here lies the necessity that each person should be born again, that he might be freed from the sin in which he was born. For the sins committed afterwards can be cured by penitence, as we see is the case after baptism.

18:3.t: As I live, says the Lord, if this parable shall be any longer to you as a proverb in Israel. Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sins, it shall die. (LXX: "As I live, says the Lord Adonai, if it shall be any longer that this parable is spoken in Israel; for all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sins, it shall die.") What As I live, says the Lord means, and parable or proverb, we have said more fully above; it will by no means be spoken in Israel, but among those who do not have the knowledge of God and cannot discern the truth.

But if they wish to say that after the return from Babylon these nations were subjected to the people of Israel, first we shall demand the authority of the Scriptures by which they may prove that this happened; then, when they are quite unable to demonstrate it, we shall grant it to them out of superfluity and say: Suppose that what you say happened; what justice of God would it be that the grandfathers blasphemed and the forefathers reproached, and afterwards it was repaid to the grandsons? Especially since that sentence by which it was formerly said in the law that the sins of the fathers are repaid upon the sons in the third and the fourth generation has been loosed through Ezekiel: As I live, says the Lord; this parable shall no longer be spoken, but the soul that sins, it shall die. And at the same time notice that what was said is a parable, and does not mean what they bring forward on the surface of the letter.

18:4.t: I know also another kind of death, in which a man dies for God; of it it is said: "The soul that sins shall itself die."
The soul dies to the Lord, not through natural infirmity but through the sickness caused by guilt. This type of death is not the release from this life but is the fall resulting from sin.
Show me a body that has never been sick or one that is sure of enjoying good health forever after sickness, and I will show you a soul that has never sinned.

The soul therefore that has not sinned shall live. Neither the virtues nor the vices of parents are imputed to their children. God takes account of us only from the time when we are born anew in Christ.

All, he says, souls are mine, according to creation, not according to merit, as Moses was called a man of God, of whom it is written, A prayer of Moses, the man of God, and Elijah, who said to the captain of fifty soldiers, And if I am a man of God, let fire come down upon you and upon the fifty men; but the man of sin and son of iniquity is not called a man of God, just as those are called servants and attendants of God of whom it cannot be said, Everyone who commits sin is the servant of sin, and again, For by whom anyone is overcome, to him he is also a servant. Just as the sins of the sons do not harm the fathers, so the sins of the fathers do not overflow onto the sons, but the soul that sins, it shall die: not by the abolition of its substance, but out of the fellowship of him who says, I am the life, and who says elsewhere, Everyone who lives and believes in me shall not die for ever, and, Amen, amen I say to you, whoever keeps my word shall not see death for ever; […]

18:5.t: ·i· If, he says, a man is righteous and does judgment. It is written in Proverbs: The thoughts of the righteous are judgments. He who possesses this virtue, so as to do nothing without reason and judgment, can say that prophetic word, The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves; and when he has judged all things rightly, so as not to accept the person of the poor in judgment, he will fulfill the precept of the Lord, As the lesser, so also shall you judge the greater, saying boldly, My soul has longed to desire your judgments at all times, and again, I have chosen the way of truth, I have not forgotten your judgments, and in the same psalm, I have known that your judgments are righteousness; and he will advance to such great blessedness that he understands the judgments of the Lord, which are a great deep, and says with the Apostle, O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! […]

And a man, if he is righteous and does judgment and righteousness, does not eat on the mountains and does not lift up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, and does not violate his neighbor's wife, and does not approach a menstruous woman, and does not grieve a man, returns the pledge to the debtor, seizes nothing by force, gives his bread to the hungry, and covers the naked with a garment, and does not lend at usury, and does not take more, turns his hand away from iniquity, does true judgment between man and man, walks in my precepts, and keeps my judgments so as to do truth: this man is righteous and shall live with life, says the Lord God. […]

18:6.t: ·iii· The third is: He does not eat on the mountains, which the Jews think pertains to the sin of idolatry; for we read frequently in the books of Kings and of Chronicles: Nevertheless he did not depart from the high places; the people still sacrificed and burned incense on the heights, Scripture signifying this: that on mountains and in groves they sacrificed victims to idols and kindled incense. We, however, say that he eats on the mountains who says with the Pharisee: I give you thanks, God, that I am not like this tax collector. I fast twice in the sabbath, I give tithes of all my substance, and so on; but on the contrary the tax collector, hearing him who had said, Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, struck his breast with his hand, that is, the treasury of the worst thoughts, and did not dare to raise his eyes to heaven. […]

18:7.t: ·vii· There follows in the seventh place: And does not grieve a man (or, as the Seventy translated, does not oppress through power). I do not know who is free of this vice and sin; for the Egyptians too oppressed the Hebrews through power, whence Habakkuk also complains that the impious oppresses the righteous. And would that this were said only of those who are outside, and not of those who are within! For the princes of the churches too are accustomed to oppress the people through pride, of whom it is written: They have made you prince: do not be lifted up; be among them as one of them, and the Savior commanded: Whoever wishes to be first among you, let him be the least of all.
