But what is said according to the Hebrew, And does not grieve a man, agrees with the apostolic testimony, Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, who dwells in you; and in the Gospel according to the Hebrews, which the Nazarenes are accustomed to read, it is placed among the greatest crimes: he who has grieved his brother's spirit. […]

18:8.t: ·xii· The twelfth number is held by: And does not lend at usury (or, as the Seventy translated, does not give his money at usury). In the Hebrew usury on all kinds of goods is forbidden, in the Seventy only on money, according to what is also written in Psalm 14 (15), Who has not given his money at usury, and as it is said, To your brother you shall not lend at interest, but to a foreigner you shall lend at interest. But see the progress: at the beginning of the Law interest is removed only from brothers; in the prophet usury is forbidden from all, as Ezekiel says, He has not given his money at usury; and further, in the Gospel there is an increase of virtue, as the Lord commands, 'Lend to those from whom you do not hope to receive back'. ·xiii· There follows in the thirteenth place: And does not take more. Some think that usury applies only to money; foreseeing this, divine Scripture removes the surplus on everything, so that you may not receive back more than you gave. […]

18:9.t: ·xvi· There follows in the sixteenth place: Walks in my precepts, ·xvii· and in the seventeenth: Judgments (or my justifications) he keeps, so as to do them, and keeps them once done; each of which has a manifold understanding, if we wish to go over all the commandments of the Law, in which there are said to be precepts of the Lord and in which justifications. Psalm 118 (119) is full of precepts and justifications, and in part Psalm 18 (19), in which it is written, The righteousnesses of the Lord are right, gladdening hearts and the precept of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes; in this the question is raised how God said in this same prophet, I gave them justifications not good, in which they should not live in them; and the answer is easy, and fuller in what follows: that the Jews, following the killing letter, do not live, and the Christians, understanding the life-giving spirit, do live. […]

18:10.t: But if he begets a son who is a robber, shedding blood, and does one of these things (or, as the Seventy translated, and does sins, does not walk in the way of his righteous father), and who does not do all these things, but eats on the mountains, and pollutes his neighbor's wife, grieves the needy and the poor (or oppresses), seizes plunder, does not return the pledge, and lifts up his eyes to idols, commits abomination, gives at usury and takes more: shall he live? He shall not live; since he has done all these detestable things, he shall die by death, his blood shall be upon him. For 'robber' in the Hebrew is written 'pharis', which the second edition of Aquila translated 'sinner', Symmachus 'transgressor', the Seventy and Theodotion 'pestilent'. Just as a pestilence creates diseases and is wont to lay waste far and wide the regions on which it has settled, so the pestilent man ravages everything.

And let us speak first according to the history, so that you may know that the iniquities of the fathers do not overflow onto the sons. If the righteous man does what the preceding discourse wove together in order, he shall live with life; but if he begets a son who departs from the service of the Lord and exchanges his father's virtues for vices, so that he does what the father did not do and does not do what the father wrought, will he be able to live? Certainly he will not live, but will be guilty of his own blood. Further, according to the spiritual understanding, if a righteous man of the Church has preached the evangelical faith, and his son and disciple has been deceived by heretical error, the son will be called pestilent, of whom it is written also in Psalm 1, And has not sat in the chair of pestilence, and in Proverbs, The bold and insolent and proud man is called pestilent. […]

18:14.t: But if he begets a son who, seeing all the sins of his father which he did, fears and does not do likewise, does not eat upon the mountains and does not lift up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, and does not violate his neighbor's wife, and does not grieve a man, does not retain the pledge, and does not seize plunder, gives his bread to the hungry, and covers the naked with a garment, turns his hand away from injury to the poor, does not take usury and surplus, does my judgments, walks in my precepts: this man shall not die in the iniquity of his father, but shall live with life. His father, because he practiced calumny and did violence to his brother, and wrought evil in the midst of his people, has died in his iniquity. […]

18:19.t: And you say: Why has the son not borne the iniquity of the father? Clearly because the son has wrought judgment and righteousness, has kept all my precepts, and has done them: he shall live with life. The soul that sins, it shall die: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, and the father the iniquity of the son; the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the impiety of the impious shall be upon him. He solves the question which the hearer could raise as an objection: 'You are accustomed', he says, 'to say: Why has the righteous son not borne the iniquity of the father?'; to which he himself replied: 'Clearly because the son has done well and has not committed his father's offenses'. And it is just that, as the sinner dies in his crime, so the righteous man should live in his virtues; and that the soul that sins should die, and he who keeps the precepts of God should live.

18:20.t: How can you fail to bear in mind that the father shall not bear the iniquity of the son, nor the son bear the iniquity of the father, but each shall die in his own sin? I have neither father nor son slandered by you; I have had neither teacher nor disciple. But if the sins of the parents must be made charges against their children, it is far fairer for the sins of Arius to be charged against his disciples; and, whoever begat the heretic Aetius, for the charges against the son to be applied to the father. If on the other hand it is unjust for any one to be accused for their sakes, it is far more unjust that I should be held responsible for the sake of men with whom I have nothing to do, even if they were in every respect sinners, and something worthy of condemnation has been written by them. I must be pardoned if I do not believe all that is urged against them. since my own experience shows me how very easy it is for accusers to slip into slander.

18:21.t: Sin is a terrible thing, and the most grievous disease of the soul is iniquity, which corrodes the fiber of the soul and makes it liable to eternal fire. It is an evil freely chosen, the product of the will.

But if the impious man repents of all his sins which he has wrought, and keeps all my precepts, and does judgment and righteousness, he shall live with life and shall not die. Of all his iniquities which he has wrought I will not be mindful. 'To such a degree', he says, 'do the sins of the fathers not overflow onto the sons, nor does a criminal father weigh down a righteous son, nor are some punished for the crimes of others, that one and the same man who was formerly impious and a sinner, if afterwards he repents and, turned to better things, blots out his former sins, is not judged by the oldness of his sin, but is received into my flock by the renewal of virtue'. And at the same time it must be considered what kind of impious man and sinner he receives as a penitent: 'If from all his sins', he says, 'which he has wrought he turns himself away, and keeps all the precepts of the Lord, so, namely, that he abandons all crimes and follows all virtues; […]

From both, then, men are in danger; both from hoping and despairing, from contrary things, from contrary affections. Who is deceived by hoping? He who says, God is good, God is merciful, let me do what I please, what I like; let me give loose reins to my lusts, let me gratify the desires of my soul. Why this? Because God is merciful, God is good, God is kind. These men are in danger by hope. And those are in danger from despair, who, having fallen into grievous sins, fancying that they can no more be pardoned upon repentance, and believing that they are without doubt doomed to damnation, do say with themselves, We are already destined to be damned, why not do what we please with the disposition of gladiators destined to the sword. This is the reason that desperate men are dangerous: for, having no longer aught to fear, they are to be feared exceedingly. Despair kills these; hope, those. The mind is tossed to and fro between hope and despair. Thou hast to fear lest hope slay thee; […]

18:22.t: In his righteousness which he has wrought he shall live. 'He shall live not so much by my righteousness as by his own, although it belongs to my righteousness to render good things to the good and evil things to the evil'.

18:23.t: He takes delight in the conversion of sinners, for he desires the conversion that follows their sins. Surely, he himself is the only sinless one.

For if it had not been His will that they should hear and be saved, He ought to have been silent, not to have spoken in parables; but now by this very thing He stirs them up, even by speaking under a veil. "For God willeth not the death of the sinner, but that he should turn unto Him and live."
18:23.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 45:2

18:23.t: Is the death of the impious man of my will, says the Lord God, and not that he should turn from his ways and live? Therefore it is of the Lord's will that all be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth; and wherever the sentence of God seems severe and ferocious, he condemns not men but sins.

18:24.t: Vain then is the labour of the righteous man, and free from blame is the way of the sinner, if a change befall, and the former turn from the better to the worse, and the latter from the worse to the better. So we hear from Ezekiel teaching as it were in the name of the Lord, when he says, “if the righteous turneth away and committeth iniquity, I will not remember the righteousness which he committed before; in his sin he shall die,” and so too about the sinner; if he turn away from his wickedness, and do that which is right, he shall live. Where were all the labours of God’s servant Moses, when the gainsaying of one moment shut him out from entering into the promised land? What became of the companionship of Gehazi with Elissæus, when he brought leprosy on himself by his covetousness? What availed all Solomon’s vast wisdom, and his previous regard for God, when afterwards from his mad love of women he fell into idolatry? […]

Remark all the sins which God threatens, thou wilt at once see that they are present sins. But if his past righteousness shall not profit the righteous in the time of his iniquity, neither shall his wickedness which he hath forsaken hurt the wicked man in the time of his righteousness; for it is written, Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the Lord, and he shall obtain mercy.
18:24.s: Letter 3: Against the Treatise of the Novatians

18:24.t: But if the righteous man turns himself away from his righteousness, and does iniquity according to all the abominations which the impious man is accustomed to work, shall he live? All his righteousnesses which he had done shall not be remembered; in the transgression by which he transgressed and in his sin which he sinned, in it he shall die. Just as old offenses do not weigh down the righteous man who was formerly a sinner, so former righteousnesses do not help the sinner who was formerly righteous; each one is judged in that in which he is found.

18:25.t: And you have said: The way of the Lord is not equitable. Hear, house of Israel: Is my way not equitable, and are not rather your ways crooked? He gives the reasons why the sentence of the Lord is just: 'Do you think me unjust', he says, 'in rendering the sins of the fathers to the sons, so that while some eat the sour grape, the teeth of others are set on edge? Behold, each one dies in his own sin and is given life in his own righteousness; in both cases, not the things past but the things present. Rather it is your sentence that is unjust, you who think that the parable is not a parable, but take it as though it were the truth of history, that the crimes of some are punished in others'.

The way of the Lord then has refreshment if it is kept to according to His law. But it is we who by troublesome distractions bring sorrows and troubles upon ourselves, while we try even With the utmost exertion and difficulty to follow the crooked and perverse ways of this world. But when in this way we have made the Lord's yoke heavy and hard to us, we at once complain in a blasphemous spirit of the hardness and roughness of the yoke itself or of Christ who lays it upon us, in accordance with this passage: "The folly of man corrupteth his ways, but he blames God in his heart;" and as Haggai the prophet says, when we say that "the way of the Lord is not right" the reply is aptly made to us by the Lord: "Is not My way right? Are not your ways rather crooked?"

18:26.t: ON THE PERSON WHO HAS RECEIVED FAITH IN CHRIST. — It is written: “The righteousness of the righteous shall not benefit him on the day that he goes astray; and the wickedness of the wicked shall not harm him when he turns back” (Ezek. 18:26–27). And the Lord in the Gospel says: “He who does not believe is already judged” (Jn. 3:18); by this indicating that the one who believes is not subject to judgment for the reception of a sentence, but will be found worthy of praise by the merit of faith. Therefore, the knowledge of God has this privilege, that it obtains the remission of sins. For the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God is deemed worthy to be freed from all sins. Long wandering in error, tossed by the waves of ignorance in various ways, he has at last been enlightened and has received the flashing light of truth, in which, after great storms, he rests in safety. It is fitting that after this knowledge he restrain himself from those things which he used to do long before when he was set in ignorance. […]
18:26.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 126: ON THE PERSON WHO HAS RECEIVED FAITH IN CHRIST

18:26.t: For when the righteous man turns himself away from his righteousness and does iniquity, he shall die in them: in the iniquity which he has wrought he shall die. This can be understood thus: the people of Israel, formerly righteous, turned itself away from its righteousness, because it abandoned the author of righteousness, and did iniquity by denying the Son of God; in the sin and crime which it wrought it will die, not in many but in one, killing the heir so that it lost the inheritance.

18:27.t: And when the impious man turns himself away from his impiety which he has wrought, and does judgment and righteousness, he has given life to his own soul; for, considering, he has turned himself away from all his iniquities which he has wrought; he shall live with life, and shall not die. 'On the contrary', he says, 'the people of the nations, not having the knowledge of God, and impious, if it turns itself away from its impiety which it formerly wrought in idolatry, and does the things which were commanded to Israel in the Law, has itself, formerly dead, given life to its own soul; and seeing that it had perished in the iniquities which it wrought, it will believe in him who says, 'I am the way and the life and the truth'; it shall live with life, and shall not die'.

18:29.t: And the sons of Israel say: The way of the Lord is not equitable. Are my ways not equitable, house of Israel, and are not rather your ways crooked? To this day Israel blasphemes God: why has he abandoned his people and taken up the multitude of the nations? The Lord rebukes them because their ways are crooked, while the sentence of the Lord is just: having despised or destroyed the former tenants, he sends other farmers into his vineyard; understanding which, in the parable of the Gospel, the Jews said: This shall not be.

18:30.t: The ministers of the grace of God have, by the Holy Spirit, spoken of repentance; and the Lord of all things has himself declared with an oath regarding it, "As I live, says the Lord, I desire not the death of the sinner, but rather his repentance;" [Ezekiel 33:11] adding, moreover, this gracious declaration, "Repent, O house of Israel, of your iniquity." [Ezekiel 18:30] Say to the children of my people, Though your sins reach from earth to heaven, and though they be redder than scarlet, and blacker than sack-cloth, yet if you turn to me with your whole heart, and say, Father! I will listen to you, as to a holy people. [2 Chronicles 7:14] And in another place He speaks thus: "Wash you and become clean; put away the wickedness of your souls from before my eyes; cease from your evil ways, and learn to do well; seek out judgment, deliver the oppressed, judge the fatherless, and see that justice is done to the widow; and come, and let us reason together. […]
18:30.s: Clement's First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 8

18:30.t: Therefore I will judge each one of you according to his ways, house of Israel, says the Lord God. Whether those who are judged are from the multitude of the Gentiles or from the people of Israel, there is no respect of persons with God, but each one will be crowned by his own faith, and condemned by impiety and unbelief.

Turn, and repent of all your iniquities, and iniquity shall not be a ruin to you. Cast away from you all your transgressions by which you have transgressed. This word is properly directed to Israel, that they should repent and abandon their iniquities, or transgressions, by which they transgressed against God. But it can also be understood of both peoples, so that both Israel and the crowd of the nations, abandoning their vices, may turn to him who is able to heal their bruises.

18:31.t: "Make for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit" that you may become a subject of joy for the citizens of heaven. For if there is joy "over one sinner who repents," according to the Gospel, how much more will the salvation of so many souls gladden the blessed saints? You have entered on a good and glorious course: run the holy race in good earnest.

'And make for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit, so that, abandoning the oldness of the letter, you may live in the newness of the spirit'. The new heart of Israel is to believe in him whom it had formerly denied; the new heart of the nations is to abandon idols and, having despised the cult of the dead, to believe in him who is the God of the living.

And why will you die, house of Israel? It is better, as we said above, to take this exhortation, in which it is written, Turn, and repent, as addressed to the person of the Jews, whom he does not wish to die and to whom he is now speaking: 'Why will you die, house of Israel, you who have as fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob — of whom it is written, The God of the living and not of the dead —? Why will you die by your own fault, you who ought to live by the merit of your fathers and by my mercy?'

18:32.t: And there are those who even while they live are dead unto God. For He laid a commandment on Adam and said to him, In the day that thou shalt eat of the tree, thou shalt surely die. And after he had transgressed the commandment, and had eaten, he lived nine hundred and thirty years; but he was accounted dead unto God because of his sins. But that it may be made certain for thee that a sinner is called dead even when he lives, I will make it clear to thee. For thus it is written in Ezekiel the Prophet, As I live, saith the Lord of lords, I desire not the death of the dead sinner.
18:32.s: Demonstration 8 (Of the Resurrection of the Dead), Section 17

18:32.t: For I do not want the death of the dying sinner, says the Lord God; return and live. 'I do not want you to die', he says, 'whom I begot in salvation: for sons indeed I have begotten and exalted, but they have despised me; return therefore and live'. Return is not said except to those who were formerly with God and afterwards deserted his company. And live through repentance, you who are dead through sin. Therefore Israel, because it does not return to its former state, must be believed to be dead.

19:1.t: And you, take up a lament over the princes of Israel, and you shall say: Why did your mother, a lioness, lie down among lions, in the midst of young lions rear her whelps? And she brought out one of her young lions, he became a lion, and he learned to catch prey and to devour man. And the nations heard of him, and not without wounds of their own they caught him, and they brought him in chains into the land of Egypt. And when she had seen that she was weakened and her expectation had perished, she took one of her young lions, she made him a lion. He went about among the lions and became a lion, he learned to catch prey and to devour men; he learned to make widows, and to bring their cities into a desert, and the land and its fullness was made desolate by the sound of his roaring. And the nations gathered against him from every side, from the provinces, and they spread their net over him; in their wounds he was caught. And they put him into a cage, in chains, and they brought him to the king of Babylon; […]

From this it is plain that both the earlier reading, in which it is said: Why did your mother, a lioness, lie down among lions?, and this one, in which it is written: Your mother is like a vine in your blood, planted upon water, pertain to Jerusalem, which lost her lions and her shoots, and there did not remain in her a rod that might rise up into a tribe or into the scepters of rulers. For it begins from a lament and ends in a lament: Take up a lament over the princes of Israel, that is, at the beginning, and now at the end: It is a lament; and the royal stock is to be attended by the lamentation and lament of the parable. […]

19:3.t: For after Jerusalem had brought out Jehoahaz the son of Josiah from the royal stock and made him king, he proved so cruel in a short time that he is related, tropologically, to have caught prey and devoured men.

19:4.t: When the Egyptian had come against him, he caught him not without wounds — or in a pit, as is properly contained in the Hebrew, so as to preserve the tropological capture of lions, which are always caught in pits — and he brought him in a muzzle, or in chains, into the land of Egypt, and there he died.

19:5.t: When his mother Jerusalem, who had borne him, who had reared him, who had set him in the kingship, had seen that her expectation had perished, she took from among the other kings Jeconiah, the son of Jehoiakim, and set him up as king.

19:6.t: He too, having imitated the cruelty of his predecessor, is described under the ferocity of a lion, in that he devoured men, made many widows, brought cities to a desert, and at the sound of his roaring the whole province was terrified, so that the nations gathered against him and spread their net and caught him in a pit and put him in a cage and in chains — not that this was done to Jeconiah: for he gave himself up to the king of Babylonia and was carried off into Chaldea; but so that the metaphor of the lion may be preserved, which is caught in pits and bound with chains and kept in cages —.

19:9.t: Otherwise, according to the history, we read this of Zedekiah, who was set up as king of Jerusalem after Jeconiah — and this is what gave occasion for most people to understand Zedekiah rather than Jeconiah, because chains are read of, and cages, and a prison is named —; he was, then, kept in prison and not put to death, and was only removed from the kingship. But the history relates that Zedekiah was led blind into Babylon and there immediately killed.

19:10.t: Your mother is like a vine in your blood, planted upon the water; its fruits and its leaves grew from many waters; and it had solid rods for the scepters of rulers, and its stature was exalted into leaves, and it saw its height in the multitude of its shoots. And it was plucked up in wrath, and cast down to the ground, and the burning wind dried up its fruits; the rods of its strength withered and were dried up, fire devoured it. And now it is transplanted into the desert, in a land impassable and thirsty. And fire went out from the rod of its branches, which devoured its fruit; and there was not in it a strong rod, a scepter of rulers. It is a lament, and it shall be for a lament. (LXX: "Your mother is like a vine, like a flower on pomegranates, planted in water; its fruit and its sprout came from much water; and it had a rod of strength for a tribe of leaders, and it was exalted in its greatness in the midst of its offshoots, and it saw its greatness in the multitude of its shoots. […]

19:12.t: The vine, then, was exalted and raised up; because God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble, it was plucked up in the fury of the Lord and cast down to the ground, so that the elegant metaphor of the vine-stock might preserve the ruins of Jerusalem; for however beautiful a vine may be and however far it stretches out with long runners, unless you raise up stakes and reeds, joined to the earth it dries up from the heat, especially if the burning wind, which the Greeks call καύσωνα [the scorching wind], has dried up its fruits, so that it withers and is burned as though by the blazing heat of fire. But as for what has been added in the Seventy, And they were avenged, in place of what is written in the Hebrew, They withered, what coherence it can have I am unable to know.

19:13.t: That vine, then, of such abundance and of such fruits and of such beauty, how is it now carried over into the desert, in a land impassable and thirsty? And it signifies the land of Babylon, to which they were carried over, or Egypt, where they fled for refuge, or the land of Judea itself, in which a few poor people remained, over whom Gedaliah was set to gather and rule the remnant of the people; against him there rose up, from the royal stock and from the rod of the branches of the vine, Ishmael, who killed him at Mizpah and devoured all the fruit of the vine; and from then on there was not in that vine a strong rod and a scepter of rulers: for none of the kings remained to govern the people, but with Johanan, the son of Kareah, they fled to Egypt. Therefore it is a lament and a parable of lamentation, so that the royal line may be lamented, which will thenceforth cease in Judea until he should come for whom it is reserved: And he was the expectation of the nations.

20:1.t: And it came to pass in the seventh year, in the fifth, on the tenth of the month, there came men of the elders of Israel to inquire of the Lord, and they sat before me. Eleven months and five days after the previous vision, the word again comes to the prophet, after some of the elders of the house of Israel had come to inquire of the Lord and had sat before him. That it was the custom of the people of Israel to seek from the Lord through the prophets whatever they desired to know, many examples testify: Saul, looking for the asses, goes to Samuel and received advice from the servant boy to offer the prophet the fourth part of a shekel; when the son of Jeroboam fell ill, his wife is sent to Shiloh to the prophet Ahijah, bringing little gifts, loaves and cakes, grapes and a small jar of honey, to learn about her son's sickness; David too, a prophet, inquires of another prophet, Nathan, whether he ought to build a temple to the Lord; and Ahab asks whether he should go up to Ramoth-gilead or not; […]

20:3.t: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, speak to the elders of Israel, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Have you come to inquire of me? As I live, I will not answer you, says the Lord God. To the saints and to those who ask fitting things a promise is given: 'While you are still speaking I will say: Behold, I am here'; but to sinners, such as the elders of Israel were, whose crimes the prophet describes in what follows, no answer is given, but a rebuke for their sins, and he adds an oath: As I live, so that the sentence of the one who refuses may be the firmer. What the Seventy said: If I answer you, Symmachus translated more plainly: I will not answer you.

20:4.t: If you judge them, if you judge, son of man. (LXX: "If I avenge them with vengeance, son of man.") 'They indeed came to inquire, wishing to learn the future concerning the things about which they are in doubt. But you, son of man, judge them, so that there may be no prophet's answer, but the sentence of one who judges, for the iniquities which they have committed, and they have followed the crimes of their fathers'; or certainly: If I avenge them with vengeance, so that the sense is: 'They are covered with such great iniquity that they are not worthy even of correction and reproof', according to what is said in the prophet: I will no longer visit your daughters and your daughters-in-law, when they have committed adultery. Hence sinners too, who have come into the depth of sin, are let go to do the desires of their heart.

Show them the abominations of their fathers. And you shall say to them. (LXX: "Testify to them the iniquities of their fathers, and you shall say to them.") If the sins of the fathers do not overflow onto the sons, how is it that the abominations and iniquities of the fathers are now set before the elders? For this reason, evidently: that they may be shown to act like their parents and, by a hereditary evil, to drag a very long rope of sins, so that they may dread the punishments of those whose vices they imitate.

20:5.t: Thus says the Lord God: On the day when I chose Israel, and lifted up my hand for the stock of the house of Jacob, and appeared to them in the land of Egypt, and lifted up my hand for them, saying: I am the Lord your God. On that day I lifted up my hand for them, to lead them out of the land of Egypt into the land which I had provided for them, flowing with milk and honey, which is excellent among all lands. (LXX: "Thus says the Lord God: From the day on which I chose the house of Israel, and became known to the seed of the house of Jacob, and was known to them in the land of Egypt, and took them up, saying: I am the Lord your God. On that day I took hold of them with my hand, saying, to lead them out of the land of Egypt into the land which I prepared for them, a land flowing with milk and honey, it is a honeycomb beyond all lands.") […]

20:7.t: And he said to them: Let each one cast away the offenses of his eyes, and do not be defiled with the idols of Egypt: I am the Lord your God. (LXX: "And he said to them: Let each one cast away the abominations of his eyes, and let him not be defiled with the inventions of Egypt: I am the Lord your God.") For 'offenses', which in Hebrew are called 'seccuse', Symmachus translated 'nauseating things', the second edition of Aquila 'cuttings-off', so as to signify that bleariness must be cast away from the eyes, and a kind of nausea which not only hinders the sight but also produces vomiting in those who look at it; 'gelule' too is a Hebrew word, which the Seventy translated 'inventions', the first edition of Aquila 'defilements', the second, and Symmachus and Theodotion, 'idols', whom we too have followed for the present. He commanded them, as they were first going out of Egypt, to forget the idols which they had served for a long time; […]

20:8.t: And they provoked me. (LXX: "And they withdrew from me.") Or, as Symmachus translated: They did not consent to me; and as soon as they are called, they withdraw from God, so that there is no interval between the calling and the withdrawal. And this is to be noted, that no one withdraws from God except one who was formerly with him; hence the dragon too in the book of Job is called ἀποστάτης, a transgressor and one who withdraws.

And they would not listen; each one did not cast away the abominations of his eyes, nor did they abandon the idols of Egypt. (LXX: "And they would not listen to me; they did not cast away the abominations of their eyes, and did not abandon the inventions of Egypt.") 'For this reason', he says, 'they provoked me and withdrew from me: because they would not listen, while man's free will is preserved, and they did all the things which I commanded in the law that they should not do, at once despairing of salvation and muttering against Moses, and distrusting the promises of God'. There follows:

And I said that I would pour out my indignation upon them, and fulfill my wrath on them in the midst of the land of Egypt. 'As soon as I commanded them to leave or cast away the offenses of their eyes and by no means to be defiled with the idols of Egypt, they provoked me and would not listen to what I said, but on the contrary did what I had commanded should not be done. Therefore I had decreed to pour out on them my fury and my indignation and to fulfill my wrath, which I had conceived in my mind, in the midst of Egypt, upon those who had not yet gone out of Egypt'. For there follows: I therefore cast them out of the land of Egypt and led them down into the desert, from which it is shown that they had not yet gone out of the land of Egypt when he wished to pour out his indignation and fulfill his wrath upon them and to strike them in the midst of the land of Egypt.

20:9.t: And I acted for my name's sake, that it might not be profaned before the nations in whose midst they were, and among whom I appeared to them, to lead them out of the land of Egypt. 'What I was thinking of doing on account of justice I did not do on account of the greatness of my clemency, lest my name be defiled and I should seem not to have been able to fulfill what I had promised to Israel. I spared my name, then, lest the nations among whom I became known to them in the land of Egypt should have occasion to blaspheme'. Up to this point the prophet describes what he promised them while they were settled in the land of Egypt, and how they at once gave offense, and what the Lord thought of doing against them and yet did not do; what follows he spoke to them after they had gone out of Egypt.

20:10.t: I therefore cast them out of the land of Egypt, and led them out into the desert. And I gave them my precepts, and showed them my judgments, which a man should do and live in them. Moreover I also gave them my sabbaths, that it might be a sign between me and them, and that they might know that I am the Lord who sanctifies them. And the house of Israel provoked me in the desert: they did not walk in my precepts, and they cast away my judgments, which, if a man does them, he shall live in them, and they violated my sabbaths exceedingly. I said therefore that I would pour out my fury upon them in the desert and consume them. And I acted for my name's sake, that it might not be profaned before the nations from which I cast them out in their sight. […]

20:12.t: For indeed the Sabbath did at the first confer many and great benefits; for instance, it made them gentle towards those of their household, and humane; it taught them God's providence and the creation, as Ezekiel saith; it trained them by degrees to abstain from wickedness, and disposed them to regard the things of the Spirit.
20:12.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 39:3

20:12.t: It is this truth that we shall realize perfectly when we shall be perfectly at rest and perfectly see that it is he who is God.

20:13.t: These precepts and ordinances and the observance of the sabbath the Lord gave in the desert, so that doing them they might live in them, not that they should pass from them to greater things, as is promised in the Gospel; and these they violated, not once nor a little but exceedingly, so that the ἐπίτασις [intensification] of the violation might be shown. He said, therefore, and decreed in his mind, that he would pour out his fury upon them in the desert and consume them, when he spoke to Moses: Let me alone, and, angered with fury against them, I will destroy them; but he would not do it, sparing the Egyptians and the other nations, lest they be scandalized, and them as well, on whom he had mercy, awaiting the repentance of those who would turn back. […]

20:15.t: I therefore lifted up my hand over them into the desert, not to bring them into the land which I gave them, flowing with milk and honey, the foremost of all lands; because they cast away my judgments, and did not walk in my precepts, and violated my sabbaths, for their heart went after idols. And my eye spared them, so that I did not kill them; nor did I consume them in the desert. (LXX: "And I lifted up my hand over them in the desert, so as not at all to bring them into the land which I gave them, a land flowing with milk and honey, it is a honeycomb beyond every land; because they rejected my ordinances, and did not walk in my precepts, and violated my sabbaths, and they walk after the thoughts of their hearts. And my eye spared them, so that I did not wipe them out; and I did not kill them to consumption in the desert.") […]

20:17.t: 'But my eye', he says, 'spared them, so that I did not kill them and wipe them out: so that I did not consume them altogether'; in which it is asked how he spared those whose corpses lay in the wilderness and, except for Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh, no one entered the land of promise. From this we understand that they live, and are not reserved for eternal punishments, nor blotted out of the book of the living, nor consumed before the face of the Lord; for if, because they were not brought into the land of promise, they must be believed to have perished, then Moses too perished, who only saw the land of promise and did not enter it, of whom the Lord speaks in the book of Joshua: Moses my servant is dead, and in Malachi: Remember the law of Moses my servant, and in Jeremiah God speaks of him as of his friend and most intimate: If Moses and Samuel should stand in my sight? […]

20:18.t: But he said to their sons in the wilderness: In the precepts (or statutes) of your fathers do not walk, and neither with their idols nor keep their judgments (or be defiled by thoughts). I am the Lord your God: walk in my precepts, and keep my judgments and do them, and sanctify my sabbaths, that it may be a sign between me and you, and that it may be known (or that you may know) that I am the Lord your God. After the slaying of the fathers who fell in the wilderness, he gives precepts to the sons, in whose salvation he had mercy on the fathers: 'And the eye of the Lord', he says, 'spared them, so as not to kill them altogether and wipe them out, but to preserve the fathers in the sons'; and he testifies to them the same things that he also spoke to the fathers: that, after they have walked in his precepts and kept his judgments and observed the sanctification of the sabbath, which was given as a sign, they may then know that he is the Lord their God. […]

20:21.t: And the sons exasperated me; they did not walk in my precepts, and did not keep my judgments to do them, which, when a man has done them, he shall live in them, and they violated my sabbaths; and I threatened to pour out my fury upon them, and to fulfill my wrath on them in the desert. But I turned back my hand and acted for my name's sake, that it might not be profaned before the nations from which I cast them out in their eyes. 'But the sons too', he says, 'followed the crimes of their parents and did all that those had done; hence they too deserved a like sentence; but they were preserved by the same greatness of my mercy as their fathers too, and for the same reasons for which I also had mercy on the fathers, so that I, the one and the same Creator of both, might soften my wrath with a like patience'. We run through the plain things so as to pass on to the more obscure.

20:23.t: How could it be shown from the testimony of the prophets, already received among the Gentiles in the New Testament, that the promise which God made to Abraham has been fulfilled through the coming of Christ? — It is written in the prophet Isaiah: “My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations” (Isa. 56:7). But perhaps the Jews will say: The house of God, that is, the synagogue, is open to all. Nor do we object; yet in such a way that, as always, the circumcised join themselves to the Law. For their Law is that by which they were commanded, after the manner of Abraham, to be circumcised. Therefore, nothing new can seem to be signified by this example of the prophet; since anyone coming from any nation has never been forbidden from the beginning of Judaism to join himself to the Law. Nothing new spoken by the prophet can be thought, indeed it would be unessential, if the Gentiles have always been admitted to serve the God of Abraham and are never found to have been forbidden. […]
20:23.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 44: HOW THE PROMISE TO ABRAHAM WAS FULFILLED IN CHRIST

20:23.t: Again I lifted up my hand against them in the wilderness, to scatter them among the nations and winnow them into the lands, because they had not done my judgments, and had rejected my precepts, and had violated my sabbaths, and their eyes had been after the idols (or thoughts) of their fathers. Therefore I too gave them precepts not good, and judgments in which they shall not live; and I defiled them in their gifts, when they offered (or made pass over) everything that opens the womb, for their transgressions (for which the Seventy translated that I might destroy them. And what they passed over:), and they shall know that I am the Lord. Where in the Old Testament the Lord lifted up his hand against the sons of those who fell in the wilderness, wishing to scatter them among the nations, Scripture does not say, but from what he relates here we must believe that it happened; […]

Wherefore speak to the house of Israel, son of man, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Still in this too your fathers blasphemed me, when they had spurned me with contempt, and I had brought them into the land over which I lifted up my hand to give it to them; they saw every high hill and every leafy tree, and they sacrificed their victims there, and there they gave the provocation of their offering, and there they set their odor of sweetness and poured out their libations. And I said to them: What is the high place to which you go in? And its name was called 'high place' to this day. (LXX: "Therefore speak to the house of Israel, son of man, and you shall say to them: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Even to this your fathers provoked me to anger in their transgressions by which they fell away against me, and I brought them into the land over which I lifted up my hand to hand it over to them; […]

20:24.t: Therefore they are said to tell fables, not the truth; for they think that one must never depart from the things that Moses handed down, as, for example, concerning foods, or marriages, or new moons, or the blood of a weasel, or a house unclean for seven days; though they know that their forefathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were justified without these things and were called friends of God; and as the prophet Ezekiel testifies that, because they had profaned the law of God and his justifications, they received precepts and commandments that were not good, in which they could not be justified. Hence the Lord too says to the Jews: Because Moses wrote these things for the hardness of your heart (Mark 10:5). Hence it is that the apostle Peter too: Why do you lay, he says, a yoke upon the necks of the brethren, which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear (Acts 15:10)? For if they had been useful, they would have been given then, when the Law too was given on the tablets; […]

20:25.t: For as regards the former people, what good or perfect thing could be commanded to those who murmured and contradicted? Indeed, a little later they even turn to idols, and forgetful of the benefits and wonders of God they set up the head of a calf. For this reason, therefore, precepts are given to them, in which they may be tested. Hence it is that also through the prophet Ezekiel the Lord says to them: "I gave you precepts and ordinances that were not good, in which you shall not live by them"; for being tested in the precepts of the Lord they are not found faithful.

We hold, then, that the law has a twofold sense—the one literal, the other spiritual—as has been shown by some before us. Of the first or literal sense it is said, not by us but by God, speaking in one of the prophets, that "the statutes are not good, and the judgments not good"; whereas, taken in a spiritual sense, the same prophet makes God say that "his statutes are good, and his judgments are good."

This Law, then, he says, works wrath; for these things were added by God when angry, so that they might be a burden upon the unbelief of the Jews. In matters so many, it is inevitable that something be omitted. Therefore the Apostle Peter says: “Why,” he asks, “do you put a yoke upon the neck of the brothers which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?” (Acts 15:10). Finally, God says through the prophet Jeremiah: “I gave them statutes that were not good” (Ezek. 20:25). For after many offenses and temptings of God, and insults against Moses and detractions from God, these things were given for them to observe, so that their stiff neck might be pressed down, and wherever they turned, they would have the Law, so that there might be no refreshment for them.
20:25.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 46: WHY THE LAW IS BOTH HOLY AND WORKS WRATH

20:25.t: WHY WERE CIRCUMCISION AND PRECEPTS GIVEN TO THE PEOPLE, WHICH PREVIOUSLY DID NOT EXIST AND NOW ARE NO LONGER HELD IN AUTHORITY? — Circumcision is a sign of Abraham’s faith, so that when this sign was seen in his sons, it might be known that they were his sons, who, believing God, had received this sign (Gen. 17:10–11). But the commandments about Sabbaths and things past were given as testimony, and about things to come which were to have a figure (Exod. 20:9–11). For the future Sabbath, in which He will grant rest in eternity, is foreshadowed by this Sabbath that was made in the completed week. The law of foods, however, was not given at the beginning of the Law, but when, under a leader, they were faithless and did not want to give faith to God’s words and promises, they received, because of the hardness of their heart, precepts that were not good, as the prophet Jeremiah says (Ezek. 20:25). This was done so that their neck might be pressed down, for their own improvement. […]
20:25.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 10: WHY WERE CIRCUMCISION AND PRECEPTS GIVEN?

20:25.t: For a paedagogus, as the word is rendered in the Latin, is the teacher of a boy; and he cannot apply perfect precepts to an imperfect age, because it cannot bear them. Again, the God of the Law says by the Prophet, I gave them also statutes that were not good, that is, not perfect. But the same God has preserved more perfect things for the Gospel, as He says, I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil the Law.

They, it is well known, when they led not a life of toil but indulged in relaxation, not being able to bear prosperity, fell away into ungodliness. What then did God upon this? He laid upon them a multitude of laws with a view to restrain their licence. And to convince you that these laws contribute not to any virtue, but were given to them as a sort of curb, providing them with an occasion of perpetual labor; hear what saith the prophet concerning them; "I gave them statutes which were not good." What means, "not good?" Such as did not much contribute towards virtue. Wherefore he adds also, "and ordinances whereby they shall not live."

And Ezekiel, in the person of God: "I led out", he says, "them", that is, the people of the Jews, "from the land of Egypt: and I led them into the desert: and I gave them my precepts, and showed them my justifications: which a man shall do, and live in them" (Ezek. 20:10). But concerning that law which works wrath, to which the Apostle too died, he adds afterward: "And I gave them precepts that were not good, and justifications in which they shall not live in them" (ibid., 25).

But let us not think that to live in them are the words of the Apostle, but of the prophet Ezekiel, who says: "And I led them out into the desert, and I gave them my precepts, and showed them my ordinances, which a man shall do, and shall live in them" (Ezek. 20:10, 11). And when he had said that those who had walked in the precepts and ordinances live, he added: "And I gave them precepts not good, and ordinances in which they should not live in them" (ibid., 25). How much care in the words! Where he said: "I gave them precepts and ordinances in which they should live in them", he did not add "good". But where he put "in which they should not live in them", he added: "And I gave them precepts not good, and ordinances in which they shall not live in them". But these things more fully in Ezekiel: now let us return to the order of the Epistle.

In another way, however, we shall affirm that the weak and needy elements are the traditions of the Jews and the base understanding according to the letter, which are statutes that are not good and precepts that are not good. For the spiritual understanding of the Law is strong and rich (Ezek. 20), so that either it ought not to be called an element at all, or it is indeed an element by comparison with the age to come and with the life in Christ Jesus, by which the angels and the heavenly powers now live. But compared with the Jewish sense, it should be called not so much an element, that is, a beginning, as perfection.

This too can be said: that before the offense they received only the Decalogue, but after the idolatry and blasphemy the manifold ceremonies of the law, so that they would rather offer to God the victims which they were offering to demons, and, by comparison with sacrilege, what was not good in itself would become lighter: by no means evil, because they were offered to God, and yet not good, because they had offended the author of good.

And to produce something still plainer, even the vital precepts of the law itself, which are said to have been "given byangels by the the hand of a mediator," and of which the same Apostle says: "So the law indeed is holy and the commandment is holy and just and good," when they are compared with the perfection of the gospel are pronounced anything but good by the Divine oracle: for He says: "And I gave them precepts that were not good, and ordinances whereby they should not live in them." The Apostle also affirms that the glory of the law is so dimmed by the light of the New Testament that he declares that in comparison with the splendour of the gospel it is not to be considered glorious, saying: "For even that which was glorious was not glorified by reason of the glory that excelleth."
20:25.s: The Third Conference of Abbot Theonas, Chapter 4

20:27.t: 'But you, son of man, speak again to them, that is, to the elders of the house of Israel who came to inquire of you: Your fathers, from whose stock you are descended, blasphemed me in this too and held me for nothing: after I had brought them into the land, which they possessed by my strength, which I had given them to possess, they turned it to provoking me; for when they had seen every high hill and leafy tree, they sacrificed on the mountains and in the groves and in the woodlands, and sacrificed victims to idols, and poured out offerings; and when I saw this, I said to them: What is 'bama' — for this means 'high place' —, or why do you go into such a place, which you have chosen for yourselves on all the hills, so that to this day places of this kind are called 'bamoth' and the ancient error keeps its former name?'.

20:29.t: For 'bama', which we rendered as 'high place', an error has prevailed in the edition of the Seventy, so that ἀβανὰ is written, which means nothing in the Hebrew language; 'bama', if you divide its two syllables into two words, can mean 'in what', but that sense does not fit the present passage; but wherever it is written in the books of Kings and Chronicles: Still the people burned incense and sacrificed on the high place, 'bama' in the singular and 'bamoth' in the plural mean 'high places'.

20:30.t: Therefore say to the house of Israel: Thus says the Lord God: You are defiled in the way of your fathers, and you commit fornication after their stumbling-blocks, and in the offering of your gifts, when you make your sons pass through the fire, you are defiled with all your idols to this day; and shall I answer you, house of Israel? As I live, says the Lord God, I will not answer you. 'You imitate the vices of your fathers and walk by the same ways, so that like offenses deserve a like punishment too; and you have advanced so far in crimes that you consecrate your sons to demons through fire, nor is it enough to have done this once, but even at present you do the same things; not that the elders in captivity do these things, but that those who were staying in Jerusalem and over whom captivity was hanging do not cease to do all these things. And when you are bound by such great outrages, do you seek', he says, 'my answer? As I live, says the Lord, and I swear by my own self, I will not answer you'. And what follows:

20:32.t: The first Passover is of the first people; the second Passover is ours. For we were "unclean in soul", we who "worshiped wood and stone" and "not knowing God served those who by nature were not gods". We also were those who "were journeying far", of whom the Apostle says that we were "strangers and sojourners from the covenants of God, having no hope and without God in this world".

Nor shall the thought of your mind come to pass, of you who say: We will be like the nations and like the families of the earth, to worship wood and stones. As I live, says the Lord God, with a strong hand and with an outstretched arm and with fury poured out I will reign over you, has this sense: 'Do not think that your thoughts, by which you blaspheme against me, can be fulfilled; for you say: We do not wish to be under the Lord nor to be called his people, but, as all the nations in the whole world are, and each people lives by its own will, so as to worship wood and stones and serve idols, we too will be one nation out of many'.

20:33.t: To which God replies, and swears by himself, and says: 'I will not leave you nor despise you, as negligent masters are accustomed to despise runaway slaves, but I will drag you back to my rule, and with arm outstretched and striking I will reduce you to your former servitude and reign over you, so that, whether you will or not, you may have me as king, and may feel as an angry king him whose clemency you neglected'.

20:34.t: And I will lead you out from the peoples, and gather you from the lands in which you are scattered; with a mighty hand, and an outstretched arm, and with fury poured out I will reign over you. 'I will not suffer you', he says, 'to be among the nations nor to be held in eternal captivity, but I will lead you out from the peoples and gather you from the lands into which hostile necessity has scattered you here and there to be slaves; and I will do these things not to destroy you and wipe you out, but to be your king'. From this we understand that even what the heretics call the cruelty of the Creator sounds of clemency, since he is angry and rages and pours out all his fury for this purpose: to draw back to his kingdom those who had chosen the tyranny of demons, and that to be its slaves.

20:35.t: And I will bring you into the desert of the peoples, and there I will enter into judgment with you face to face. As I contended in judgment against your fathers in the desert of the land of Egypt, so will I judge you, says the Lord, and I will subject you to my scepter, and bring you into the bonds of the covenant. And I will pick out from you the transgressors and the ungodly, and I will lead them out of the land of their sojourning, and they shall not enter the land of Israel, and you shall know that I am the Lord. 'I will do', he says, 'to you who are in Babylon and now serve idols what I did to your fathers in Egypt: I will lead you out into the desert of the peoples and there enter into judgment with you face to face, as I contended in judgment against them when they went out of Egypt; […]

20:37.t:
[Passage quoted, Ezek. xx. 36.]

Here, again, is a clear witness that but few will come under God's staff, and that this will be when the rest of Israel has fallen away from the promises.
20:37.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 2, Chapter 3

20:38.t: But the transgressors and the ungodly, who in hardness of heart persevere in evil works, I will pick out from you, not to possess them but to cast them away; and I will indeed lead them out of the land of their sojourning, so that, once led out, they may not enter the land of Israel but perish in diverse regions, and that, by the distinction of the good and the evil, you may know that I am the Lord who do all things with judgment'. The discourse hastens on to what remains, and we run briefly through each point, so as to offer readers only the sense.

20:39.t: And you, house of Israel, thus says the Lord God: Walk each of you after your idols, and serve them. But if in this too you do not listen to me, and pollute my holy name any more with your gifts and with your idols. (LXX: "And you, house of Israel, thus says Adonai the Lord: Let each one take away his inventions; and after this, if you listen to me, and do not pollute my holy name any more with your gifts and with your pursuits.") Symmachus translated this passage more plainly: Each of you, go and serve your idols, since you would not listen to me. But my holy name do not pollute any more through your gifts and images. But on my holy mountain, on the high mountain of Israel, says the Lord God, there all the house of Israel shall serve me. Symmachus' translation has this meaning: 'Since you do not wish to serve me, go, serve idols and tread in the footsteps of your images; […]

20:40.t: On my holy mountain, on the high mountain of Israel, says the Lord God, there all the house of Israel shall serve me: all, I say, in the land in which they shall please me; and there I will require your firstfruits and the beginning of your tithes in all your sanctifications. In an odor of sweetness I will receive you, when I have led you out from the peoples and gathered you from the lands into which you were scattered, and I shall be sanctified in you in the eyes of the nations. And you shall know that I am the Lord. Of this mountain, on which all the house of Israel is to serve God, Isaiah and Micah sang with one voice: In the last days the mountain of the house shall be manifest on the summit of the mountains and shall be raised above the hills; and all the nations shall flow to it, and many peoples shall go and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will teach us his ways and we will walk in his paths; […]

20:42.t: When I bring you into the land of Israel, into the land for which I lifted up my hand to give it to your fathers. 'Then you shall know that I am the Lord, when I bring you', he says, 'into the land of Israel, for which I lifted up my hand to bring your fathers into it, which they lost by their own fault and which you have received back not so much by your own merit as by my clemency'.

20:43.t: And you shall remember your ways and all your crimes, with which you were defiled in them; and you shall be displeasing to yourselves in your own sight in all your wickednesses which you have done. And you shall know that I am the Lord, when I have done good to you for my name's sake, not according to your evil ways nor according to your most wicked crimes, house of Israel, says the Lord God. We cannot remember our crimes and vices unless we have been brought into the land of Israel and, set there, say with the Apostle: I who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God. And you shall be displeasing, he says, to yourselves in your own sight in all your wickednesses which you have done (or, as Symmachus translated: And you shall seem little to yourselves because of all your wickednesses which you have wrought), so that, after they have been exalted, they may believe themselves to be lowly, because: The Lord gives grace to the humble, and in another place it is written: Before crushing […]

But that, when we do not always resist or remain persistently unwilling, everything is granted to us by God, and that the main share in our salvation is to be ascribed not to the merit of our own works but to heavenly grace, we are thus taught by the words of the Lord Himself: "And you shall remember your ways and all your wicked doings with which you have been defiled; and you shall be displeased with yourselves in your own sight for all your wicked deeds which you have committed. And you shall know that I am the Lord, when I shall have done well by you for My own name's sake, not according to your evil ways, nor according to your wicked deeds, O house of Israel."
20:43.s: The Third Conference of Abbot Chaeremon, Chapter 18

20:44.t: And you shall know that I am the Lord, when I have done good to you: and we came to know the Lord Savior the more at that time when he did good to us and suffered for our sins and bore our iniquities and grieved for us, not for any merit of those who are saved but for his name's sake; otherwise our ways and most wicked crimes deserved not mercy but punishment. But whatever we have said of the people of Israel, which, freed from Egypt, committed many things in the wilderness and offended God, and afterward, brought into the land of promise, venerated idols and worshiped wood and stones, and afterward was preserved by the clemency of God, let us refer to those who have been freed from the Egypt of this world by the high hand of the Lord and, brought into the wilderness of vices, sighed again for Egypt and did the things for which they ought to have been punished, but nonetheless, through repentance, not by their own merit but by the clemency of the Lord, have been preserved.

20:46.t: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set your face against the way of the south, and drip toward the southwest, and prophesy to the forest of the southern field. And you shall say to the southern forest: Hear the word of the Lord: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will kindle a fire in you, and I will burn up in you all green wood and all dry wood; the flame of the kindling shall not be extinguished, and every face shall be burned in it from the south to the north: and all flesh shall see that I the Lord have kindled it, and it shall not be extinguished. And I said: Ah, ah, ah, Lord God; they say of me: Does not this man speak in parables? (LXX: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, make firm your face upon Theman, and look toward Darom, prophesy upon the forest, the leader Nageb. And you shall say to the forest Nageb: Hear the speech of the Lord: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will kindle a fire in you, and it shall devour in you all green wood and all dry wood; […]

And beautifully, at the beginning: Drip, he says, toward the southwest, so that not the whole wrath of God may seem to be poured out, but a kind of drip and a part. But if there is such savagery in a drip, what must be reckoned of whole downpours, so that all flesh, which is to see the salvation of God, may know through the burning of the woods and through the flame that is extinguished by no one's help that he himself is the Lord?

Tropologically, however, Theman and Nageb and Darom can be understood as Egypt; for we read in Daniel that the south is frequently taken for Egypt; and Egypt refers to the straits of this world. Ezekiel therefore prophesies the evils that are to come upon the world, which he calls a forest, one that has no fruit-bearing trees but is a dwelling-place of beasts, of which it is also said in Psalm 28 (29): The voice of the Lord perfecting the stags, and he will uncover the thickets of the woods. These are the woods and forests that devoured more of Absalom's army in the battle than the sword killed. And in the forests the green wood is kindled first, and then the dry: those who live in evil, and those who are dead to righteousness. […]

20:47.t: The divine word, then, speaks through the μεταφορὰν [metaphor] of a forest against Jerusalem, which is a dwelling of beasts and of fierce men, saying that he will set it on fire and that all its wood will be burned up together; by no means does he call trees those that were lacking in fruit, but wood, as if made ready for burning. And first he burns in it the green wood, according to what we read in this same prophet: And begin from my holy ones, and afterward the dry, which could have nothing living in itself; that is, the saints and the sinners together, so that some by captivity may escape an evil death, while others are handed over to eternal punishments. And what he adds, From the south to the north, indicates this: from Jerusalem to Babylon, so that the whole road of those going into captivity may be filled with those falling by sword, famine and pestilence; […]

20:49.t: Understanding this, the prophet answered: Ah, ah, ah, Lord God (or, as the Seventy translated: By no means, Lord), and he adds: They say to me: Does not this man speak in parables? (or: Is this a parable which is spoken?), and the sense is: 'Speak more plainly; we do not understand what you are saying in a parable; open to us the meaning of God in plain speech'.

And the prophet prays that what the Lord has threatened may not come to pass, that is, that the forest may not be set on fire and all the wood burned up together, so that either they may still receive room for repentance, or the necessity of announcing sad things may not be laid upon him, especially since the people do not understand them and are provoked rather to madness by the obscurity of the sayings.

21:2.t: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set your face toward Jerusalem, and distil toward the sanctuaries, and prophesy against the ground of Israel. And you shall say to the land of Israel: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, and I will cast out my sword from its sheath, and I will kill in you the righteous and the wicked. But because I have killed in you the righteous and the wicked, my sword shall go forth from its sheath against all flesh, from the south to the north, and all flesh shall know that I the Lord have drawn my sword from its sheath, irrevocable. (LXX: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Therefore prophesy, son of man, and set firm your face against Jerusalem, and look toward their holy places, and prophesy over the land of Israel. And you shall say to the land of Israel: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, and I will draw out my sword from its sheath, and I will slay out of you the lawless and the unrighteous. […]

21:5.t: And what he had said there: And all flesh shall see that I the Lord have kindled it, that is, the forest or the flame, and it shall not be quenched, here he says in other words: That all flesh may know that I the Lord have drawn my sword from its sheath, irrevocable. For truly, for Jerusalem the flame has not been lulled to sleep, nor the fire quenched, nor the sword recalled, because there was a short time in between, and Jerusalem, with its temple, was set ablaze by Babylonian fire.

21:6.t: And you, son of man, groan in the breaking of the loins, and in bitternesses groan before them. And when they say to you: Why do you groan?, you shall say: For the report, because it comes, and every heart shall melt, and all hands shall be loosened, and every spirit shall grow weak, and waters shall flow down all knees; behold, it comes, and it shall be done, says the Lord. (LXX: "And you, son of man, groan in the breaking of your loins, and in griefs groan in their sight. And it shall be, if they say to you: Why do you groan?, then you shall say: Because of the tidings, because it comes, and every heart shall be seized, and all hands shall be loosened, and all flesh and every spirit shall be tested, and all thighs shall be defiled with moisture; behold, it comes, and it shall be, says the Lord God.") First he had said: 'Prophesy, or distil, toward the south, the southwest and the noonday, and toward the southern forest'. […]

21:9.t: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, prophesy, and you shall say: Thus says the Lord God: Speak. The sword, the sword is sharpened and filed; it is sharpened to slaughter victims, and it is filed that it may gleam: you who move the scepter of my son, you have cut down every tree. And I have given it to be polished, that it may be held in the hand; this sword is sharpened, and this one is filed, that it may be in the hand of the slayer. Cry out and howl, son of man, because this one has come among my people, this one among all the leaders of Israel who had fled; they have been handed over to the sword with my people, therefore clap upon your thigh, because it has been proved, and this when it has overturned the scepter and it shall be no more, says the Lord God. You therefore, son of man, prophesy, and strike hand against hand, and let the sword be doubled, and let the sword of the slain be tripled. […]

According to the ἀναγωγὴν [anagogy, the higher sense] we can take the sharpened sword, prepared for slaughter, as the devil, of whom the Apostle says: To hand over such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved; and in another place: Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme; and in the Psalms it is written: He sent fury and wrath and distress, a sending by most evil angels. Some think that this sword was also in the hand of the angel when Jerusalem was struck under David. Others, however, suspect that it is also said of that sword of which it is written in the Gospel: 'I came not to send peace upon the earth, but a sword, and to divide among themselves every bond of kinship, so that the wicked may fall and the saints rise again'. […]

21:12.t: Therefore, O prophet, cry out and howl, and bear witness to the impending evils with the lamentation of your voice. This sword has spared no one, nor left anyone without a share in the impending evils. It has come among the people, it has come among the leaders of Israel, it has come among my guests and the priests who dwelt in my temple. Therefore strike your thigh, or your hand, and take on the bearing of a mourner. For this sword has been proved by me, and this when it has overturned my scepter and kingdom, which shall be no more and shall come to its end in King Zedekiah.

21:14.t: Again I command you, prophet, that you, who had struck your thigh in astonishment and wonder, should strike your hands also, so that not only once but a second and a third time the sword may come to slay'. For Nebuchadnezzar had come the first time when he carried off Jeconiah, and the second time when Jehoiakim reigned, the third time when Zedekiah did. 'And this is the tripled sword, when a great slaughter took place, and it multiplied the ruins to such a degree that they were stunned in mind and melted in heart, and it caused confusion in all their gates'.

21:16.t: It is commanded therefore to it, that is, to the sword sharpened and filed to flash, clad and ready and prepared for slaughter, that it go to the right if it so wishes, or to the left. 'Wherever', he says, 'it pleases your face, enter boldly, having me as your leader and helper. I will clap hand against hand, so that, as your patron and exhorter, I may spur you on as you rage against my adversaries. Do not hesitate, do not dread and fear to suffer what Sennacherib suffered; I the Lord have spoken; you are the minister of my will, carry out my sentence'.

21:18.t: 'When', he says, 'the divine word had said to me: Prophesy, son of man, and speak to the sword, and say: The sword, the sword, and the rest that the prophecy of the sword contains, a second time the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Do you wish, son of man, to know who this sword is, and to learn more openly the person of the raging sword? Listen to what I say: Set two ways, so that by them the sword of the king of Babylon may come, who will indeed go forth by the one road of the Chaldeans but, when he has come through the desert and the wilderness to the fork of the land of Arabia which is called that of the Ammonites, of which one way leads to Jerusalem on the right-hand side, but the left to Rabbath of the Ammonites' — which is a metropolis and today is named Philadelphia.

21:19.t: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: And you, son of man, set for yourself two ways, and let the sword of the king of Babylon come: both shall go forth from one land; and with his hand he shall take a conjecture, at the head of the way of the city he shall cast it. You shall set a way for the sword to come to Rabbath of the Ammonites, and to Judah, into Jerusalem the most fortified. For the king of Babylon stood at the fork, at the head of the two ways, seeking divination, mixing arrows; he questioned idols, he consulted entrails. At his right hand the divination came out against Jerusalem, to set battering rams, to open the mouth in slaughter, to lift up the voice in howling, to set battering rams against the gates, to heap up a mound, to build siege works. And in their eyes he shall be as one consulting an oracle in vain, and imitating the idleness of the sabbaths; but he himself will remember the iniquity, so as to capture. […]

21:21.t: 'Mindful', he says, 'of the slaughter that befell the Assyrian king when a hundred and eighty-five thousand were cut down in one night, he will be afraid to turn aside to the right-hand side and go against most fortified Jerusalem, but he will stand at the very crossroads and, according to the rite of his nation, will consult the oracle, putting arrows into the quiver and mixing them, inscribed or marked with the names of each, to see whose arrow comes out and which city he ought to attack first' — this the Greeks call βελομαντίαν [belomancy, divination by arrows] or ῥαβδομαντίαν [rhabdomancy, divination by rods] —. 'He questioned the idols, therefore, he consulted the entrails. To the right came his divination, that he should go against Jerusalem and attack it, heap up mounds, set battering rams, build siege works and shut in the city, and in slaughter open his mouth and rouse the roar of an exulting and howling army.

21:23.t: Doing this', he says, 'he will seem to the inhabitants of Jerusalem to consult the oracle in vain, and as it were to wear away the idleness of the sabbaths, namely to play and accomplish no work. But the king of Babylon will trust not in his own strength but in the iniquity of the people, by which he knows that they have offended God and have heaped up the sins of their fathers with new offenses, and that their transgressions have been laid open to all; and therefore he will not doubt of victory, because he will trust in the iniquity of Jerusalem'. This is according to the Hebrew, from which the Seventy disagree in most places, not so much in sense as in words.

21:25.t: But you, profane, wicked leader of Israel, whose day has come, foreordained in the time of iniquity, thus says the Lord God: Take off the miter, take away the crown; is not this that which raised up the lowly and brought low the lofty? Iniquity, iniquity, iniquity I will set it; and this shall not be until he comes whose is the judgment, and I will deliver it to him. (LXX: "And you, profane, lawless leader of Israel, whose day has come in the time of iniquity, the end, thus says the Lord God: You have taken off the miter and put on the crown; this shall not be alike; you have humbled the lofty and raised up the lowly. Iniquity, iniquity I will set it; nor shall this be such, until he comes to whom it is due, and I will give it to him.") Symmachus translated this passage thus: But you, profane, lawless leader of Israel, whose day has come, appointed in the time of iniquity, thus says the Lord God: He has taken off the miter and taken away the crown; neither this nor that; […]

21:26.t: For the miter is the insignia of the high priest; the crown, that is, the diadem, is the mark of a king. 'Is not this the miter and this the crown, which did nothing by judgment but, in imitation of the Babylonian king: Whom he wished he exalted, and whom he wished he humbled?

In the place where we translated: Is not this, Symmachus rendered beautifully: Neither this nor that; for because he had said: Take off the miter, take away the crown, he added: 'Neither this nor that is', that is: 'Both the kingdom and the priesthood shall cease'. Hence, of those who afterwards, until the coming of Christ, were kings and priests alike, one, Hyrcanus the high priest, placed a diadem on his own head and wished in vain to claim both this and that for himself, since the kingdom was not owed to him after Zedekiah, but to him for whom it was laid up and who was the expectation of the nations; of whom Malachi also speaks: You priests, who defile my name, and a little after: My will is not in you, and I will not accept victims from your hands. For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is great among the nations, and in every place sacrifice is made and a pure offering is offered to my name; […]

21:27.t: Therefore, not once nor — according to the Seventy — twice, but a third time I will set iniquity upon you forever, which was not reckoned to you at once, but until Christ comes, whose is the judgment, and the Father delivers to him the kingdom and the priesthood, or the Church gathered from the nations'. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son; and in another place: O God, he says, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king's son; this is he for whom the everlasting rule and priesthood are laid up, of whom Jacob also spoke: A prince shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until he comes for whom it is laid up; and he shall be the expectation of the nations.

21:28.t: And you, son of man, prophesy and say: Thus says the Lord God, to the Ammonites and to their reproach; and you shall say: Blade, blade, unsheathe yourself to slay, file yourself that you may kill and flash, while vain things were seen for you and lies were divined, that you might be set upon the necks of the wounded wicked, whose day has come, foreordained in the time of iniquity; return to your sheath, to the place in which you were created; in the land of your birth I will judge you, and I will pour out my indignation upon you, in the fire of my fury I will blow upon you, and I will give you into the hands of foolish men and of those who fashion destruction.
