27:19.t: Dan and Greece and Mozel set out wrought iron in your fairs; stacte and calamus were in your trade. (LXX: "※ Dan and Iauan and Mozel in your fairs ⁚" — which in their edition were added from Theodotion —; "iron made by workmanship and a wheel is in your mixture.") From the name of the patriarch Dan both the tribe and the place in which the tribe dwelt received their name, where today is Paneas, which was formerly called Caesarea Philippi, whence the river Jordan too obtained its name: 'Ior', that is, stream, 'Dan', which flows from Lebanon; 'Iauan', moreover, sounds 'Greece', which means, as we have said, 'is and is not'; for 'Mozel' too Symmachus translated 'bringing', so that the sense is: 'Dan and Greece brought wrought iron into your fairs, and the rest'; but Aquila for 'Mozel' put 'from Uzal', from which regions we must believe that iron and stacte and calamus were carried to the fairs of Tyre. […]

27:20.t: Dadan were your dealers in carpets for sitting. (LXX: "Dedan were your traders with choice beasts for chariots.") The Hebrew and the Seventy differ much in the present place, except for the name of the region, which is close: 'Dedan' and 'Dadan'. For there is an infinite distance between 'carpets for sitting' and 'choice beasts for chariots'; nor is there any doubt that four-horse teams, chariots and horses are taken in the bad sense if they are earthly; otherwise, of heavenly ones, Elijah too is carried off in a chariot, and is called by Elisha: Father, father, charioteer and chariot of Israel, and the eyes of Gehazi are opened, so that he sees chariots on the mountain and horses without riders, prepared for the Lord's seat; but in the carpets the beauty of words is shown, on which the dealers of Dedan ride and rest, in a composed sitting, coming to the fairs of Tyre.

27:21.t: Arabia and all the princes of Kedar, they were the traders of your hand; with lambs and rams and kids they came to you. For 'lambs, rams and kids' the Seventy translated 'camels and rams and lambs'. Arabia and the princes of Kedar — which today is the region of the Saracens —, as has been shown most fully in the discourse of Jeremiah which is written against Kedar, abound in these animals, namely lambs and rams and kids — and it multiplies the fairs of Tyre by this importation —, and it is also a region most fertile in camels, because of the breadth of the desert's pastures and the mildness of the air, in which this animal delights. 'Arabia', moreover, means 'evening', and 'Cedar' 'darkness', of which it is also said in the Psalms: I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; these regions bring to Tyre camels weighed down with the heaviest burdens of sins, or lambs and rams and kids, which they sacrifice on their altars, which they have feigned out of an iniquitous, rebellious heart. […]

27:22.t: The sellers of Sheba and Rema, they were your traders, with all the first spices and with most precious stone and gold, which they set out in your market. In the Psalms, where it is written: The kings of the Arabians and of Saba will offer gifts to you, in the Hebrew it has: The kings of Saba and Saba will offer gifts to you, of which one 'Saba' is written with the letter 'sen', the other with 'samech', which is like our letter. Since, then, 'Saba' means 'conversion', this must be said: that in the present place it signifies not 'conversion' but 'aversion', from which gifts are brought to Tyre, with all spices and the best odors and precious stone and gold, all of which are set out in the fairs of Tyre; […]

27:23.t: Aran and Chenne and Eden were traders, Saba, Assur, Chelmad your sellers. They were your traders in many ways, in wrappings of hyacinth and of many-threaded cloths and of precious treasures, which were wrapped and bound with ropes. (LXX: "Charran and Channa and Edne, these were traders, Saba, Assur and Chalmad your dealers, bringing trade ※ in Machalim and in Galima ⁚ hyacinth, and ※ polymita ⁚ choice treasures bound with ropes.") These too are nations containing the names of various places. What was added in the Seventy from Theodotion: In Machalim and in Galima, Symmachus translated: In precious wrappings; 'polymita' too, for which Theodotion translated 'varied', we added from Aquila and Symmachus — the garments of the traders were so precious that they were carried in wrappings and bound with ropes of hyacinth —; 'Aran', or, as the Seventy said, 'Charran', sounds in our language 'holes'; 'Chenne', 'preparation'; 'Eden', 'delights', for which among the Seventy is 'Edne', which is not found in the Hebrew; […]

27:24.t: And they have manifold equipment, distinguished with incredible variety, which is bound in wrappings of hyacinth; or their treasures, which they have treasured up for themselves on earth, are bound with ropes, according to what is written: Each one is bound with the ropes of his own sins, and they did not have a free trade, but bound everything with the chains of sins. The wrappings of hyacinth, because of the similarity of the color, I shall refer to the powers of the air, which lavish their treasures on the fairs of the world.

They also had cedars in your trades. The ships of the sea (or, as is contained in the Hebrew: Tharsis) were your princes in your trade. For 'cedars' the Seventy translated 'cypresses'. And since we have spoken of both above, it is superfluous to increase the reader's weariness.

27:25.t: And she was filled and glorified (or weighed down) exceedingly in the heart of the sea. 'Nothing,' he says, 'was lacking to you that pertains to the riches of the islands; yet that glorification was a weighing down of the possessor, since you cannot bear riches with moderation, although poverty too is often a temptation' — whence Solomon too asks only for necessities, and detests riches and poverty alike, lest pride creep in in the one, and in the other impatience and lying.

27:26.t: Your rowers brought you into many waters. Above we read that the rowers of the Tyrian city were the 'Sidonians' and the 'Aradians', of whom the one mean 'hunters', the others 'those who put down': for they hunt the souls of those whom they lead by their own will amid the waves of this age, and they do not lift them up to the heights but sink them into the depths; nor do they imitate those who, sailing until the morning watch, broke the raging waves of the sea and were found worthy to receive the Lord Savior, and at once, with such a passenger and companion, reached the harbor of rest. Of which it is written more fully in the Gospel.

The south wind has shattered you in the heart of the sea. All the riches of Tyre perish when the 'south wind' blows, which more expressively is called in Hebrew 'cadim', and is rendered in Greek καύσων, which we can translate as 'burning wind'; of which the holy man also said: By day the sun will not burn you, nor the moon by night. By this wind Jacob had been burned, and yet not shattered, when he says: I was burned by day by the heat and by the frost of night; those too who were hired from the first hour bore the heat and burning of the whole day, and yet they receive the denarius, because they were burned and not shattered; whence the bride too says in the Song: I am black and beautiful, because there has looked down on me (or, as is better contained in the Hebrew, there has discolored me) the sun.

27:27.t: Your riches and your treasures and your manifold equipment. Many read thus: In the heart of the sea are your riches and your treasures and your manifold equipment, so that all the riches of Tyre and all its substance are set in the heart of the sea and are overwhelmed by the waves of the world, and its inhabitants have nothing stable and lasting, that Gospel word being fulfilled: Fool, this night they will take your soul from you; and what you have prepared, whose will it be?, and that apostolic one: Those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and many snares, and are dragged down into the depth. The history is plain; and therefore we fit short little comments to almost each little verse. For our discourse is already hastening to the end of the book.

Your sailors (or rowers) and your pilots, who held your equipment and were over your people; and your men of war who were in you, with all your multitude which is in your midst, will fall in the heart of the sea on the day of your ruin. The rowers, or sailors, of the Tyrian city — we read that they are the Sidonians and the Aradians, of whom we have already spoken, and, according to the edition of the Seventy, the counselors of 'Byblus', which in Hebrew is called 'gebal' —, its men of war too — Persians, Lydians and Libyans —, will all fall and be shown to be of no account, when Tyre has fallen and all its glory has had the end of ruin; but the multitude — which the Seventy translated 'mixture' —, apart from the princes, signifies the common people, who, without titles of dignity, will be crushed by a like judgment. And the prophecy is mixed between the city and the ship, so that from the one you may understand the other; and yet both pertain to the consummation of the age and to shipwreck.

27:28.t: At the sound of the cry of your pilots the fleets will be troubled, and they will come down from their ships, all who held the oar (or the sailors and all the pilots of the sea), and the passengers and the prow-men will stand on the land, and they will wail over you with a loud voice and cry out bitterly, and they will cast dust upon their heads and be sprinkled with ash (or will strew ash for themselves). But what follows, ※ And they will shave baldness over you, and gird themselves with sackcloth, and weep for you in bitterness of soul with most bitter weeping, and take up over you a mournful song, and lament you ⁚, is not found in the Seventy, but was added from the edition of Theodotion. When Tyre has fallen, its pilots will be troubled and will come down from the fleets, and the rowers and passengers and prow-men — or the sailors and all the pilots of the sea —, tossed by the waves, will at last stand with a firm step; […]

Some, ridiculously — but still, what we have read must be told — interpret the 'pilots' as the bishops of the heretics, the 'counselors' as the presbyters, the 'prow-men' as the archdeacons, the 'rowers' and 'sailors' as the deacons, and they refer the 'passengers' to the whole people — if they had added the 'shipmaster' as the devil, they would have completed the tragedy —, who will all wail together and weep most bitterly and do penance after they have perceived the shipwreck of their ship and have stood on land, and have lost all the beauty of the knowledge falsely so called, and in place of joy and gladness have marked their penance with grief in bitterness of heart.

27:31.t: And they will weep for you, he says, in bitterness of soul with most bitter weeping — for it is better to go into the house of mourning than into the house of feasting —, so that they may lament Tyre and redouble the mournful song; which the following Scripture adds. But that we may know that there is profit for those who lament her as she falls, and who formerly dwelt in the heart of the sea and in its midst, let the example of the prophet teach us, who himself too is commanded to lament Tyre, so that, when the time of penance has been completed, she may be restored to her ancient state, and, having taken up the harp, may sound forth to the Lord: read Isaiah.

27:32.t: Who is like Tyre, which has become dumb (or has fallen silent) in the midst of the sea? — which is not found in the Seventy —. You who, in the going out of your trades (or what reward you found), from the sea filled many peoples, in the multitude of your riches and of peoples enriched many kings; now you have been crushed by the sea (or in the sea), your wealth is in the depths of the waters (or your trade); and all your multitude which was in your midst have fallen. All the inhabitants of the islands were astonished (or were crushed) over you, and all their kings, struck by the storm (or turned to madness), changed their countenances (or wept); the traders of the nations (or of the peoples) hissed over you: you have been brought to nothing (or you have become perdition), and you will be no more for ever (or in perpetuity). […]

27:33.t: 'With how great wares, O Tyre, have you been enriched? And what have you sought with so much labor, that by day and by night you should gather what was to perish by shipwreck? You did indeed fill many peoples and enriched kings with your wealth — of whom it is written: The kings of the earth stood by, and the princes gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ —; but now you have been crushed in the sea and in the depths of the waters' — according to what is written of Pharaoh: The chariots of Pharaoh and his strength he cast into the sea, who sank into the depth like a stone and could say: I came into the depth of the sea, and the storm sank me —.

All these things, moreover, we can refer to the person of the heretics, who, in the crushing and shipwreck of Tyre, will perceive their error, and, set in the midst of the sea, will long to free their souls, and will lament the riches wrongly gathered, with which they had enriched many kings, namely their patriarchs, and the ignoble common people, whose wealth will collapse in the midst of the sea; the inhabitants too of all the islands — if, however, we wish to refer what has been said to the good sense — will be astonished over the crushing of Tyre, and the kings of all the islands either will themselves, as if struck by a storm, change their countenances, or at least will show the grief of their heart with weeping and tears, and will testify to the greatness of their stupor with wonder and hissing, at how she has been brought to nothing and has perished who promised salvation to many nations; […]

27:35.t: 'All the islands, or the inhabitants of the islands, which are beaten by the waves of this age, will be astonished over you, and their kings, struck by the storm, will perceive their own destruction, and, imitating the voice of the serpent, will hiss and say: You have been brought to nothing (or you have become perdition) — so that you had not the nature of perdition, but the will —, and you will not be' — if he had spoken up to this point, a great question would arise: how it should not be, when we now see it built up; but from what follows: 'for ever', he shows the time of one age, which, according to the age of man, is reckoned in a cycle of seventy years —, or 'you will not be to God' — as the Apostle says: Who called the things that were not, and Isaiah the prophet: Behold, all your adversaries will be confounded and will blush; […]

28:2.t: And if thou dost glory in thy wisdom, thou dost not in it excel the Prince of Tyre, whom Ezekiel reproached, saying unto him:—Art thou wiser than Daniel, or hast thou seen by thy wisdom the things that are hid? And if thy mind is puffed up by thy years, that they are many; they are not more in number than those of the Prince of Tyre who ruled the Kingdom during the days of twenty-two Kings of the house of Judah, that is, for four hundred and forty years. And since the years of that King of Tyre were many, all the time he thus said in his heart, I am God and sit in the seat of God in the heart of the seas. But Ezekiel said to him: Thou art a man and thou art not God.

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, say to the prince of Tyre: Thus says the Lord God: Because your heart has been lifted up, and you have said: I am God, and I have sat in the chair of God in the heart of the sea; though you are a man and not God, and you have set your heart as the heart of God. Behold, you are wiser than Daniel, no secret is hidden from you; in your wisdom and your understanding you have made strength for yourself, and you have acquired gold and silver in your treasuries; in the multitude of your wisdom, in your trading you have multiplied strength for yourself, and your heart has been lifted up in your might. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because your heart has been lifted up as the heart of God, therefore behold, I will bring upon you strangers, the mightiest of the nations; and they will bare their swords against the beauty of your wisdom, and they will defile your comeliness. […]

Therefore let us discuss what is written according to both understandings, that of proud kings and equally that of apostate princes: 'Though you are', he says, 'in the midst of the sea, and are held in the narrow confines of an island, and, I will say more, though you are a man and surrounded by the frailty of human flesh, lifted up by the swelling of your heart you have supposed that you dwell on the throne of God, in the heavens; and at the same time, because you boast of wisdom, so much so that the men of your kingdom challenged Solomon with riddles: are you then wiser than Daniel, who by the grace of God overcame all the magi and soothsayers and is now the wisest in Babylon?' […]

28:3.t: Who would refuse the counsel of Daniel, of whom God said, "Who is wiser than Daniel?" How can people doubt about the minds of those to whom God has given such grace? By the counsel of Moses wars were brought to an end, and for his merit's sake food came from heaven and drink from the rock. How pure must have been the soul of Daniel to soften the character of barbarians and to tame the lions! What temperance was his, what self-restraint in soul and body! Not unworthily did he become an object of admiration to all, when—and all people do admire this—though enjoying royal friendships, he looked not for gold or counted the honor given him as more precious than his faith. For he was willing to endure danger for the law of God rather than to be turned from his purpose in order to gain human favor.
28:3.s: On the Duties of the Clergy 2.11.57-58

28:3.t: The same apostle writes that God alone is wise, although both Solomon and many other holy people are called wise, and it is said, according to the Hebrew, to the prince of Tyre, "You are wiser than Daniel." Therefore, just as he alone is called the light, immortal and wise, although they are many who are immortal, and who are lights and who are wise, so also the human perfection that proceeds not from nature but from grace shows that those who seem to be perfect are imperfect.

This is the reason, if I am not mistaken, why in the above-mentioned Prophet Ezekiel a certain most haughty person is asked, "Art thou then wiser than Daniel?" Nor on this point can that be possibly said which some contend for in opposition to the Lord's Prayer: "For although," they say, "that prayer was offered by the apostles, after they became holy and perfect, and had no sin whatever, yet it was not in behalf of their own selves, but of imperfect and still sinful men that they said, 'Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.' They used the word our," they say, "in order to show that in one body are contained both those who still have sins, and themselves, who were already altogether free from sin." Now this certainly cannot be said in the case of Daniel, who (as I suppose) foresaw as a prophet this presumptuous opinion, when he said so often in his prayer, "We have sinned;" ... […]
28:3.s: ON THE MERITS AND FORGIVENESS OF SINS AND ON INFANT BAPTISM 2:13.10

28:4.t:
Even so we read that the Lord spoke also of the king of Tyre through his prophet: ''Son of man, take up a lamentation upon the king of Tyrus, and say unto him, 'Thus saith the Lord God: thou hast been the seal of likeness, and a crown of beauty in the delights of paradise; every precious stone was thy covering, the sardius and topaz and emerald.' " Again he says: ''With silver and with gold hast thou filled thy treasuries, from the multitude of commerce hast thou filled thy storehouses." Do not all these things seem to have been said expressly of the people of Africa? Where are greater treasuries, where is greater commerce, where are fuller storehouses? "With gold," he says, "hast thou filled thy treasuries from the multitude of thy commerce." I add more: Africa was once so rich that the abundance of her commerce seems to have filled not only her own treasuries but those of the whole world as well.

What did the prophet say next? […]
28:4.s: On the Government of God, Book 7, Chapter 14

28:12.t: The chief author of sin, then, is the devil, the author of all evil. Not I but the Lord has said, "The devil sins from the beginning." Before him no one sinned. Nor did he sin because by nature he was of necessity prone to sin—or else the responsibility for sin would reflect on him who created him in this way—but after being created good, he became a devil by his own free choice, receiving that name from his action. Though he was an archangel, he was afterwards called devil (slanderer) from his slandering, and though he was once a good servant of God, he was afterwards rightly named Satan, for Satan is interpreted "the adversary." This is not my teaching but that of the inspired prophet Ezekiel. For taking up a lament against him, he says, "You were a seal of resemblance and crown of beauty; you were begotten in the paradise of God," and a little further on, "Blameless you were in your conduct from the day you were created until evil was found in you."

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, raise a lament over the king of Tyre, and you shall say to him: Thus says the Lord God: You, the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in comeliness; you were in the delights of the paradise of God, every precious stone was your covering: sardius, topaz and jasper, chrysolite and onyx and beryl, sapphire and carbuncle and emerald; gold, the work of your comeliness, and your openings were prepared on the day on which you were formed. You, a Cherub stretched out and protecting; and I set you on the holy mountain of God; you walked in the midst of the fiery stones, perfect in your ways from the day of your formation, until iniquity was found in you. In the multitude of your trading your inner parts were filled with iniquity, and you sinned. And I cast you out from the mountain of God, and I destroyed you, O protecting Cherub, from the midst of the fiery stones. Your heart was lifted up in your comeliness; […]
He who was nurtured in a paradise of delight as one of the twelve precious stones was wounded and went down to hell from the mount of God.

Further, in Ezekiel we find it written thus: You are the seal of likeness and the crown of beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God. You were clothed with every first stone: sardius, topaz and emerald, carbuncle and sapphire and jasper, silver also, and gold and ligure, and agate and amethyst, and chrysolite and beryl and onyx; and with gold you filled your treasuries and your storehouses within you. From the day you were created, I set you with the Cherubim on my holy mountain; you were in the midst of the fiery stones, spotless in your days, from the time you were created until your iniquities were found in you (Ezek 28:12ff.). For who is so foolish and of so senseless a mind as to think that the prince of Tyre, whoever he believes him to be, set in the paradise of God, and created among the Cherubim, and dwelling among the fiery stones (which we understand without doubt as the Angels and heavenly Powers), was one adorned with earthly stones and having the likeness and the seal?

But the devil, who was a prince, and fell, did not die. For angelic dignity cannot receive death, but only ruin. Therefore he said, you shall fall like one of the princes. 'How is Lucifer fallen, who rose in the morning?' Behold, both here he fell, and there he fell. He fell for this reason, because he always dwelt among the heavenly things. This is he to whom it is said in Ezekiel: 'You are the unsealing of the likeness.' See what he says, the unsealing of the likeness. He did not say, You are the seal of the likeness: but, the unsealing of the likeness. God had sealed you, and had made you like himself: but you afterwards unsealed yourself. After the likeness and image of God you too were formed. Finally it is said in that same prophecy: 'In the midst of the cherubim you were nourished, among the stones of jasper and carbuncle you were in the paradise of God. And you fell,' he says, 'and were wounded from the mountain of the Lord.' […]

The Hebrews, among their other fables and γενεαλογίας [genealogies] and endless questions, are accustomed to understand these things as spoken against Hiram king of Tyre, although from Solomon to Ezekiel there are a great many years, which it is evident men did not live at that time; and to pronounce it thus, as if the prophet were speaking to him in irony: 'Are you the seal of the likeness of God, full of wisdom and perfect in comeliness, you adorned with all stones, you a Cherub, or created with a Cherub, when on the contrary you have sinned and are to be dissolved into ashes?'; and they add to their fable a marvel, so that, against the authority of Scripture, or rather without the authority of Scripture, they say: Hiram lived a thousand years. But how forced this interpretation is, the prudent reader understands without our judgment.

And So we are clearly shown that out of that number of them some of the leaders fell, by the lamentations of Ezekiel and Isaiah, in which we know that the prince of Tyre or that Lucifer who rose in the morning is lamented with a doleful plaint: and of him the Lord speaks as follows to Ezekiel: "Son of man, take up a lamentation over the prince of Tyre, and say to him: Thus saith the Lord God: Thou wast the seal of resemblance, full of wisdom, perfect in beauty. Thou wast in the pleasures of the paradise of God: every precious stone was thy covering: the sardius, the topaz and the jasper, the chrysolyte and the onyx and the beryl, the sapphire and the carbuncle and the emerald: gold the work of thy beauty, and thy pipes were prepared in the day that thou wast created. Thou wast a cherub stretched out and protecting, and I set thee in the holy mountain of God, thou hast walked in the midst of the stones of fire. Thou wast perfect in thy ways from the day of thy creation, until iniquity was found in thee. […]
28:12.s: The Second Conference of Abbot Serenus, Chapter 8

28:12.t: We should notice that the nature of angels is not said to have been made in the likeness of God but as the seal of the likeness, since as its essential nature is finer, it is suggested that God's image is expressed with greater likeness in it. The prophet immediately adds, every precious stone was your covering, carnelian, topaz and jasper, chrysolite, onyx and beryl, sapphire, carbuncle and emerald. He gave the names of nine stones, since there are nine ranks of angels. The first angel was adorned and covered with these nine since when it was set ahead of the whole multitude of angels, it was more illustrious in comparison with them. Why have I briefly listed these choirs of steadfast angels, if I am not also to comment more specifically on their functions? In Greek, angels are "messengers," and archangels are the most important messengers. We should know too that the word angel is the name of a service, not of a nature. […]

28:13.t: Hence it follows that the serpent in Paradise was certainly not brought into being without the will of God. In the figure of the serpent we see the Devil. That the Devil existed even in Paradise we are informed by the Prophet Ezechiel, who in discussing the Prince of Tyre says: Thou wast in the pleasures of the paradise of God. We maintain that the Prince of Tyre stands for the Devil.

There follows: You were in the delights of the paradise of God — for which in the Hebrew there stands 'in eden' — which the history of Genesis also narrates — and 'eden' is rendered as 'delights' —, and fittingly, for distinction, he names the paradise 'of God', to show that there is also a contrary paradise, 'not of God', among those who change the truth into a lie and boast that they have paradise; by which word he shows that the one of whom it is written is by no means a man, but a contrary force that once dwelt in the paradise of God; although the Jews think that this is prophesied of Hiram king of Tyre through the τρόπον [figure of speech] which is called ὑπερβολὴ; and to him to whom it is said: You were in the delights of the paradise of God, or 'you were made', it shows what he had, and what he lost. […]

The Manichaeans do not understand that if the devil is evil by nature, there can be no question of sin at all. They have no reply to the witness of the prophets, for example, where Isaiah, representing the devil figuratively in the person of the prince of Babylon, asks, "How you are fallen from heaven, O Day Star, son of the dawn?" or where Ezekiel says, "You were in Eden, the garden of God; every precious stone was your covering." These texts indicate that the devil was for a time without sin.

28:14.t:
For while the Prince of Tyre was walking without fault in the midst of the stones of fire, there was mercy upon him. But when his heart was lifted up, the cherub who overshadoweth, destroyed him.

Now, what are the stones of fire, but the children of Zion and the children of Jerusalem? For in the ancient time, in the days of David and of Solomon his son, Hiram was a friend to those of the house of Israel. But when they were carried away captive from their place, he rejoiced over them and spurned them with his feet, and did not remember the friendship of the house of David. And as to that which I said that the children of Judah were called the stones of fire, it was not of my own thought that I said it, but Jeremiah the Prophet spake concerning them; for when he was calling forth tears for them in the Lamentations, he said:—The children of Zion were more excellent than precious stones. And again he said:—How are the stones of the Sanctuary cast down at the head of all the streets? […]

After this it is said, according to the Hebrew: You, a Cherub stretched out and protecting — it is understood: the ark of God and the mercy seat; or, according to the Seventy, 'that he himself was anointed and created with the Cherub'; from which it is shown that this cannot apply to a man, the prince of the city of Tyre, but to a force once holy and preeminent, which was set as prince of the city of Tyre —; and I set you, he says, on the holy mountain of God — no doubt it signifies paradise, to which the apostle Paul says he was caught up after the third heaven —; now 'Cherub' is said in the masculine gender, singular number, and in the plural they are called 'Cherubim', which means 'multitude of knowledge', upon whom God rests and sits, and he uses this chariot, as the prophet says to him: You who sit upon the Cherubim, show yourself, and in another place: He ascended upon the Cherubim and flew upon the wings of the winds; […]

28:15.t: And what follows: Perfect in your ways from the day of your formation (for which the Seventy set down: You were unblemished in your days, from the day on which you were formed), until iniquity was found in you, shows that every creature was formed good by God and had perfect virtue, and through this that the prince of Tyre too was unblemished, so that the blemish thereafter is not of nature but of will.

'Until', he says, 'iniquity was found in you — found by God —, which was held shut up in the treasury of your breast, through pride and the abuse of the power you had received'; in the multitude of his trading, too, his inner parts, or storerooms, were filled with iniquity — for while he seeks out many things, and is not content with the knowledge he had received nor with the power over which he had been set, he filled the storerooms and inner parts of his breast —; so that, sated and grown fat, he kicked against his Creator: for Jacob ate indeed and was sated, and the beloved kicked back; he grew fat and was fattened and was enlarged, and forsook God who had made him, and: Out of the heart proceed the worst thoughts, on account of which God says: You sinned. And I cast you out from the mountain of God (or you were wounded from the mountain of God); […]

28:17.t: And he gives the reasons why he was led out, or cast out, from the midst of the fiery stones: 'For lifted up indeed was your heart in your comeliness, while you think yours what is God's'; whence the Apostle too says he received a goad of the flesh and an angel of Satan to buffet him, lest he be proud through the multitude of revelations and fall into the judgment of the devil. And therefore: 'Your learning has been corrupted', he says, 'with your comeliness (or you have lost your wisdom in your comeliness), so that, while you wish to be more than you were formed and to be wiser than you had received from God, you lost even what you had, and instead of beauty and learning, deformity and folly possessed you; […]

28:18.t: Wherefore he also polluted his sanctification, which he had had when he dwelt on the mountain and lived in the midst of the fiery stones. There follows: I will bring forth fire in your midst which may devour you; this fire would be kindled in the heart of the king of Tyre by him whose darts are fiery, and of whom it is written: All adulterers, their hearts are like an oven, of which fire Isaiah also speaks: Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame which you have kindled, so that, going forth outward, it may devour its possessor, according to what is written in the same Isaiah: It will devour the matter like hay; on that day the mountains and hills and forests will be quenched, and it will devour from the soul even to the flesh; this fire, which is called strange, Nadab and Abihu had offered at the altar of the Lord, and therefore they were consumed by divine fire; whence Moses too says: This is the word which the Lord spoke: In those who draw near to me I will be sanctified; […]

It is profitable too that all evil works be turned into ashes, so that the harmful fire may be utterly extinguished, and all may see and be astonished that the Tyrian king has perished and been made nothing, not for many ages, but for one, or certainly for ever, so that what is written may be fulfilled: I will not spare you, and I will not have mercy.

28:21.t: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set (or make firm) your face against Sidon, and you shall prophesy concerning it, and you shall say: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, Sidon, and I will be glorified in you (or in your midst), and they shall know that I am the Lord, when I have executed judgments in it (or in you) and have been sanctified in you (or in it). And I will send upon it (or into you) pestilence and blood in its streets (or your), and the slain (or the wounded) shall fall in its midst by the sword (or by swords) round about, and they shall know that I am the Lord. And there shall no longer be for the house of Israel a stumbling block of bitterness and a thorn bringing pain on every side round about, from those who oppose them (or who were doing them insult), and they shall know that I am the Lord God. […]

Further, according to the spiritual understanding, this seems to us the sense. 'Sidonians' means 'hunters', of whom it is also written in the Psalms: Our soul has been snatched like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters, and again: For he will rescue me from the snare of the hunters and from the harsh word, and in Proverbs the eye of a harlot is the snare of a sinner; but there are also hunters in the good sense, contrary to these, of whom Jeremiah writes: Behold, I will send fishers and hunters who will hunt you from every hill and mountain, whom the Lord also sends to fish, and makes them from fishers of fish into fishers of men; whence the little village of Peter and Andrew too is called by this name — for 'Bethsaida' means in our tongue 'house of hunters' —. Against these, then, the worst hunters, the word of God is directed, and the prophet is commanded to set, or make firm, his face against Sidon, and by no means to waver with every wind of doctrine, but, standing firm in the truth, he will slay the hunters.

28:22.t: What, then, are the things with which the Lord threatens Sidon?: 'Behold, I myself will come to you, and I will be glorified in you when I have slain you; and all who live will know that I am the Lord, when I have repaid you what you deserve. And I will send pestilence and blood into your streets' — and rightly are the streets said to be Sidon's: for broad indeed and spacious is the way that leads to death —; and those who stood badly will fall slain by the sword round about, that sword which the Lord came to send upon the earth to separate what was badly joined; and those who remain will know that he is the Lord.

Now the divine word foretells that it too is to be taken by the Babylonians, and that by the weight of its evils it is to know that he is the Lord, when he has judged it and been sanctified in it and consumed it by famine and pestilence and the sword, so that it falls in its streets and is no longer a stumbling block to the people of God, nor assails them frequently; and when this has been done, the people of Israel, whom he had scattered among various nations, are to return to their own land, and he is to be sanctified in them, not, as in Sidon, in the bad sense but in the good, when he has had mercy on them, and they have dwelt in the land which he gave to their father Jacob; and they have dwelt secure and trusting in the Lord, and have built houses and planted vineyards, when he has fulfilled his promises; and then they are to know that he is the Lord, whose promises are most firm. Many refer this to the time of Zerubbabel, Ezra and Nehemiah, when the people of Israel returned and dwelt in the land of Judea; […]

28:24.t: And when they have ceased, there will no longer be a stumbling block of bitterness and a thorn of pain pricking and wounding the people of God.

28:25.t: All these things, moreover, are said against the adverse powers: that in the last time they are to be destroyed, and there will be eternal security, when the Lord has gathered the house of Israel, those who discern God with the mind, and has been sanctified in them, and that will be fulfilled which is written: Be holy, for I am holy, and they have dwelt in their own land, of which we also read elsewhere: I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living, which he had given to Jacob, who had supplanted his elder brother and had deserved to receive his birthright; and they will dwell in it secure, or in hope, and they will build houses and plant vineyards, and they will dwell a second time in hope, according to what is read in Isaiah: You who have been weaned from milk, who have been drawn from the breast, expect tribulation upon tribulation, hope upon hope; […]

29:1.t: In the tenth year (or, according to the Seventy, the twelfth), in the eleventh month (or, according to the Hebrew, the twelfth), on the first (or one) day of the month, the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set (or make firm) your face against Pharaoh king of Egypt, and you shall prophesy concerning him, and concerning all Egypt you shall speak, and you shall say: Thus says the Lord God. After Sidon, which itself too is situated on the coast of Phoenicia, the word comes to the prophet in the tenth year of the captivity of King Jehoiachin, and in the twelfth month, and on one day of the month, that he should set his face, or make it firm, against Pharaoh king of Egypt and speak concerning all, or to all, Egypt; and that the province of Egypt, situated on the same coast on the other side of Judea, should be described, and the things that are to come upon it be prophesied. […]

29:2.t: But this above all must be inquired: whether it is the same Pharaoh who is named in Exodus and in Isaiah and Jeremiah and Ezekiel and in many other places, and in the Song: To my cavalry among the chariots of Pharaoh I have likened you, my near one, or one and then another; and it seems to me that he is not one, but that among the Egyptians the royal dignity is indicated by this word, just as among the Romans their kings are called 'Caesars' and 'Augusti' — from the first, Gaius 'Caesar', and the second, his adopted son Octavian, who was afterwards named 'Augustus' —, and among the Syrians 'Antiochuses', among the Persians 'Arsacids', among the Philistines 'Abimelech', and, after Alexander, in Egypt 'Ptolemies' down to Cleopatra, at whose defeat at Actium Egypt was made a Roman province; therefore at present the word of the Lord is spoken against any one whatever of the kings of Egypt, who is interpreted as διασκεδάστης, namely 'slayer' and 'mangler' and 'one who cuts down and divides all things with the sword'. […]

29:3.t: These things are said by μεταφορὰν [metaphor] as to the king of Egypt, because the province itself too was by no means hostile to Israel, but, while it promised great things, it separated them from the help of God; but according to ἀναγωγὴν [anagogy, the higher sense] we often read the 'dragon' as the opposing power — whence also Pharaoh is called διασκεδάστης, because he separates and disjoins from God, and 'Egypt', that is, μεσραὶμ, is rendered 'those who afflict' and 'those who distress', namely those whom it has been able to subjugate to itself. This dragon is the transgressor of whom Job speaks most fully, and in the Psalms it is written: You broke the heads of the dragon, you gave him as food to the Ethiopian peoples —, and the dragon is called 'great' in comparison with lesser dragons — of which it is sung: You broke the heads of the dragons in the waters, and in another place: This sea, great and spacious, there are creeping things of which there is no number, small animals with great. […]

Behold, I am against you, Pharaoh king of Egypt, great dragon who lie (or sit) in the midst of your rivers and say: The river is mine, and I made myself (or them). And I will put a bridle (or a snare) in your jaws, and I will make the fish of your rivers stick to your scales (or wings), and I will draw you out of the midst of your rivers, and all your fish shall cling to your scales. And I will cast (or set down) you swiftly (or into the desert), and all the fish of your river upon the face of the earth (or of your field); falling, you shall not be gathered up nor brought together; to the beasts of the earth and the birds of heaven I have given you to be devoured. […]

29:4.t: Let us consider, then, what the dragon's penalty is, or what his punishment. There follows: And I will put a bridle (or a snare) in your jaws — like which is that passage of Job: But you will bring the dragon with a hook and you will put a halter around his nostrils. He will trust that the Jordan may enter into his mouth; with his eye he will take it in. But he will pierce his nostrils, with a ring his lip —. Now the Lord puts a bridle in the jaws of this dragon and pierces his lips and binds them with the circle of a ring when, through churchmen who are learned in the holy Scriptures, he imposes silence on him and all the doctrines of perversity are dissolved; and he glues the fish of his rivers to his wings or scales — by which the heretics through pride hasten to the heights —, so that they too, joined with the dragon, may make one body with him; and they are coupled to him either in fellowship of error or in likeness of punishment, just as: He who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit. […]

29:5.t: 'And I will cast you,' he says, 'into the desert, so that you will by no means find any to deceive, or certainly I will set you down from the summit of your pride, and I will set you down swiftly' — according to that saying of the Apostle: But may the God of peace crush Satan under your feet swiftly —, so that, when the dragon is crushed and set down, the fish of his river too may be set down, and the author of crimes may fall, who formerly thought that he stood and ran about through the whole world; and let him fall upon the face of his own earth, to which he was cast headlong from heaven, so that he may by no means any longer be gathered in the churches of the heretics, nor be brought together or buried in those who believed him, once they have been freed from him, but may be given to be devoured by the beasts of the earth and the birds of heaven: the beasts, of which it is written: Do not hand over the soul that confesses to you, and the birds of heaven, which eat the seed beside the way and are interpreted by […]

29:6.t: Of a reed staff of this kind Rabshakeh too vainly reproaches Hezekiah king of Judah, saying: Behold, trusting in this reed rod, and a broken one, upon Egypt; whoever leans on it, it goes into his hand: so is Pharaoh king of Egypt and all who trust in him; and he indeed was lying about a righteous king in recalling these things — he who is interpreted as 'much with a kiss': for he was drunk from the golden cup of Babylon, and therefore he was thrusting his own things upon the people, while it was confessing the Lord —; here, however, Pharaoh is reproached for having been to the house of Israel a rod or reed staff, promising them help that was vain and fragile and soon to be shattered. But that we may be able to know which is the reed staff on which the house of Israel ought not to trust, we shall be able to understand it from the contrary staff and rod of the Lord, of which it is said to the Lord: Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me; […]

29:8.t: Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will bring a sword upon you, and I will kill from you man and beast; and the land of Egypt shall be a desert (or destruction and solitude), and they shall know that I am the Lord. Because he said (or you said): the river is mine, and I made it (or the rivers are mine, and I made them); therefore behold, I am against you and against your rivers, and I will make the land of Egypt into solitudes, laid waste by the sword (or destroyed) from the tower of Syene (or from Migdol and Syene) to the borders of Ethiopia. The foot of man shall not pass through it, nor shall the foot of beast walk in it, and it shall not be inhabited for forty years; and I will make the land of Egypt deserted in the midst of deserted lands, and its cities in the midst of overthrown cities: they shall be desolate for forty years, and I will scatter (or sow) the Egyptians among the nations, and I will winnow them into the lands. […]

Now the cloud of allegory must be discussed, and with the same brevity we shall try to avoid the length of this explanation too. The word is to the dragon, who had said: The rivers are mine and I made them, that the Lord himself is bringing upon him the sword of which it is written in Isaiah: My sword has become drunk in heaven: now it will descend upon the earth, to destroy from him man and beast, whatever seems to have either reason or simplicity; and to destroy not absolutely, but as to the dragon, so that they may perish to the dragon and live to God; and that the land of Egypt may become destruction, according to the sense given above, in which it perishes to the dragon, and after destruction be reduced to solitude, ceasing to have the worst of guests; […]

29:10.t: He says, therefore, that all Egypt is to be ravaged up to the borders of Ethiopia, to which the farthest region of Egypt is joined, so that the foot of man does not pass through Egypt nor are beasts found in it, and it is not inhabited for forty years — for the Egyptians are spared, and, because they were once hosts to Israel, their sentence is shorter in time: Tyre kept its sabbaths for seventy years and so was restored to its former state; the captivity of Judea too and the overthrow of the temple completed seventy years, until Cyrus king of the Persians: For the mighty shall mightily suffer torments.

29:11.t: Nor may the foot of man, that is, anything rational, pass through Egypt, nor the foot of beast walk in it — so that it may not hold any of the simple, whom Pharaoh, letting the men go, wished to keep in Egypt, while Moses opposed him and wished to free the beasts too from the captivity of Egypt —. And it shall not, he says, be inhabited for forty years — which number is always one of affliction and punishment: whence Moses and Elijah and the Savior himself fasted forty days and nights, and for forty years the people was in the wilderness, so that afterwards, circumcised at Gilgal, it might be freed from the reproach and disgrace of Egypt; in the mystery of this number this same prophet too slept forty days on his right side for the tribe of Judah, and the people is announced as about to serve in Egypt four hundred years, which make forty decades or four ἑκατοντάδας [hundreds]; […]

29:12.t: And when he says: I will make the land of Egypt deserted in the midst of deserted lands, he means the Philistines, the Edomites and the Moabites and all the other regions against which the prophet's oracle stands above —; then he will scatter or sow the Egyptians among the nations and winnow them into the lands, and, because The Lord is merciful and compassionate, patient and of many mercies, after forty years there is the restoration of Egypt, and the whole captivity will be brought back to its ancient soil and settled in the metropolis, which is called Pathros, where it arose and from which it set out, only on condition that, for its own good, it loses its ancient pride and is a lowly kingdom, indeed the lowliest of all nations, and is no longer lifted up against the nations nor has rule over them, but, reduced to fewness, by no means deceives the house of Israel by confidence in itself, nor teaches them iniquity, or recalls them to the memory of iniquity, in that, having forsaken the help of God, they sought the […]

29:15.t: And so that, even when they have been restored to their former state, they may cast themselves down through humility because they lived in Egypt and built cities of brick, and among the many kingdoms of the Church may be lowly, and may know against whom they have sinned; and that Egypt may no longer be lifted up over the churches spread through the whole world, but be reduced to fewness, and few may remain in it among the nations, according to what is written: Give them, O Lord. What will you give them? Give them a barren womb and dry breasts, so that they may by no means rejoice and exalt themselves in the multitude of the deceived, but be reduced to a few: For many are called, few chosen. And may they no longer deceive the house of Israel, that is, the Church, nor promise them a vain hope and confidence, teaching iniquity, so that they flee the discipline of the Church and follow Egyptian pleasures. And these things will happen so that a third time the Egyptians may know that he himself is the Lord; […]

29:17.t: And it came to pass in the twenty-seventh year, in the first and on one day of the month, the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made his army serve a great service against Tyre; every head made bald and every shoulder rubbed bare, and wages were not paid to him, nor to his army, over Tyre for the service with which he served me against it. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will give Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon in the land of Egypt, and he will carry off its multitude, and plunder its booty, and seize its spoils, and it will be wages for his army, and for the work for which he served against it. I have given him the land of Egypt because they labored for me, says the Lord God. In that day a horn shall sprout for the house of Israel; and to you I will give an open mouth in their midst, and they shall know that I am the Lord. […]

And lest we seem to pass anything over, according to the spiritual understanding we inquire where we have read this number, that is, the twenty-seventh: in the book of Genesis Scripture testifies that in the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the second month, the waters of the flood were brought upon the face of the earth, and afterwards in the seventh month of the same year, which is near to the sabbath, and on the twenty-seventh day of the same seventh month, the waters of the flood ceased, and the ark of Noah rested upon the mountains of 'Ararat', which means 'of Armenia'; from which we understand that the number is a middle one and can be applied to either side: since in it both the wrath of God begins with the flood, and his clemency is shown in the seventh month on the same number of days; […]

29:18.t: And as for that He said again:—I will destroy the overshadowing Cherub. For the Cherub that He will destroy is Nebuchadnezzar, as it is written:—He performed a work in Tyre, and there was given him by Tyre no hire for his host, and in return for the work of Tyre there was given him the land of Egypt. And why was hire not given by Tyre to Nebuchadnezzar? Clearly because its wealth went away in the sea, so that Nebuchadnezzar did not receive it. And at that time He destroyed the overshadowing Cherub, which is Nebuchadnezzar.

For in another prophecy too, which is seen to be against the Egyptians, the same Scripture weaves in: Son of man, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has made his army serve a great service against Tyre: every head made bald, and every shoulder rubbed bare, and no wage has been paid to him, nor to his army, for Tyre (Ezek 29). By this he signifies that a mound was heaped up over a long time by the army of Babylon, so that he tried beforehand to do what Alexander did afterwards, joining the island to the mainland (Quintus Curtius, book 4).

We read in the histories of the Assyrians that the besieged Tyrians, when they saw no hope of escape, embarked on ships and fled to Carthage, or to other islands of the Ionian and Aegean sea. Hence too it is said in Ezekiel: No wage has been paid to him, nor to his army, for Tyre (Ezek 29): because all the wealth of the city had been carried away, and all the nobles had left it empty.

Let us speak first, then, according to the letter. When Nebuchadnezzar was besieging Tyre and could not bring rams, engines and mantlets up to the walls — because it was surrounded by the sea —, he ordered the countless multitude of his army to carry stones and earth for a mound and, having filled up the sea in between, or rather the very narrow strait, he made the neighboring shore continuous with the island; when the Tyrians saw this now all but completed, and the foundations of the walls were being shaken by the battering of the rams, whatever precious things the nobility had in gold, silver, clothing and various furnishings, it put on ships and carried off to the islands, so that, when the city was taken, Nebuchadnezzar found nothing worthy of his labor; and because in this respect he had obeyed the will of God, some years after the captivity of Tyre Egypt is given to him; […]

Let these things have been said of the prophecy according to the letter, or rather according to the truth; but from the fact that Nebuchadnezzar received the wage of a good work, we understand that even in the case of the heathen, if they have done anything good, it is not passed over without reward by the judgment of God; whence also through Jeremiah Nebuchadnezzar is called the dove of God, because he served God's will against a sinful people. And I will bring, he says, my servant Nebuchadnezzar; from which it is clear that we are condemned by comparison with the Gentiles, if they do by natural law the things which we neglect even when written; of which the apostle Paul argues most fully to the Romans.

29:21.t: The cause of the Lord's anger against Egypt is this: that it deceived the people of God by its help, so that it would not hope in the Lord and would provoke him to wrath: 'In that day,' he says, 'on which Egypt has been taken, the horn of the house of Israel will sprout' — no doubt signifying the royal line; which some refer to Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, who was born of the stock of David through Jeconiah, others to the last time, when they think that Elijah too will come; but we, understanding the horn of the Lord as concerning Christ, touch lightly on the present history —. 'And when,' he says, 'O prophet, this has first been fulfilled, then your mouth will be opened, and your prophecy will by no means hang on a doubtful promise but will be seen accomplished in deed, so that those who have heard may know that I am the Lord, for whom to have said is to have done'.

30:1.t: We have set down these things like elementary lessons for little children, so that through letters, syllables and nouns and the joining of words they may arrive at the reading of prose or verse. Now let us approach the tropology, and let us display the vast sea of discussion on a small panel, as it were, of a painting. The Word of the Lord, which was always in the Father, came to the prophet and calls him not by his own name but 'son of man', which in the holy Scriptures is always taken in a good sense, at least in the singular number — as in this same prophet and in Daniel and in the Gospel —; otherwise, in the plural number, it is read in the opposite sense — as in that verse: Sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword, and again: Sons of men, how long heavy of heart? The lion indeed will roar, and who will not fear? The Lord has spoken, and who will not prophesy? —. Howl, he says, woe, woe for the day, for the day is near, and the day of the Lord draws near, a day of cloud; […]

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, prophesy and say: Thus says the Lord God: Howl, woe, woe for the day, for the day is near, and the day of the Lord draws near, a day of cloud; it will be the time of the nations. And a sword will come upon Egypt, and there will be terror in Ethiopia, when the wounded have fallen in Egypt and its multitude has been carried off and its foundations destroyed. Ethiopia and Libya and the Lydians, and all the rest of the common throng, and Chub, and the sons of the land of the covenant with them will fall by the sword. Thus says the Lord God: And those who prop up Egypt will collapse, and the pride of its dominion will be destroyed; from the tower of Syene they will fall in it by the sword, says the Lord of hosts. And they will be laid waste in the midst of desolate lands, and its cities will be in the midst of deserted cities; and they will know that I am the Lord, when I have set fire in Egypt, and all its helpers have been crushed. […]

30:4.t: There follows: A sword will come upon Egypt — the 'sword' turning and flaming: the divine word, which divides the good from the evil and consumes the most wicked with its fire; and 'upon Egypt': of this world —, so that there is terror in Ethiopia: those who dwell beyond Egypt in the night of error and in darkness, and whose blackness is turned to whiteness either with difficulty or not at all. And the wounded will fall in Egypt, those who had stood badly in wickedness. 'And the multitude of Egypt will be carried off' — For wide and spacious is the way that leads to death —. And its foundations will be destroyed, so that nothing of its former firmness may remain in Egypt, but, the most wicked foundations abandoned, the foundation of Christ may be laid, on which the Church may be built — every indeed planting which the heavenly Father has not planted will be rooted up; whence Jeremiah too is commanded to destroy what had been built, so that he may build better things —.

30:5.t: 'There will perish in Egypt also the Ethiopians, Libyans, and Lydians — or, according to the Seventy, Persians, Cretans and Lydians and Libyans — and Chub, that is, the Arabs, and all the rest of the common throng — whom the Seventy translated as hybrids and mixed peoples —'; all of whom, according to the diversity of vices and the interpretation of the names which we set out in the vision of Tyre, we can understand as different nations — whence the Apostle too: You, he says, Gentiles in the flesh, who are called the foreskin: for he would never have said Gentiles in the flesh unless there were others in the spirit; and in another place: Behold Israel according to the flesh —; […]

30:6.t: Then 'the supports and props of Egypt will collapse', which held it up in wickedness: the subtleties of the dialecticians and the argumentation, the tricks, of the philosophers; 'the insolent and proud dominion will also be destroyed', of those who speak all things through arrogance and count the simplicity of the Church as nothing; for 'from the tower of Syene they will fall in it' — which lies at the farthest limits of Egypt, bordering on Ethiopia and the Blemmyes, where the Nile is unnavigable, and there is the roar of the cataracts, and everything is pathless and full of serpents and venomous creatures —; but if, as we said above, 'Magdolus' means 'magnificence' and 'Soene' 'circle', it is clear that the wealth of Egypt and its insolent strength and magnificence, that is, boasting and exaltations, perish by force as far as the circle of Egypt, where nothing is stable but rolls in an uncertain fall, and comes to ruin.

And so that we might know that all these nations had been in aid of Egypt, the following passage shows it: 'And those who prop up Egypt will collapse — or the supports of Egypt, that is, its allies —, and all the pride of its dominion — or the insolence of its strength — will be destroyed and brought down from the tower of Syene — which we have said is situated at the farthest borders of Egypt; or 'from Migdol to Syene', as the Seventy translated —. All the cities of Egypt will be deserted, so that they may acknowledge the Lord when the fire of the Chaldeans has laid everything waste and its helpers have been crushed.

30:7.t: 'Then the Egyptian cities will be laid waste and the land will be deserted and no congregation will remain that has any firmness, so that, at the end of things, they may know that he himself is the Lord, when he has sent fire into Egypt', which the Lord desires to burn, so that the hay, wood, stubble that have been built upon the foundation of Christ may be burned up, 'and all the helpers of perverse doctrines may be crushed' — from which it is to be understood that the knowledge falsely so called, and those of whom it is written: Scatter, O Lord, the nations that want wars, are called the allies and helpers of Egypt —.

30:9.t: And messengers will have come — according to Aquila and Theodotion 'siim', which Symmachus translated 'hastening', and we rendered as 'triremes': for so we received it from the Hebrews — so that all the confidence of Ethiopia may be crushed, and, when the neighboring province has been made desolate, terror may seize those nearest'.

'On that day', he says, 'messengers will go out from the face of God' — of whom it is written in the Gospel: Their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven; and in the parable of the sowing 'the reapers, the angels', that is, 'they are messengers', are sent: To gather all stumbling blocks and cast them into the furnace of fire: where there is weeping of eyes and gnashing of teeth —, and they will hasten to fulfill the command, 'to frighten off, or crush, the confidence of Ethiopia', those who have reached the highest peak of malice; 'and, in the overthrow of Egypt, Ethiopia may be crushed and tremble, because the day of the Lord is one of vengeance and retribution', by which the darkness of sins is put to flight and the light of virtues remains.

30:10.t: But so that we might know what this sword was that would lay Egypt waste and terrify Ethiopia, there follows more plainly: And I will make the multitude of Egypt cease by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who will not only come, but will come accompanied by many nations, so that all Egypt will be filled with the blood of the slain.

And I will make, he says, the multitude of Egypt cease by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, to whom they were handed over for him to punish — for he is the enemy and avenger who also received a wage because he had served in the siege of Tyre — the multitude of Egypt: so that the many may cease to be in Egypt, who are always in it — but if anyone should object, asking how that is said in Deuteronomy: In seventy souls your fathers went down into Egypt, but now you have become like the stars of heaven in multitude, it is easily resolved: for he did not set down an example of an earthly multitude but of a heavenly one, which shines with virtues and is full of lights —; against which multitude of Egypt 'the mightiest' of the nations are brought, to destroy the land — for whom the Seventy translated 'pestilent men', which I do not know how it suits those who are brought by the Lord, unless perhaps according to that example: A sending by most wicked angels —; […]

30:12.t: And so great will be the wrath of the Lord that the channels of the rivers — that is, the διωρύγες [canals] of the Nile — will be dried down to the ground, and the fullness of Egypt will be made desolate by the hand of pestilent men — or of the most wicked men —.

30:13.t: 'For my words cannot be void; and my indignation will advance to this point: that the images of Egypt are destroyed and the idols cease from Memphis', which to this day is the metropolis of Egyptian superstition — or the nobles and princes from Memphis and from the land of Egypt —.

There follows: And I will destroy the images (which the Seventy translated abominations), and I will make the idols (or the nobles) cease from Memphis, and a leader (or princes) in the land of Egypt; they will be no more: for it belongs to the most merciful Lord to overthrow evil works, so that no likeness that falsely counterfeits the image of truth may remain in Egypt; and that the nobles too may perish from 'Memphis', which means 'from the mouth', from which they fashioned all the idols, so that, with the heads and masters of the idols cut off, there may be no prince in Egypt, and 'all Egypt may be filled with terror and destruction'; of whose cities it is said: And I will destroy the land of Pathros, and I will set fire in Tahpanhes (or in Tanis), and I will execute judgments in 'No' (which the Seventy translated 'Diospolis'); and I will pour out my indignation upon Sain, the strength of Egypt; […]

30:14.t: And so great a terror will possess all Egypt that the whole land of Pathros will perish, and fire will lay waste Tahpanhes — or, as the Seventy translated, Tanis —. And I will execute, he says, judgments in 'Alexandria', which is so called today; but it has the ancient name 'No', which Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion translated as it stands in the Hebrew; in its place the Seventy, intending I know not what, said 'Diospolis', which is a small city of Egypt; but we have put 'Alexandria' for 'No' — by 'anticipation', which in Greek is called πρόληψις, according to that line of Vergil: and he came to the Lavinian shores: not that at that time, when Aeneas came into Latium, they were called Lavinian, but because they were later named Lavinian, so that the passage might become clearer to the reader's understanding —.
Diospolis [Thebes]: refusing. But better, in Greek: city of Jupiter.

30:15.t: And I will pour out, he says, my indignation upon 'Sain', which we rendered as 'Pelusium'; and it is called the strength of Egypt because it has a very safe harbor and the trade of the sea is carried on there most of all — whence the poet too calls the lentil Pelusian, not because this kind of legume is grown there, or chiefly there, but because the greatest quantity of it is brought there from the Thebaid and all Egypt along the stream of the Nile —. And I will slay, he says, the multitude of 'Alexandria', which again is set down in the Hebrew as 'No', for which the Seventy translated not 'Diospolis', as above, but 'Memphis'. And, to show that the city was already populous at that time: I will destroy, he says, the multitude of 'No'.

After this it is said: And I will slay (or destroy) the multitude of 'Memphis' — in place of which the Hebrew has 'No', which above the same Seventy translated 'Diospolis', which means 'rest' —: for there are many who seek rest and want to lie on ivory beds and eat suckling lambs; or — according to the Seventy, who translated 'Memphis' —: there are many who say to others: Allow me to remove the speck from your eye, when they themselves have beams.

30:16.t: And I will set fire, that is, the king of Babylon, in Egypt, who, like fire, is to ravage everything. Like a woman in labor 'Sain' will be in pain, that is, 'Pelusium' (or will be thrown into confusion with confusion), and in 'Alexandria' (that is, in 'No') there will be a breach, and waters will be poured out (for which again the Seventy translated 'Diospolis'). Now it is the custom of the Egyptians, because of the flooding of the Nile, to build high embankments along the banks of the Nile; and if these have been broken through the negligence of the guards or by the excessive volume of the waters, the waters do not irrigate the fields lying below but overwhelm and ravage them; by these it is signified that Egypt was to be occupied by the army of the Chaldeans just as it is usually covered and ruined when the waters of the Nile flood and rise beyond measure. […]

'And fire is set in Egypt', to consume wordiness and pleasures with its burning. 'All temptation will be in pain, and in Diospolis — which again in the Hebrew is set down as 'No' — there will be a breach', so that the waters are poured out, and every most wicked congregation is scattered and perishes here and there; or, according to the Hebrew: 'In Memphis there will be daily distresses', so that they may render account for every idle word and understand that nothing of their sayings escapes the judgment of the Lord.

30:17.t: 'The young men also of Heliopolis — which in Hebrew is called 'On' — and of Bubastus, another city, will fall by the sword, so that the cities themselves, that is, their inhabitants, or their women, are led into captivity — the sex that lies exposed to outrage —.

The young men also of Heliopolis and of Bubastus will fall by the sword — 'Heliopoleos' is called 'On' in Hebrew, which means 'pain'; and 'Bubastus', in the Egyptian language, means 'trial of the mouth' —; all these, who could not bear the pain of the world but pursued the pleasures of Diospolis and trusted in their fluency of speech and, disputing against the other doctrines, had had experiences of victory, will fall by the sword of the word of God; and those who are called not young men at all but, from weakness of mind, women, will be led captive; or the cities themselves, through pain and the boasting of the mouth, will be brought into captivity.

30:18.t: And in Tahpanhes, he says, the day will grow black; 'Taphnae' means 'yielding to the mouth', 'of the devil' being understood; those who have yielded to him will lose the light of truth and exchange day for night, and will perceive that the scepters of Egypt and all its dominion have been broken in Tahpanhes, so that the insolent strength, or the pride of its power, fails in it, and the rays of the sun of righteousness are blinded by a cloud, and not women at all, but daughters, are led into captivity.

But in Tahpanhes, which is a royal city, the scepters of Egypt will be broken, that is, the whole royal line; and when its power has failed, its princes slain, then the day will grow black and everything will be filled with gloom and darkness, so that the city itself is covered with a cloud of sorrow and mourning, and its daughters, that is, the remaining towns, are led into captivity; so that, after I have executed judgments in Egypt and shown myself judge to all, then the Egyptians may know that I am the Lord'.

30:19.t: 'And let the Lord execute not one judgment but many judgments in Egypt' — for just as there are various mansions of the good with the Father, so also there are various judgments of the punishments of Egypt — so that, when all these things have been done, the Egyptians may know that he himself is the Lord, whose judgments are true, justified in themselves.

30:20.t: And it came to pass in the eleventh year, in the first, on the seventh of the month, the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and behold, it has not been bound up so that health might be restored to it, that it might be tied with cloths and packed with linen bandages (or that it might receive a poultice) and, its strength recovered, might be able to hold a sword. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against Pharaoh king of Egypt; and I will shatter his arm, strong but broken (or arms strong and set in order), and I will cast the sword down from his hand, and I will scatter (or I will sow) Egypt among the nations, and I will winnow them into the lands. And I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, and I will give my sword into his hands; […]

30:21.t: Now let us see what the prophecy against Pharaoh, or about Pharaoh, is. He says that he has broken his arm, and that it has not been bound up nor tied nor packed with linen bandages nor received a poultice — according to what is written: Not to apply a poultice, nor oil, nor bandages —; had this been done, surely, its strength recovered, he could hold a sword and go forth to wars. Therefore the merciful and compassionate God shatters his arm again, or his arms, so that the sword may fall utterly from his hand and Egypt be scattered among the nations and winnowed into the lands — but in the arm understand strength and might, as Scripture says: Crush the arm of the sinner and the evil one —; and this is crushed in our adversaries when they persecute us indeed but cannot overwhelm us; and for the salvation of the servants of God the Babylonian king often rises up against Pharaoh, so that a more powerful one overwhelms the powerful and the evil are handed over to the worse; […]

31:1.t: Let these things be said for the present according to the history; most understand them as things that will happen at the consummation of the world, and that King Pharaoh, that is, the power to which Egypt is subject, is compared to the most mighty king of the Assyrians, that is, the Antichrist; and if he falls, surely the other rulers too of this darkness and the princes of the world will fall the more easily. Let us speak, therefore, of the particulars, touching on everything briefly, so that we may seem not so much to discuss and explain obscure things as to have given material to those who wish to explain them. And first it must be discussed why in the eleventh year, the third month, on the first day of the month, the word of the Lord came to Ezekiel, saying: Son of man, say to Pharaoh king of Egypt and to his multitude. To one who is about to speak to Pharaoh, the word of the Lord comes in the eleventh year; […]

31:2.t: And it is said to the king of Egypt: Whom have you become like in greatness (or height) of yours? — because he too exalted himself and is subject to that sentence: Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled —, but yet he is not like the height of the one who was like a cedar, or cypress, in Lebanon: Beautiful in branches and thick with leaves, and lofty in height, and raised his head right up to the clouds — to which, according to David, the truth of God reaches, and which are commanded not to rain a shower upon Israel —.

And it came to pass in the eleventh year, in the third, on the first of the month, the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, say to Pharaoh king of Egypt and to his people: Whom have you become like in your greatness? Behold, Assyria like a cedar (or cypress) in Lebanon, beautiful in branches and thick with leaves, and lofty in height, and among the dense leaves (or in the midst of the clouds) its top was raised up; the waters nourished him, the deep raised him up, its rivers flowed round about its roots, and it sent out its streams to all the trees of the region. Therefore its height was raised above all the trees of the region (or of the field), and its shrubs (or branches) were multiplied ※ and its branches (or shrubs) were raised up ⁚ because of many waters. And when it had stretched out its shade, all the birds of heaven made nests in its branches, and under its leaves all the beasts of the forests brought forth young, and under its shade dwelt the assembly of all the nations; […]

31:3.t: His beauty too is proclaimed, which was changed into ugliness by a depraved will — so that it is said of him: The Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon —, and he, lofty and set on Lebanon, the highest of mountains, would fall the more heavily the more sublime he had been; and holy Scripture, wishing to show his height, calls him a great top which the waters nourished — not the waters of Siloam: Which go with silence, but the waters of Rezin and the waters of Egypt, of which it is written: What is it to you, that you should drink the water of Geon (or Sior, which means 'turbid' waters)? —. The deep also exalted him — the deep over which darkness was borne at the beginning of the world, and into which in the Gospel the demons beg not to be sent —; […]

31:5.t: Therefore he was lifted up and grew up above all the tallest trees, and his shrubs were multiplied, and he possessed the empire of the whole world, saying: All these things have been delivered to me; and his branches were lifted up, which had been watered by the waters of the deep.

31:6.t: He stretched out, or spread, his shade, so as to subject all to his sway. In its branches all the birds of heaven made nests — For everyone who commits sin is born of the devil and is counted among the number of his branches; and those birds made nests in his branches which ate the seed beside the way in the Gospel, or, since All have sinned and are in need of the mercy of God, of whom it is said: All have turned aside, together they have become useless, for this reason they made nests in his branches —; there follows: And under its leaves all the beasts of the forests brought forth young, those which have lost the gentleness of Christ, and under its shade dwelt the assembly of very many nations, so that there was no one who was not touched by his shade — except the one who said: Behold, the prince of this world comes, and will find nothing in me. Through one indeed man sin entered into the world, and through sin death, and so death passed through to all men, in which we all sinned; and in Adam we all die; […]

31:7.t: Now Assyria was most beautiful in its greatness and in the spreading of its shrubs, because its root had been watered by many waters, so much so that in the paradise of God none of the cedars and cypresses was higher, nor did firs and pines equal its loftiness, or plane trees were not equal to its leaves; and for this reason none of the trees planted in paradise had been made equal to it, because: No tree of the paradise of God was likened to it and to its beauty — for they were by no means lifted up through pride, but knew their humility, nor did they try with a sacrilegious mind to claim likeness to God for themselves —, and what follows: And all the trees of delights that were in paradise emulated it, we expound thus: 'The trees of paradise emulated the multitude of its branches' — For many are called but few chosen, and: Wide and spacious is the way that leads to death —; for it longs to have as many for salvation as Assyria had for perdition.
