31:10.t: Whence, because Assyria was lifted up in height, and set its loftiness green and dense (or raised its top right up to the clouds), and its heart was lifted up, so that he said: I will be like the Most High, therefore he was delivered into the hand of the mightiest of the nations — which let us understand as another detestable power, to which he is delivered for punishment: for he is the enemy and the avenger; so that Assyria is understood as the Antichrist, and the mightiest of the nations, to whom he was delivered, as Satan, according to that saying of the Apostle: Whom I have delivered to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme —, who: Doing will do to him whatever has been commanded him by the Lord: and this cypress was cast out of the paradise of God on account of its impiety.

31:11.t: And what follows: I delivered it into the hand of the mightiest of the nations, he calls the Babylonian king, so that he may understand that his conquering the Assyrian was not of his own might but of divine power. According to its impiety, he says, I cast it out, so as secretly to warn the Babylonian that he ought not to be cruel nor oppress the people of God which had been delivered to him, lest he suffer things like those of the Assyrian, who was cruel and impious.

31:12.t: And strangers and cruel men will cut it down (or the pestilent among the nations) — so that that which is written may be fulfilled: When the pestilent man is scourged, the fool will become wiser, and again: Already the axe is laid to the roots of the tree —, and they will cut it down upon the mountains, so that it falls in its pride. In all moreover the valleys its branches will fall, so that all who were in his retinue are led down to Tartarus and withdraw from its shade and leave it, so that the birds of heaven and the beasts of the earth, which before had been under it and were covered by its shade, afterwards become partakers of its punishment.

And strangers and the most cruel of the nations will cut it down (or, according to the Seventy, the pestilent), which he would never say while placed in Chaldea, lest he stir up their madness against his own nation; it is also thrown down upon the mountains, and in all the valleys its branches fall and are broken on the crags, and it is abandoned by all the peoples, that is, by the birds of heaven and the beasts of the field, and it will come to such great destruction that all the trees which were thought lofty in comparison with the Assyrian tree cease, by its example, to be lifted up any longer and raised on high, nor do they stand in their height, but, once it has been cut down, all are cut down together by fear; […]

31:14.t: And when the other trees of the forests, or of paradise, see that Assyria the cypress has fallen by the sentence of the Lord, they will not be lifted up in pride, nor will they think themselves anything, nor will they consider the watering of their waters their own riches: because all the branches and the birds of heaven and the beasts of the earth which were under the rule of Assyria are led down to death, to the lowest land — of whom it is written: In his sight all who go down into the earth will fall, and in another place: They will go into the uttermost parts of the earth —, and they will be by no means with the angels, but with the sons of men: Who go down into the pit (or into the ditch) everlasting.

31:15.t: After the cutting down of the Assyrian tree, or on the day when the Assyrian went down to the underworld, the Lord proclaimed mourning, and again by metaphor speaks of him, that he was covered with the deep — according to that which is written: I came into the depth of the sea, and the tempest overwhelmed me —, and that all the rivers, namely all the nations, ceased to water him any longer; and that Lebanon was saddened, or darkened, over her, that is, the tree, or over him, that is, the Assyrian.

But when he has gone down into the uttermost part of the earth and has become the portion of foxes, by which he is to be torn, then there will be mourning, either of all his allies or of the holy powers, who will grieve that he has gone down to the underworld; whence the Lord says: I covered him with the deep, by whose waters he had before been nourished, and I held back its rivers, that is, the deep's, and restrained many waters, so that they would not water him but rather overwhelm him; Lebanon was saddened over him, in which he had been exalted, and all the trees of the field were shaken, dreading a like cutting down.

31:16.t: And lest we should think the discourse is about a tree, there follows: At the sound of its fall I shook the nations — for what fall of a single tree can be so great that all the nations are shaken at its sound? —, when I led it, he says, down to hell — according to the letter, a tree cannot be led down to the underworld — with the others who were going down into the pit, that is, to the underworld; and were consoled in the lowest land, namely in the heart of the earth, all the trees of pleasure (or of delights, which in Hebrew is called 'eden', so as to signify wooded glades and forests), choice and splendid, which were in Lebanon and were watered by waters. […]

At the sound of its fall I shook the nations, so that no one would be ignorant of his destruction and of his being led down to the underworld with his other allies; and all the trees of pleasure, that is, of paradise, received consolation, while they see evil things repaid to the evil and good things to the good — and these are the trees of Lebanon, watered by the waters of the rivers of the Lord, with which that tree too which fell had been watered; or all the trees which once were good and were watered by waters and dwelt on the height of Lebanon will receive consolation when they see their prince suffer like torments —; for they too will go down to hell to those slain by the sword of the Lord, and all the strength of the trees will dwell under its shade, that is, in punishment, in the midst of all the nations which will be held by the bars of hell.

31:18.t: At the end an apostrophe is made to the Assyrian himself or to Pharaoh: To whom have you been likened, O renowned and lofty one among the trees of pleasure? 'No one', he says, 'was your equal, but you surpassed all kings in power, and yet with the other kings who were in your retinue you have been brought down to the lowest lands, that is, to the underworld' — as Scripture says: They will go into the uttermost parts of the earth, they will be delivered into the hands of the sword, they will be portions for foxes —. In the midst, he says, of the uncircumcised you will sleep with those who were slain by the sword: he shows what the trees were, what the cedar or cypress, wounded by swords and lying with the uncircumcised; and, to join the last things to the earlier, since he had said above: Whom have you become like in your greatness? […]

After this the discourse is turned to Pharaoh himself, to whom it had been said at the beginning: Whom have you become like in your height?, and it is said to him: To whom have you been likened, O renowned and lofty one among the trees of pleasure? — to the Assyrian, of course, who fell —: 'You too were renowned and lofty among the trees of Eden — that is, of delights and of paradise —, and behold, you have been led down like the Assyrian, with all the trees that were once in delights, to the lowest land and to the underworld; and you will sleep not in rest but in punishments, in the midst of the uncircumcised — that is, the unclean — and with those who fell by the sword of the Lord'; and so that we may know who it is to whom he said: O renowned and lofty one among the trees of pleasure, he puts it more openly: He is Pharaoh and all his multitude (or, according to the Seventy: So is Pharaoh and all his multitude), so that, as the Assyrian above was cut down and fell, so also the Egyptian may be overthrown.

32:1.t: And it came to pass in the twelfth year, in the twelfth month (or the tenth), on the first day of the month, the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, take up a lament over Pharaoh king of Egypt, and you shall say to him: You have been likened to the lion of the nations, and to the dragon that is in the sea; and you tossed with your horn in your rivers, and you troubled the waters with your feet, and you trampled their rivers (or your rivers). Therefore thus says the Lord God: I will spread my net over you in a multitude of many peoples, and I will draw you out in my dragnet (or I will draw you out on a hook); and I will cast (or I will draw) you onto the land, upon the face of the field I will throw you (or the plains will be filled with you), and I will make dwell (or sit) upon you all the birds of the sky, and I will glut the beasts of the whole earth with you; and I will put your flesh upon the mountains, and I will fill the hills (or the valleys) with your gore (or with your blood). […]

32:2.t: Pharaoh is compared to a lion — not of one nation but of many nations — or to a dragon in the sea, so that he possesses land and waters; he was lifted up into 'pride' by the watering of the rivers — which he calls 'horn' — and, by the multitude of his army, passing through all the waters, he was able to trouble them.

Let it suffice to have said these things in passing on the simple letter, so that we may come to the spiritual understanding. Nor do I think one must labor greatly to know who Pharaoh king of Egypt is, since we have spoken of it more fully above: namely that power to which Egypt was entrusted, whether one province or the Egypt of the whole world, which was not created a lion but by its own vice was likened to the lion of the nations — for Man, indeed, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to the senseless beasts, and was made like them; of this lion Peter also speaks: Our adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion, and in Psalm 9 (10) it is written: He lies in wait in secret like a lion in his den; he lies in wait to seize the poor, and Jeremiah says by the Holy Spirit: A lion from the forest has struck them —; […]

32:3.t: Therefore thus says the Lord God: I will spread my net over you, in a multitude of many peoples; the Lord's net, woven by the plan of the Old and New Testament, is cast over the dragon — who dwells in the multitude of peoples, and delights in crowds and multitude —, so as to draw him out in his dragnet, or on his hook — this is the dragnet that is cast into the sea of this world and draws out many fish, some to be chosen and others to be thrown away; or this is the hook of which it is written in Job: But you will draw out the dragon with a hook and put a halter around his nostrils, for which Aquila translates: Drawing out Leviathan with a hook, and with cords you will bind his tongue —; […]

Therefore he says that he will spread his net over his multitude and draw him out with his dragnet — or hook —, and cast — or stretch — him out upon the land, him who like a serpent had been wound in many coils, so that he may be devoured by all the birds of the sky. And when not only the birds but all the beasts of the earth have torn him, the rest of his flesh will fill the mountains and valleys and plains, so that all things swarm with worms — and he says this by way of metaphor, so that, after the birds of the sky and the beasts have been glutted with his flesh, that is, his army and the whole multitude, the remaining part may be turned into worms and gore —:

32:5.t: and what follows: And I will put your flesh upon the mountains, and I will fill your hills with your gore (or I will fill the valleys with your blood), has this sense, that we should understand the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth as the peoples of the deceived and the cruelty of the Gentiles, and refer the mountains to the leaders of heresies — such as Valentinus and Marcion were —, and the hills to their successors who are glutted with the dragon's gore, or the valleys which are filled with the dragon's blood to all the lower sort of believers; or certainly the mountains are the hostile powers that roam about in the air, and the valleys those which penetrate the underworld and have been consigned to eternal punishments.

32:6.t: Further, what is said: And I will water the land with the stench of your blood upon the mountains (or the land will be watered with your dung upon the mountains), and the valleys will be filled with you, signifies this, that all the pride and arrogant swelling of the heretics is filled not so much with living and pure blood as with putrid and stinking blood — according to what is written: Make them like the dung of the earth, from which the holy man is delivered by the Lord: Who raises the needy from the earth, and lifts the poor from the dung, to set him with princes, with the princes of his people —; and the valleys, sunk into the depths, as we said above, signify either the underworld or the lowly mind of the heretics, who do everything for the sake of pleasure and earthly wealth;

32:7.t: and what is joined: And when you have been extinguished I will cover the sky, and I will make its stars grow black: I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon will not give its light; all the lights of the sky I will make mourn (or grow dark) over you, and I will put darkness upon your land, says the Lord God, if we follow the letter, cannot be understood at all: for when, after Pharaoh — or the dragon — was slain, did the sun and moon and stars not give their light, and the sky was covered with darkness — according to that poetic line: And the impious ages feared eternal night —? This, then, must be said: that when Pharaoh has been extinguished — who transformed himself into an angel of light, of whom it is written in another place: The light of the impious will be extinguished —, the sky, or the heavens, will be covered with darkness — of which Paul also speaks: And the spiritual things of wickedness in the heavenly places —; […]

'Then,' he says, 'the heavens will be wrapped in darkness: the sun and the moon and the other lights will not give their light, but over you all things will grow black, and nothing will be joyful for you.

32:8.t: all the lights also, and whatever of doctrine seems to be among the heretics, will be blinded when the dragon has been extinguished, or they will mourn the loss of their prince, so that the Lord himself covers the land of the heretics with darkness, namely ignorance of the truth, so that the blind lead the blind into a ditch and the inhabitants of the land are sent into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

32:9.t: After this it is said: And I will provoke the heart of many peoples, when I bring your destruction (or your captivity) among the nations upon a land which you do not know, so that those who formerly served Pharaoh are angered against him, seeing that his captivity has been led away to another land, which the dragon did not know. Nor ought we to doubt that the lands which Pharaoh does not know are good, namely when the captivity of Pharaoh is exchanged for another captivity — of which it is said to the Savior: Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he received (or, according to the Apostle, gave) gifts among men —.
And at your destruction all peoples and all their kings will tremble with exceeding horror, seeing my sword flying this way and that and sparing no one, and in your ruin they dread a like ruin.

32:10.t: And I will make, he says, many peoples stand astonished over you, so that those who formerly admired Pharaoh's power may afterwards marvel at him for having fallen from his summit; the kings of the peoples, too, will tremble over him with exceeding horror — whose kingdoms the devil showed to the Lord, and of whom it says in the psalm: The kings of the earth stood up, and the princes gathered together —; and this will come about when the sword of the Lord begins to fly over their faces, understood as those of the kings, or of the peoples — and the sword of the Lord is to be understood as the word of God, living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, which flies and darts about and dazzles the eyes of those who behold it and frightens their faces —, so that, astounded at the ruin of Pharaoh, they may see themselves cast down in him; […]

32:11.t: But so that you may know what this sword is, hear it more plainly: The sword of the king of Babylon will come to you; by the swords of the mighty (or of giants) I will cast down all your multitude — which giants are the invincible nations that were held in the army of the Babylonian king —; these will lay waste (or will destroy) the pride of Egypt and all its multitude, and nothing will remain in Egypt, but together with the men the beasts and brute animals too will be carried off alike.

But the sword of the king of Babylon will come upon the Egyptian dragon, so that by the swords of the mighty — or of giants — the Lord may cast down his multitude, which followed the king of Egypt: Invincible, he says, (or pestilent ones from the nations) are all these, so that the evil are handed over to worse ones to be punished — of whom it is written: A sending by most evil angels, and the Apostle: Whom I have handed over, he says, to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme, or for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved —.

32:13.t: And when by ministers of this kind the pride of Egypt has been cast down and its multitude scattered, all its beasts that were beside many waters will perish, and the foot of man will trouble them no more — for if Blessed is he who sows upon the waters, where ox and ass tread, conversely unhappy is he who will be able any longer to hold the simple by his terror, so that the foot of man does not tread in them, whereby the Egyptian waters seem not to have in them even a sign of wisdom and reason —; nor will the hoof of beasts trouble them, so as to make them 'turbid and muddy' instead of most limpid and shining.

And so great will be the desolation in Egypt that its waters will be troubled neither by the foot of man nor by the hoof of beast, but all things will be quiet; and the waters of its rivers will flow like oil, most pure and shining, with no one passing through them nor troubling their streams' — and this will come about because of the desolation of Egypt, which will be reduced to a desert, stripped of all its multitude, when the Lord has struck its inhabitants, so that those who remain may understand that he himself is the Lord —.

32:14.t: Then the waters that had been troubled by the dragon's dominion will be rendered most pure, not by another but by the Lord himself, so that their rivers are rendered like oil and are the nourishment of the true light; and these things will come about when the Lord has made the land of Egypt desolate and has destroyed its fullness and all its inhabitants have been struck, so that by this progress they may be able to know that he himself is the Lord.

32:16.t: Therefore it is a lament for Pharaoh, and the daughters of the nations round about will lament him, and not only over him, but also over his multitude which, as the Lord laid it waste, was blotted out.

And what is joined: It is a lament, and they shall lament him; the daughters of the nations shall lament him; over Egypt and over its multitude they shall lament him, says the Lord God, makes it plain that the souls of all the nations which had formerly been oppressed by him, or of those nations which by no means dwelt in Egypt but in the region of the living, lament the slain dragon and all his multitude: not in hope of salvation, but because from so great a power, by his own vice and pride, he has been cast down into eternal punishments.

32:17.t: Now, with the same brevity, so far as the difficulty of the explanation permits, let us gather the chief points of the spiritual understanding. Above, the word of the Lord came to the prophet on the first day of the month; here, on the fifteenth — now on the first day, that is, on the calends, is the beginning of the month; on the fifteenth, when the whole orb of the moon is filled; and if it was the first month, it is the first day of Unleavened Bread, but if the seventh, of Tabernacles, when the tents are pitched, which feasts are among the very greatest among the Hebrews —; and the lament is made over the strength of Egypt, so that he who is strong in evil may cease to be so and take on weakness, and when he is weaker, then he may be stronger. For the 'strength' of Egypt, the Hebrew has 'multitude' — For wide and spacious is the way that leads to death, and many enter by it, just as, on the contrary, it is said to Israel: But you are few among all the nations; […]

And it came to pass in the twelfth year, on the fifteenth of the month, the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, sing a dirge over the multitude of Egypt, and drag it down, it and the daughters of the mighty nations, to the lowest land with those who go down into the pit. Than whom are you more beautiful? Go down, and sleep with the uncircumcised. In the midst of those slain by the sword they shall fall; the sword has been given; they have dragged her away and all her peoples. The mightiest of the strong will speak to him from the midst of hell, they who went down with his helpers; and they have slept uncircumcised and slain by the sword. There is Assyria and all her multitude, round about her are their graves, all of them slain, and they who fell by the sword; whose graves have been set in the uttermost parts of the pit, and her multitude is round about her grave; all of them slain and falling by the sword, who once had spread dread in the land of the living. […]

32:19.t: And what follows: Than whom are you more beautiful? Go down, and sleep with the uncircumcised, the word is properly addressed to Pharaoh king of Egypt — or, as was added in the Seventy from Theodotion, to Egypt itself: From the most beautiful water go down, and sleep with the uncircumcised; which pertains especially to him who, reborn in the baptism of Christ, hearing with the Church: Who is she that comes up made white, leaning upon her kinsman?, afterwards, defiled either by fornication or by other vices, is cast out of the Church, and it is said to him: From the most beautiful water go down, and sleep 'with the uncircumcised', that is, 'with the unclean', according to that sense which the Apostle sets down: We are the circumcision, who serve God in the spirit, and glory in the Lord, and put no confidence in the flesh —.

32:20.t: All these will fall with Pharaoh in the midst of the wounded — or the slain —, by that sword which is the opposite of the sword which the Lord came to send upon the earth: for just as the sword of Christ separates the good from the evil — as he says: I came not to send peace upon the earth, but a sword —, so the sword of the heretics cuts down all peoples and leads the wounded down to the underworld; these are the giants, most mighty and rebellious and setting their mouth on high, and the more they raise themselves up to the heights through pride, the more they are dragged down to the depth of the ditch and the uttermost parts of hell, all of whom have been slain by the sword.

32:22.t: And so that either Pharaoh or the whole strength of Egypt, which has been dragged down to the underworld, might know whom he had as companions in punishment, the following word shows: There is Assyria and all the multitude (or synagogue) of her; for the prince of the heretics is the devil — whose congregation is truly a synagogue, of which it is said in the Revelation: Who are the synagogue of Satan —.

But the following short verses, which are marked in front with an obelus, I think should be passed over, and what is found in the Hebrew should be stated: Round about her are their graves, namely of those deceived by him, who are all wounded (or slain) by the sword, and therefore have fallen; whose graves have been set in the uttermost parts of the pit — and that hell is called a pit is plainly shown by that psalm in which the penitent says: I have been likened to those who go down into the pit; which we ought by no means, according to the proper sense of the Latin word, to understand as that which in Greek is called λίμνη [lake] — such as the lake of Tiberias, and lakes Larius and Benacus, and many others —, but as what we are accustomed to call cisterns; which pits, because they chill the waters and take from them all the warmth of the spirit, sinners and all heretics dig; […]

32:24.t: After this it is said: There is Elam, and all her multitude round about her grave, no doubt the Assyrian's. 'Elam' is rendered into our tongue as 'their ascent'; for all who, despising the humility of Christ, have ascended to the pride of the devil and have thought themselves to be something in the knowledge falsely so called, are to be named Elamites, who go round the grave of the Assyrian king and have been slain and wounded by the sword; and although they set their mouth on high, yet they went down unclean and uncircumcised to the lowest land, so that the more loftily they had been raised up, the more heavily they might fall; these set their terror not once but a second time in the land of the living — for who among the churchmen is safe from the terror of Elamites of this kind and has not lost someone of his flock? —; and beautifully the Church of Christ is called the land of the living, so that, on the contrary, the conventicles of the heretics may be believed to be the land of the dead.

And they have borne, he says, their shame (or their torment) with those whom they dragged down with them into the pit and the depth of hell, whose bed is in the midst of the slain; namely of those whose throats they cut with their blade, and they are surrounded by peoples of this kind; these peoples are the peoples of the Assyrian king, and although they boast that they are circumcised, yet they are uncircumcised and slain by the sword, and a third time they have spread terror and dread in the land of the living; hence they have borne their torment and punishment in the midst of those whom they deceived by their frauds.

32:26.t: There also is — that is, beside the Assyrian — Meshech and Tubal and all her multitude, round about her grave, all uncircumcised and slain and falling by the sword, who had set their dread in the land of the living. For 'Mosoch and Thubal', Symmachus and Theodotion translated 'their bed', to show that the beds of the heretics, or rather their everlasting ditches, are the punishments of the Assyrian king; 'Mosoch' means 'madness', 'Thubal' 'conversion' — not to good from evil but from good to evil — or 'all things', to show that all heretics are mad and with equal zeal are turned to worse things; nor is it surprising if those who are mad and heaped together for evil have a multitude, since they are companions of the Egyptian king, who rejoices in multitude; all these have been slain by the sword, who set their dread, not once nor a second time, but a third time, in the land of the living, of which we have spoken more fully above.

32:27.t: There follows: And they will not sleep with the mighty (or the giants) who fell, and the uncircumcised, who went down to hell with their weapons and set their swords under their heads, and their iniquities were in their bones, because they became the terror of the mighty in the land of the living. 'These,' he says, 'who stood out as leaders of the heretics, have come to such a summit of malice and of torment, that they do not deserve to bear like punishments even with the mighty and the giants who fell from the beginning; who, having by no means done penance for their error, went down to the underworld with their weapons, rebels against God and his Church, carrying their spirit with them' — of whom it is written: Sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows —, 'and they set,' he says, 'their swords under their heads, resting in a hostile spirit, and, as their supreme victory, embracing the darts of their opinions, to such a degree that their iniquities were in their bones — that is, their strongest fabrications […]

32:28.t: After this it is written: 'And you therefore will be crushed in the midst of the uncircumcised' — which is said either to Pharaoh or to the strength, or multitude, of Egypt, that it too is crushed, according to what is written: But may God crush Satan under your feet swiftly — 'and you will sleep,' he says, 'with those slain by the sword, in perpetual sleep'.

32:29.t: There, with the Assyrian and with the Egyptian multitude, will be Edom and her kings, all who have served earthly works or delighted in blood — for 'Idumaea' [Edom] sounds both 'earthy' and 'bloody' —; all the kings and all the princes — of whom the Apostle also frequently speaks: 'brooding over earthly works and daily shedding the blood of those whom they have deceived by their fraud' — have slept with the uncircumcised and unclean and with those who went down into the pit, of whom we have spoken above.

32:30.t: In the same company will also be the princes of the north, from which evils blaze up upon the earth — and from which, whether in Jeremiah or in this same prophet, that pot full of flesh and bones is set alight —, and not only the princes of the north, but every magistrate of 'Assur' — for which in the Hebrew is more truly set down all the 'Sidonians', whom we have rendered as 'hunters', according to what is written: Our soul has been snatched like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters (for which in the Hebrew is set down of the Sidonians); which Sidonians — or hunters — will be led down to the underworld trembling, who once trusted in their own strength; and they will sleep unclean, and they will bear their confusion — or torment —, having the everlasting remorse of an evil conscience, so that their fire is not quenched and their worm does not die.

32:31.t: When Pharaoh has seen all these, he will be comforted, either still having his former malice and seeing that he has many companions of his punishment, or at any rate he was comforted seeing that they too are confounded in their punishments and their terrors, over all his multitude which was slain by the sword: that is, Pharaoh's, or that of all his companions, and especially of the Assyrian king and Meshech and Tubal and the Edomites, and of the princes of the north and of the Sidonians; for these had set their terror in the land of the living — which is said for the fifth time, so that we ought to beware of and flee all nations of this kind, which have deceived us in all our senses, and know that they are dreadful and cannot easily be avoided unless we keep our heart with all vigilance —. 'He has slept,' he says, 'Pharaoh himself too, with his companions slain by the sword', which companions are his multitude, going by the wide and spacious way to everlasting punishments.

33:1.t: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, speak to the sons of your people, and you shall say to them: A land, when I bring the sword upon it, and the people of the land take one man from the last of them (or one man from among them), and set him over themselves as a watchman, and he sees the sword coming upon the land, and sounds the trumpet and announces it to the people; but whoever he is who hears the sound of the trumpet does not take heed for himself, and the sword comes and takes (or seizes) him: his blood shall be upon his own head; he heard the sound (or voice) of the trumpet and did not take heed for himself, his blood shall be upon him. But if he guards himself, he has saved his soul. But if the watchman sees the sword coming, and does not sound the trumpet, and the people do not guard themselves; and the sword comes and takes a soul from among them: that one indeed has been taken in his iniquity, but his blood I will require from the hand of the watchman. […]

33:2.t: Passing by the elders in the book of Daniel; for it is better to pass them by, together with the Lord's righteous sentence and declaration concerning them, that wickedness came from Babylon from ancient judges, who seemed to govern the people; how are we affected by Ezekiel, the beholder and expositor of the mighty mysteries and visions? By his injunction to the watchmen not to keep silence concerning vice and the sword impending over it, a course which would profit neither themselves nor the sinners; but rather to keep watch and forewarn, and thus benefit, at any rate those who gave warning, if not both those who spoke and those who heard?

An important medicine for evil is confession, and care to avoid stumbling. I will be first to do so, as I have made my report to my people from on high, and performed the duty of a watcher. For I did not conceal the coming of the sword that I might save my own soul and those of my hearers. So will I now announce the disobedience of my people, making what is theirs my own, if I may perchance thus obtain some tenderness and relief.

We can, however, discuss this passage in a threefold way: so that the land which appoints a watchman for itself is either, according to the letter, the land of Judea, or, according to the spiritual understanding, the Church, which often chooses a watchman from the last of its people — namely that one whom the Apostle too, writing to the Corinthians, takes as judge —, or certainly the soul of the believer, which sets the mind and reason over the people and crowd of its thoughts — so that it may not admit every incitement of the thoughts, but may judge and discern which things it should pursue and which it should flee —. The watchman of the land of Judea can be understood as either the king or the prophet; but the watchman of the Church as either the bishop or the presbyter, who has been chosen by the people and, knowing and foreseeing through the reading of the Scriptures what is to come, is to announce it to the people and correct the one who goes astray. […]

33:6.t: And: "From the hand of the watchman I will require your blood." What blood does God demand from the hand of the watchman, if not that of which the sinner is deprived? So the heart of the foolish one is destroyed, according to the saying: "Listen to Me, you who have lost heart!" — because the sinner is deprived of the blood and vital force of the soul.

O watchers, watch well, and admonish all the people concerning the sword, lest it come and take away the soul. For that soul is taken away in its sins, and its blood will be required from your hands. But if the soul is taken away after admonition, that soul will be taken away in its own sins, and ye will not be trodden down.

For this reason, overseers or rulers are set over the churches to reprimand sin, not to spare it. Nor is a person fully free from blame who is not in authority but who notices in those persons he meets in social life many faults he should censure and admonish. He is blameworthy if he fails to do this out of fear of hurting feelings or of losing such things as he may rightfully enjoy in his life but to which he is unduly attached.

33:7.t: From these words we learn: that a man, though unrighteous and wicked, can be saved from his wickedness if he hears the words of the teacher and repents; and no less, that the teacher incurs peril if he is unwilling to teach, whether from fear of peril or from despair of the sinner, since he is guilty of the blood of one who could have been delivered and rescued from death, had he not fallen through the teacher's silence; and that in both free will is preserved, since it lies both in the teacher's will either to keep silent or to speak, and in the hearer's choice either to hear and do and be saved, or to despise and perish by his own contempt. Nor does it immediately follow that, because a prophet foretells something, what he foretold comes — for he does not foretell it so that it may come, but so that it may not come —; nor, because God speaks, must what he threatens necessarily happen; […]

33:10.t: You therefore, son of man, say to the house of Israel: Thus you have spoken, saying: Our iniquities and our sins are upon us, and we are wasting away in them; how then shall we be able to live? Say to them: As I live, says the Lord God; I do not want the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn back from his way, and live; and turn from your most evil ways; and why will you die, house of Israel? You therefore, son of man, say to the sons of your people: The righteousness of the righteous shall not deliver him on whatever day he sins, and the wickedness of the wicked shall not harm him on whatever day he turns from his wickedness; and the righteous shall not be able to live in his righteousness on whatever day he sins. Even if I say to the righteous that he shall live by life, and, trusting in his righteousness, he commits iniquity; all his righteous deeds shall be consigned to oblivion, and in his iniquity which he has wrought, in it he shall die. […]

33:11.t: He who has thus satisfied God, who by repentance for his deed, who by shame for his sin has conceived more of both virtue and faith from the very sorrow for his lapsing, after being heard and aided by the Lord, will cause the church to rejoice, which he recently had saddened, and will merit not only the pardon of God but a crown.

If you have any hope of salvation; if you have the least thought of God, or any desire for good things to come; if you have any fear of the chastisements reserved for the impenitent, awake without delay, lift up your eyes to heaven, come to your senses, cease from your wickedness, shake off the stupor that enwraps you, make a stand against the foe who has struck you down. Make an effort to rise from the ground. Remember the good Shepherd who will follow and rescue you. Though it be but two legs or a lobe of an ear, spring back from the beast that has wounded you. Remember the mercies of God and how He cures with oil and wine. Do not despair of salvation. Recall your recollection of how it is written in the Scriptures that he who is falling rises and he who turns away returns; the wounded is healed, the prey of beasts escapes; he who owns his sin is not rejected. The Lord willeth not the death of a sinner but rather that he should turn and live.

And yet God is gracious and merciful. He is called a God "of mercies and a God of comfort"; good as none else is good, and kind, and gentle, and full of pity, Who "willeth not the death of a sinner, but that he should be converted and live." Whence then, whence is that Day so full of agony and anguish? A stream of fire is rolling before His face. The books of our deeds are opened. The day itself is burning as an oven, the angels are flying around, and many furnaces are prepared. How then is He good and merciful, and full of lovingkindness to man? Even herein is He merciful, and He shows in these things the greatness of His lovingkindness. For He holds forth to us these terrors, that being constrained by them, we may be awakened to the desire of the kingdom.

Nothing makes God so angry as when people from despair of better things cleave to those which are worse; and indeed this despair in itself is a sign of unbelief. One who despairs of salvation can have no expectation of a judgment to come.

Hear the Scripture: “I will not the death of a sinner, but rather that he should turn, and live.” By these words of God, he is brought back to hope; but there is another snare to be feared, lest through this very hope he sin the more. What then didst thou also say, thou who through hope sinnest yet more? “Whensoever I turn, God will forgive me all; I will do whatsoever I will.” Say not then, “To-morrow I will turn, to-morrow I will please God; and all to-day’s and yesterday’s deeds shall be forgiven me.” Thou sayest true: God hath promised pardon to thy conversion; He hath not promised a to-morrow to thy delay.

For the purpose of God whereby He made man not to perish but to live for ever, stands immovable. And when His goodness sees in us even the very smallest spark of good will shining forth, which He Himself has struck as it were out of the hard flints of our hearts, He fans and fosters it and nurses it with His breath, as He "willeth all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth," for as He says, "it is not the will of your Father which is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish," and again it says: "Neither will God have a soul to perish, but recalleth," meaning that he that is cast off should not altogether perish. For He is true, and lieth not when He lays down with an oath: "As I live, saith the Lord God, for I will not the death of a sinner, but that he should turn from his way and live." For if He willeth not that one of His little ones should perish, how can we imagine without grievous blasphemy that He does not generally will all men, but only some instead of all to be saved? […]
33:11.s: The Third Conference of Abbot Chaeremon, Chapter 7

33:11.t: Let us consider the grace of merciful God, and let us condemn the multitude of our own guilt. Behold, he sees sinners and endures them, tolerates those who resist, and yet daily calls them mercifully through the Gospel. He desires our confession from a pure heart, and has forgiven all that we have done wrong. The mercy of the Redeemer has tempered for us the severity of the law. For in it was written: If anyone does this or that, let him surely die. If anyone does these or those things, let him be overwhelmed with stones. Our Creator and Redeemer appeared in the flesh, promising not punishment but life to the confession of sinners; he receives the woman confessing her wounds, and sends her away healed. He bent the hardness of the law toward mercy, because those whom the law justly condemns, he himself mercifully frees. Hence it is also well written in the law that the hands of Moses were heavy; therefore taking a stone, they placed it underneath, upon which he sat; and Aaron and Hur supported his hands. […]

33:12.t: We must press on and persevere in the faith and virtue and in the consummation of heavenly and spiritual grace, that we may be able to arrive at the palm and the crown.
In the lives of Christians we look not to the beginnings but to the endings. Paul began badly but ended well. The start of Judas wins praise; his end is condemned because of his treachery.

For what does it profit a man to be in continence for twenty years, and afterwards to fall? — according to what is written in the prophet: 'The justice of the just man shall not profit him on whatever day he goes astray: it shall not free him, nor save him. And the sin of the sinner shall not harm him on whatever day he turns and does penance.' Neither ought the just man to be secure, nor ought the sinner to despair of his salvation: for in both of them there is both fear and hope.

And from the particular admonition with which he was speaking to the house of Israel, he passes to a general discussion: that past acts of righteousness do not save the righteous man if he has become taken up with new crimes, and old sins do not destroy the sinner or the wicked if he has amended his old errors by works of righteousness, and that God in both cases judges not past things but present ones: 'If I say,' he says, 'to the righteous: You shall live by life, and promise him the rewards of righteousness, and he, trusting in this, sins, all his former righteous deeds will be consigned to oblivion and he will die in his present iniquity; nor has my sentence changed, since I cannot render to the same man, now a sinner, what I had promised to the righteous man; […]

But behold, while we search out the secrets of the heavenly citizens, we have digressed far from the order of our exposition. Let us therefore sigh toward those of whom we speak, but let us return to ourselves. For we ought to remember that we are flesh. Let us be silent meanwhile about the secrets of heaven, but before the eyes of our Creator let us wipe away the stains of our dust with the hand of repentance. Behold, divine mercy itself promises, saying: There shall be joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance; and yet through the prophet the Lord says: In whatever day the just man shall sin, all his righteousnesses shall be in oblivion before me. Let us consider, if we can, the dispensation of heavenly loving-kindness. To those who stand, if they should fall, he threatens punishment; but to the fallen, that they might desire to rise, he promises mercy. He terrifies those, lest they presume upon their good works; he comforts these, lest they despair in their evils. You are just—fear wrath, lest you fall; […]

33:13.t: If you are righteous, fear his wrath lest you slip; if you are a sinner, believe in his mercy so that you can arise. But see, we have already fallen, we are not strong enough to stand, we lie prostrate in our evil desires. He who created us to be upright still waits, and he appeals to us to rise. He opens up his heart of love and seeks to get us back to himself again through repentance.

33:18.t: Be ye not afraid, O penitents, lest the hope which is written in the Scriptures be cut off; for it is fitting for the Spirit of God thus to warn, for a fearful warning is set in Ezekiel the prophet when He said to him: "If all his days a man shall do judgment and righteousness, and at the end of his days he shall do iniquity, in his iniquity he shall die. And if a man shall do iniquity all his days, and he shall repent and do judgment and righteousness, his soul shall live" (Ezek. 33: 18-19). By this one word He has warned the righteous that he should not sin and lose his course; and He gave hope to the wicked that he should turn from his iniquity and live.

33:21.t: And it came to pass in the twelfth year, in the tenth month, on the fifth of the month of our exile (or captivity), there came to me one who had fled (or who had been saved) from Jerusalem, saying: The city has been laid waste (or taken). Now the hand of the Lord had come upon me in the evening, before he who had fled came; and he opened my mouth until he came to me in the morning, and, my mouth being opened, I was silent no longer. In the eleventh year of the reign of Zedekiah, in the fifth month, the city of Jerusalem was taken. But this prophecy is dated the twelfth year, the tenth month, the fifth of the month, of the captivity or exile, when he was taken captive with Jeconiah. From this it is shown that one year, four months and twenty-five days after Jerusalem was taken, one of the citizens of Jerusalem came to Babylon to report that the city had been taken and laid waste.

This is according to the letter; but according to the ἀναγωγὴν [anagogy, the higher sense]: if 'Hiezechiel' [Ezekiel] means 'strength of God' — and Christ, moreover, is the power of God and the wisdom of God! —, this is to be understood: that, Jerusalem having been taken and overthrown, whoever has been able to escape the faithlessness of the Jews — such as were the apostles and the remnant that was saved —, he himself announces to Christ that all the ceremonies of the Jews have been overthrown — which certain people think must be observed even to this day, not hearing that saying of the Apostle: You have fallen from grace, you who are justified in the law. And I marvel at the obstinacy of men in wishing to defend in word what they do not dare to fulfill in deed, unless perhaps Jewish wolves are hiding under the skin of sheep, that is, of Christians. Why does a defender of the Synagogue make his voice resound in the churches of Christ? —. […]

33:22.t: One day before the one who was to tell these things came, in the evening the hand of the Lord came upon the prophet Ezekiel, and it opened his mouth, which had long been closed; and whatever that man was going to say, this one recounted beforehand as already done, and he was silent no longer, seeing his prophecy fulfilled in deed, and that the people who were in Babylon, or those who were captives, by no means doubted the prophetic oracle; for the mouth of the prophet is opened at the moment when he has shown accomplished in deed what he had announced before; and he proclaims with all freedom who points out not future things at all, but things either present or past.

33:24.t: Jerusalem having been taken, as we have said, and the temple overthrown, the poor of the land, of whom Jeremiah writes, had alone been left in Jerusalem, to tend the vineyards and the fields and to dwell in the ruins of the burned city; and though they ought to have repented over the things on account of which the captivity had come, deceiving themselves with an empty hope, they said: 'Our father Abraham was one, and yet he possessed this land by inheritance — not that he himself possessed it, but that his seed received the land of promise; if therefore that one man was multiplied into such great peoples, we, who are many more, who have been left in the land of Judea and dwell in deserted and ruined cities, shall surely be multiplied much more, so that we, being many, may possess what that one man possessed'.

Now let us come to the tropology and, according to our custom, draw the broad discussion together rather than spread it out. Every heretic dwells among crumbling walls and in deserts, and thinks that he possesses the land of Israel: 'If Abraham, one man, by his faith came to such great blessedness that his seed was multiplied like the sand of the sea and like the stars of heaven, how much more shall we, being many, possess the land of 'Israel', that is, 'of those who see God', and 'Iudaea' [Judea], 'of the Lord's confession'?'; to them the Lord answered: 'He possessed the land by the merit of faith; but your unbelief, or rather blasphemy, will not be able to possess the land of Israel, that is, the Church.

33:25.t: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, those who dwell in these ruins upon the soil of Israel speak, saying: Abraham was one, and he possessed the land; but we are many, to us the land has been given as a possession. Therefore you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: You who eat in blood, and lift up your eyes to your uncleannesses, and shed blood, shall you possess the land by inheritance? You have stood upon your swords, you have done abominations, and each of you has defiled his neighbor's wife, and shall you possess the land by inheritance? These things you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: As I live, those who dwell in the ruins shall fall by the sword, and he who is in the field shall be given to the beasts to be devoured, but those who are in strongholds and in caves shall die of pestilence. […]

To them the Lord answered that Abraham, one man, had possessed the land of promise by faith — For Abraham believed, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness —, but that these, taken up with unbelief and crimes, even if they are more, cannot possess it; and at the same time he enumerates by what deeds they offend God, namely six kinds of sins: 'You who eat in blood, and lift up your eyes to uncleannesses, that is, to your idols, and shed blood, that is, commit homicide; doing these things, will you be able to keep the land by inheritance? Nor are you content with this limit of crimes, but you stand upon your swords daily, ready to kill and imitating Esau, who stood, and lived by his sword; you do incredible abominations, namely the foulnesses of lusts; and each one defiles his neighbor's wife, so that he is the more wicked in this, that he had defiled the wife of a friend and neighbor. Would you do these things,' he says, 'and suppose that you will hold the land by inheritance?

For first, you eat in blood, pouring out the blood of those whom you cause to stumble; next, you lift up your eyes to uncleannesses or to your abominations which you have fabricated out of your own mind — when you ought to have imitated the man of the Church and said: To you I have lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in the heavens —; third, you shed blood, not giving life to those whom you have led astray, but killing them; nor is it enough for you to have done these three things, but you stand upon your swords, that is, you persevere in the depravity of your opinion, and are ready for slaughter; and you have done abominations, doing in bedchambers things that are shameful to speak of; and you have defiled the wife of your neighbor, hastening, namely, to snatch away daily from the embrace of Christ, by deceiving them, those of the Church's way of life. And when you have done these things, do you think that you will hold the land of Israel by inheritance?'

33:27.t: Answer them therefore, O prophet, and bring forth this sentence upon them from my word: I swear by myself that those who dwell in the ruins and the crumbling walls shall fall by the sword, and those who are in the fields — or in the open country — shall be devoured by beasts, and those who are in walled places — or in strongholds — and in caves shall not be able to escape the wrath of God, but shall die by famine and pestilence.

To them God says that whoever has dwelt in the ruined conventicles of the heretics shall fall by the sword of the Church — of which it is written: And two-edged swords in their hands, and in the Gospel: I did not come to send peace, but a sword, and: 'The servant who gives himself over to luxury and leisure shall be divided, that is, shall be struck with the blade, and his portion shall be placed with the unbelievers' —, and he who is in the field, or in the open country, shall be given to the beasts to be devoured — the beasts which the prophet, desiring to avoid them, prays against: Do not give to the beasts the soul that confesses to you —, but he who is in strongholds and in walled places — of which it is written: The righteous man went up against the strongest cities and destroyed their fortifications, in which the wicked trusted — and lingers in caves — of which it is said: It is written: The house of my Father shall be called a house of prayer; […]

33:28.t: And I will give,' he says, 'the land of Judea into solitude, and its proud strength shall fail — which had once been strength: The proud, however, God resists, and gives grace to the humble —; the mountains too and everything shall be deserted, and they shall come into such solitude that no one passes through them; and then the few who had remained shall by no means trust in their multitude, but shall know, by the greatness of the solitude, that I am the Lord, who gave the land into desert because of all the abominations which they have wrought'. Let these things be said against those who, Jerusalem having been taken and the whole region of the Jews laid waste, dwelt, a few of them, in the ruined and deserted cities and little villages.

33:30.t: There follows — on the same day indeed and at the same time, that is, in the twelfth year, the tenth month, on the fifth of the month, when the one who had fled from Jerusalem came, and when the prophet spoke to those who were in the land of Judea and promised themselves the hope of an everlasting possession — and he commands the prophet to speak to the people that lives in Babylon and dwells with him, and to rebuke them for their flattering snares, those who desire to hear the words of the prophet not for the salvation of the soul but for the pleasure of the ears; these walk beside the walls and in the doorways of the houses, by no means desiring to enter into the prophet's meaning, but they urge one another on and say: Come, and let us hear what is the word that comes forth from the Lord.

33:31.t: 'And so they come like a people entering the Church of God, and they sit before you, my people, which says that it is mine, and they are unwilling to do what they have heard; people of this sort seem to me like those who are beguiled by theatrical songs and listen either to tragedians or to comedians and are there caressed with pleasure, so that, when they have gone out from you, they repeat these things and sing them over and deceive themselves with the sweet sound: And they will hear,' he says, 'your words and will not do them'. Such, even to this day, are many in the churches, who say: 'Come, let us hear this man and that man', as he rolls out the words of his preaching with marvelous eloquence; and they stir up applause and shout and wave their hands; […]

34:1.t: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, prophesy concerning the shepherds (or to the shepherds) of Israel, prophesy and say to the shepherds: Thus says the Lord God: Woe to the shepherds of Israel who were feeding themselves (or O shepherds of Israel, do shepherds feed themselves); are not the flocks fed by the shepherds (or do not the shepherds feed the sheep)? You ate the milk and covered yourselves with the wool, and what was fat you slaughtered, but my flock you did not feed; what was weak you did not make firm (or strengthen), and what was sick you did not heal, what was broken you did not bind up, and what was cast off (or was straying) you did not bring back, what had perished you did not seek, but you ruled over them with harshness and with power (or and what was strong, you afflicted with toil). And my sheep were scattered, because there was no shepherd (or shepherds); and they were made to be devoured by all the beasts of the field, and they were scattered. […]

34:2.t: But those pastors who did not care for the sheep, those were hirelings who used to feed themselves alone. On this account the Prophet addresses them, saying to them:—O ye pastors who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture, hear the word of the Lord. Thus saith the Lord: Lo! I will visit My sheep as the pastor visits his flock in the day of the whirlwind, and I will require My sheep at your hands. O foolish pastors, with the wool of the sheep do ye clothe yourselves and the flesh of the fatlings do eat, and the sheep ye do not feed. That which was sick ye did not heal, and that which was broken ye did not bind. The weak ye did not strengthen, and the lost and the scattered ye did not gather together. The strong ones and the fatlings ye did guard, but with harshness ye subdued them. The good pastures ye yourselves graze upon, and what remains ye trample with your feet. The pleasant waters do ye drink, and whatever remains ye defile with your feet. […]

For you must know, and not be in doubt, that while before your election you lived to yourself, after it, you live for your flock. And before you had received the grace of the episcopate, no one knew you; but after you became one, the laity expect you to bring them food, namely instruction from the Scriptures. When then they expect, and suffer hunger, and you are feeding yourself only, and our Lord Jesus Christ comes and we stand before Him, what defence will you offer when He sees His own sheep hungering? For had you not taken the money, He would not have blamed you. But He would reasonably do so if upon taking it you dug and buried it,—in the words which God forbid that your piety should ever hear: ‘Thou oughtest to have given my money to the bankers, that when I came I might demand it of them.’

34:3.t: Let him use those tenths and first-fruits, which are given according to the command of God, as a man of God; as also let him dispense in a right manner the free-will offerings which are brought in on account of the poor, to the orphans, the widows, the afflicted, and strangers in distress, as having that God for the examiner of his accounts who has committed the disposition to him. Distribute to all those in want with righteousness, and yourselves use the things which belong to the Lord, but do not abuse them; eating of them, but not eating them all up by yourselves: communicate with those that are in want, and thereby show yourselves unblameable before God. For if you shall consume them by yourselves, you will be reproached by God, who says to such unsatiable people, who alone devour all, "You eat up the milk, and clothe yourselves with the wool;" [Ezekiel 34:3] and in another passage, "Must you alone live upon the earth"? […]

As for what follows: You ate the milk and covered yourselves with the wool, it is by a μεταφορὰν [metaphor] of shepherds that he speaks to the princes — of whom it is also written in another place: Who devour my people like a meal of bread —; in the milk understand all wealth, in the wool the manifold variety of garments. And what is said: And what was fat you slaughtered, speaks of the rich of the people, whom the wicked princes in the churches are said to slaughter, in that they praise them and dare not rebuke their vices — of whom the prophet also says: My people, those who call you blessed lead you astray, and trip up the path of your feet; […]

34:4.t: And since it is incumbent on us who seem to be in charge and in the place of shepherds to guard the flock, if we should be found negligent, what will be said to us was said to our predecessors who were such negligent leaders.

If we scorn the repentance of those who have in some degree the assurance of a bearable conscience, immediately they are drawn by the devil's invitation into heresy or schism with their wife and children, whom they had kept unharmed. And it will be charged against us on judgment day that we have not cared for the wounded sheep and have lost many innocent ones because of one wounded.

Having therefore mentioned the marks of a shepherd, Christ hath put two kinds of spoilers; one, the thief who kills and steals; the other, one who doth not these things, but who when they are done doth not give heed nor hinder them. By the first, pointing to Theudas and those like him; by the second, exposing the teachers of the Jews, who neither cared for nor thought about the sheep entrusted to them. On which account Ezekiel of old rebuked them, and said, "Woe, ye shepherds of Israel! Do the shepherds feed themselves? Do not the shepherds feed the sheep?" But they did the contrary, which is the worst kind of wickedness, and the cause of all the rest. Wherefore It saith, "They have not turned back the strayed, nor sought the lost, nor bound up the broken, nor healed the sick, because they fed themselves and not the sheep."... From both Christ distinguisheth Himself; from those who came to spoil, by saying, "I am come that they might have life, and that they might have more abundantly"; […]
34:4.s: Homily on the Gospel of John 60

34:4.t: For one who had been cast away is brought back, when any one who has fallen into sin is recalled to a state of righteousness by the vigour of pastoral solicitude. For ligature binds a fracture when discipline subdues a sin, lest the wound should bleed mortally for want of being compressed by the severity of constraint. But often a fracture is made worse, when it is bound together unwarily, so that the cut is more severely felt from being immoderately constrained by ligaments. Hence it is needful that when a wound of sin in subordinates is repressed by correction, even constraint should moderate itself with great carefulness, to the end that it may so exercise the rights of discipline against delinquents as to retain the bowels of loving-kindness.

34:5.t: And the people of God was scattered, either by vices or by heretical error, because there was no good shepherd who would lay down his life for the sheep, but all were hirelings, who consider only the profits from the flocks and flee when they see the wolf; through whose negligence the Lord's flock is devoured by the beasts of the field — of which it is written: You set darkness, and night came: in it all the beasts of the field will pass through, the lions' whelps roaring, to seize and to seek their food from God —.

34:6.t: And they are scattered, and they wander on all the mountains, who are lifted up against the knowledge of God, and on every high hill, who through heretical pride despise the simplicity of the Church, and they are scattered over the whole face of the earth, seeking earthly things, not heavenly: And there was none who would seek, nor who would bring back, because, occupied with their pleasures, they do not care about the losses of the Lord's flock.

34:7.t: Hence the word of the Lord comes to the wicked shepherds, 'because you have done this and that', the things which I expounded above and which he enumerates a second time. 'Behold, I myself will come to the shepherds and will require my flock at their hand, for whom it is better that a donkey's millstone be tied to their neck than that they scandalize the least of my people; and this will be their punishment, even the greatest: That they no longer feed my flock, lest, under the pretext of the sheep, they feed themselves and amass wealth; and I will deliver my people from their mouth'.

34:10.t: 'I will require', he says, 'from the hand', and 'I will deliver from the mouth', by which they are devoured with greedy jaws; and when he has sought out the sheep, he visits them as sick and lean and scattered through the negligence of the shepherds; and he will deliver them from all places in the day of cloud and gloom — of which Joel too speaks: The day of the Lord is at hand, and it is near; a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and mist —.

34:13.t: Then they are led out from the lands, so as to be brought into their own land, which is the land of the living, and so that he himself may feed them on the mountains of Israel — of which David speaks: I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, whence help will come to me —, and not only on the mountains, but by the streams and in all the dwelling places of the land, in the richest pastures and on the high mountain — of which Isaiah and Micah prophesy more fully —, or on the high mountains, Israel; there they will rest in green grass — and they will say: The Lord feeds me, and nothing will be lacking to me: in a place of pasture, there he has set me; beside the water of refreshment he has brought me up —, and they will feed in the fattest pastures upon the mountains of Israel.

There, life is wisdom, through which all these things come into being, both those that have been and those that will be. Yet, it is not made but is as it was, and thus it will be forever. Or rather, to have been in the past or to be in the future does not pertain to it, but simply to be, for it is eternal. To be in the past or to be in the future is not to be eternal.

34:15.t: And it is an infinite promise and a hope of blessedness, when the Lord himself promises, saying: 'I will feed my sheep, and I will by no means entrust them to wicked shepherds, and I will make them lie down, says the Lord God, so that they may rest in the bosom of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob'.

34:16.t: O shepherds, disciples of the Lord, feed the flock and lead (it) well! Strengthen the sick, support the weak, bind up the broken, make whole the lame, and take heed to the fattened ones for the Lord of the flock. Be not likened unto an unskilled and foolish shepherd, who in his foolishness is not able to feed the flock, and whose arm is dried up, and whose eye has been blinded, because he said: "dying, let it die; and perishing, let it perish, and the flesh that is left shall be eaten by its companions ". And when the Chief of the shepherds comes He will condemn the unskilled and foolish shepherd who has not cared well for his fellow servants. And he who has shepherded the flock and led (it) well shall be called "a good and skillful servant" (cf. S. Mt. 25: 21), who has presented the flock to the Shepherd while it was intact.

He is The Way, because He leads us through Himself; The Door, as letting us in; the Shepherd, as making us dwell in a place of green pastures, and bringing us up by waters of rest, and leading us there, and protecting us from wild beasts, converting the erring, bringing back that which was lost, binding up that which was broken, guarding the strong, and bringing them together in the Fold beyond, with words of pastoral knowledge.

Then what had perished among the peoples of the nations will be sought, and what had strayed through the persuasion of heretics will be brought back, and what had been broken will be bound up, and what is crushed and weak will be made firm — that what is written may be fulfilled: Who heals their infirmities, and binds up their bruises. A heart, indeed, crushed and humbled, God does not spurn; whence the holy man too says: Heal me, for my bones are troubled, and in Psalm 37 (38), repenting: There is no peace, he says, for my bones before the face of my sins —. And what will be fat, he says, and strong I will guard, lest it be devoured by beasts; and he will feed his sheep in judgment, knowing what pastures are owed to which sheep — for Diverse indeed are the dwellings with the Father. And the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son —. These things, then, he spoke against the shepherds.

But surely if we neglect our duties, does Almighty God abandon His sheep? By no means; for He Himself, as He promised through the prophet, feeds them by Himself, and He instructs all whom He has predestined to life through the goads of afflictions and the spirit of compunction.

We must all of us strive zealously to make known to the church both the dreadfulness of the coming judgment and the kingdom of heaven's delight. Those who are not in a position to address a large assembly should instruct individuals, offering instruction in personal talks; they should try to serve those around them through simple encouragement.… You who are pastors, consider that you are pasturing God's flock. We often see a block of salt put out for animals to lick for their well-being. Priests among their people should be like blocks of salt. They should counsel everyone in their flocks in such a way that all those with whom they come in contact may be seasoned with eternal life as if they had been sprinkled with salt. We who preach are not the salt of the earth unless we season the hearts of those who listen to us. […]

34:17.t: Now he speaks to the sheep, that is, to the people, and to the flock of both kinds of cattle, that is, of sheep and of goats, and not only to the sheep and goats, but to the rams and he-goats, who are the princes in the flocks; to whom he says: 'Was it not enough for you that you fed on the good pastures of the Scriptures? But on top of that you will trample the remnants of your pastures with your feet, and when you drank the purest water of God's utterances, you fouled the rest of the waters with your feet, so that my people ate the pastures trampled by you and drank the fouled waters, and, through your fault, received corrupted and violated what was good in itself'. This indeed all heretics do, picking at the utterances of the Scriptures and, as far as in them lies, staining them; but churchmen who do not guard the truth of doctrines, but fabricate them from their own heart and have their own presumption for their teacher, are held fast in a like error; […]

34:18.t: For indeed the shepherds drink most pure water, when with a right understanding they imbibe the streams of truth. But to foul the same water with their feet is to corrupt the studies of holy meditation by evil living. And verily the sheep drink the water fouled by their feet, when any of those subject to them follow not the words which they hear, but only imitate the bad examples which they see. Thirsting for the things said, but perverted by the works observed, they take in mud with their draughts, as from polluted fountains.

34:20.t: Let us see, then, what the judgment between cattle and cattle is, and with what judgment the good and true shepherd judges them, he who received all judgment from the Father: Behold, he says, I myself judge between fat cattle and lean (or between strong and weak): for the strong thrust with their sides and shoulders and dash against the weak cattle and toss them with their horns, not knowing that in the law the goring bull must be punished; and they thrust with their sides and tossed with their horns until they scattered the sheep and drove them out: for through the pride of the greater and the iniquity of those set over them, they are frequently driven from the church, so that those whom the Lord himself saved are scattered away from him; but the Lord will no longer abandon them to be a prey, and he will judge between cattle and cattle: not between the names of dignities with which those set over others swell, but between man and man, according as each is a servant of the Lord.

34:23.t: On this principle again all the kings whom they had in honor after his time were named from him, both by the people themselves and by God. For both Ezekiel and other prophets besides speak of David as coming and rising again; not meaning him that was dead, but them who were emulating his virtue. And to Hezekiah He saith, "I will defend this city, for mine own sake and for my servant David's sake."
34:23.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 2:6

34:23.t: Then he will raise up one shepherd — who says in the Gospel: I am the good shepherd —, his servant David — inasmuch as he deigned to take on the form of a servant; and 'David' means 'strong of hand' —; he himself will feed them.

Hence also in the same Ezekiel it is written: I will raise up over them one shepherd, and he shall feed them, my servant David; and he shall be their shepherd, and I the Lord will be their God, and David a prince in their midst. I the Lord have spoken, and I will make with David a covenant of peace (Ezek 34:23-25). In this it is to be considered that, long after the time of David, the gluttonous shepherds being rejected, he says he will raise up our Lord, who is of the stock of David, to gather the lambs and cherish them in his bosom, and himself to carry on his shoulder the young of the sheep, or the ewes with young; as we read in the Gospel that he carried back to the fold on his shoulders the sheep that had strayed and stayed behind from its accustomed flock (Luke 15).

34:24.t: And the Lord will be to them for God — either the Son and the Father, or certainly the shepherd according to the flesh he assumed. But 'Lord' and 'God' according to: The 'Word' that was in the beginning with 'God' —. This David, when the cattle have advanced to being a rational animal, will no longer be called shepherd but prince in the midst of them — of whom it is written: In the midst of you stands he whom you do not know —.

34:25.t: Then he will make with them a covenant of peace — by no means of wars and discord, for: His place was made in peace, but of the peace of Christ: Which surpasses all understanding —, who says: My peace I give to you, my peace I leave to you; and he will make the most evil beasts cease from the land — more mildly: either the passions by which human souls are troubled, or the adverse powers by which they are assailed —, and those who dwell in the desert will sleep secure in the woods — for the Lord will lay bare the thickets of the forests, and in his temple all will speak glory.

And when the beasts have been driven out and the land reduced to a solitude, they will sleep secure from animals of this sort and will say: The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear? —; and he will set them, those who will sleep secure, round about his mountain or hill, and they will be a blessing; then he will give rain in its season, and there will be rains of blessing — which he promises in the blessings of Deuteronomy —.

34:27.t: And the tree of life, he says, will give — of which it is written in Genesis —, and the tree of wisdom — of which it is said: It is a tree of life to all who take it up —: it will give its fruit when the earth too has given its fruit, or the trees of the regions, the very great multitude of the saints; and the earth will give its shoot: for Truth indeed has sprung from the earth; and they will be in their own land without fear, or in hope of peace, in the land of the living — the land of the meek, of which it is written: Blessed are the gentle, for they shall possess the land —, so that through the felicity of all things they may know that he himself is the Lord, when he has broken the chains or the iron ring of their yoke, by which they were pressed down as by a most heavy rule, and has rescued them from the hand of those ruling over them, or of those afflicting them with servitude: For each one is the slave of him by whom he is overcome.

34:28.t: And they will by no means be a prey any longer to the demonic nations, nor will the beasts of the earth, of which we have spoken, devour them, but they will dwell confidently without any terror, according to the exposition above.

34:29.t: And I will raise up for them, he says, a renowned shoot (or a planting of peace) — which speaks in the Gospel: I am the true vine —, and they will no longer be diminished by famine in the land — so the famine is in earthly things; but the famine of hearing the word of God, which, under the good shepherd, and the renowned shoot, celebrated in the speech of all, and the planting of peace, will by no means be in the land —, nor will they be subject any longer to the reproaches of the nations — so that they say: Where is the Lord their God? —; and after all these things they will know, not only that he himself is the Lord — which he had also said above —, but, with an addition, that the Lord of all is properly their God, with them — who says in the Gospel to the apostles: Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age —; and when he himself is the Lord their God, then they too will be his people: not just anyone, but those who have deserved to be called the house of Israel.

34:31.t: And lest we should think that all that has been said pertains to shepherds and sheep and he-goats and rams, he solves the riddle, or rather the μεταφορὰν, and sets it down more plainly: But you, my sheep, and the sheep of my pasture, are men; the whole discourse, therefore, is about men, to whom he says: I the Lord your God, says the Lord God.

35:1.t: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set (or turn) your face against Mount Seir, and you shall prophesy concerning it (or to it), and you shall say to it: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, Mount Seir; and I will stretch out my hand over you, and I will make you desolate and deserted. I will demolish your cities (or in your cities I will make a waste), and you shall be deserted, and you shall know that I am the Lord. Because you have been a perpetual enemy, and have shut up the sons of Israel into the hands of the sword (or and have laid siege to the house of Israel deceitfully in the hand of the sword) in the time of their affliction, in the time of the final iniquity; therefore, as I live, says the Lord God, I will hand you over to blood (or since you have sinned in blood), and blood pursues you, and since you have hated blood, blood pursues you. […]
