Lucidly and distinctly, the course of virtues shows. itself so.

From works performed by compulsion, in solitude there is born a blazing and immeasurable heat, which is generated in the heart by fervent deliberations, newly born in the spirit.

Works and watchfulness polish the mind by their heat and give it sight. And sight gives birth to the fervent deliberations mentioned, because of the depth of psychic sight which is called contemplation.

Contemplation gives birth to fervour; from this fervour sight given by grace is born; and then outbursts of tears begin. At first partial ones; this means that a man’s tears will flow several times every day. Then he will come to [the state of] tears without a break. Through the tears the soul receives peaceful deliberations. From peaceful deliberations it rises unto serenity of insight. And by serenity of insight a man reaches the sight of hidden things. For purity is brought about by being free from war. […]

In his final vision, Ezekiel was shown a stream that issued from the temple and flowed into the sea. He speaks of it in these words: “The angel led me a thousand cubits, and brought me through the water up to my ankles. He led me a thousand cubits, and brought me through the water up to my knees. He led me a thousand cubits, and brought me through the water up to my loins. He led me a thousand cubits, and I could not cross the stream, because its waters had risen; the stream could not be crossed” (Ezek. 47:3–5). By the stream we should understand divine Scripture, which flows out of the temple, that is, the Church, from the mouths of preachers. The angel signifies the Lord, while the prophet represents those who wish to study the divine Scriptures so that they may themselves advance in them and instruct others through their knowledge. The number one thousand often signifies the perfection of something. […]

47:4.t: And after the thousand cubits which reach as far as the ankle: He measured another thousand cubits in the water and led me across up to the knees: since after the remission of sins and the beginnings of progress, when we strive to climb a little from earthly things to higher ones, we bend the knees to the Lord — as the Apostle says: That every knee should bend, of things in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father —. Thirdly: He measured a thousand cubits, and led me, he says, across through the water up to the kidneys: for by these steps we come to the heights, which heights themselves, however, reach up to the loins and kidneys, so that all lust in us may be cut off, and we may possess the sanctification of the body without which no one will see God — whence also in this same prophet God is seen fiery from the feet up to the loins: for the works of the loins need fire and purgation, as the righteous man says: For my loins have […]

47:5.t: Whence now fourthly it is said: And he measured a thousand, 'cubits' being understood, a torrent — which the Seventy did not translate —, which I could not pass across (much better than the Seventy, who said: which he could not pass across): for the prophet, and all human nature, cannot after the loins pass across the torrent of thoughts and the incitements of vices; but that man: Who was clothed in 'baddi' [linen], and the guide of the prophet, clearly passes across: Who did no sin, nor was guile found in his mouth. And he gives the reasons why the prophet could not pass across the fourth thousand cubits: For, he says, the deep waters of the torrent had swelled, which cannot be forded — and how is it written, with the prophet glorying: Our soul has passed across the torrent? But it is easily resolved if we know that in place of this it is written in the Hebrew: The torrent has passed across my soul —. […]

47:6.t: That man, who was Ezekiel's guide, admonishes the prophet to look more carefully and see, and to attend with the eyes of the mind to hidden mysteries; and he calls him 'son of man' either as a figure of the Lord Savior — for 'Hiezechiel' means 'strength' or 'dominion of God' —, or certainly as a reminder of human frailty — lest he forget his condition while great things are shown to him —; and having admonished him he leads him and turns him to the bank of the torrent so that, since he could not cross the middle depth, he might at least recognize the things that are on the banks.

And he said to me: Surely you have seen, son of man; and he led me out, and turned me to the bank of the torrent (or of the river). And when I had turned (or he had turned me), behold, on the bank of the torrent (or of the river) a great many trees (or very many trees) on either side; and he said to me: These waters, which go out to the mounds of sand of the east and go down to the plains of the desert (or this water which goes out into Galilee, which slopes toward the east, and goes down to Arabia), will enter the sea; and they will go out, and the waters will be healed: and every living soul (or of animals) that creeps (or of creeping things), wherever the torrent (or the river) comes, will live, and there will be very many fish after these waters have come there, and all things will be healed and will live to which the torrent (or the river) comes. And fishermen will stand over them from En-gedi to En-eglaim; there will be a drying of nets; […]

47:7.t: And when, he says, I had turned (or he had turned me, who was guide and admonisher), behold, on the bank of the torrent (or of the river) many trees (or a great many trees) exceedingly, on either side: this 'torrent', which on account of the abundance of its waters is borne along in the manner of a torrent and receives rains from heaven, of which we spoke in the preceding reading, is itself called by the Seventy 'river', because it has perpetual waters, not collected from rains here and there but abiding from a living and perpetual spring — of which river we read many things in the holy scriptures, but for the present a few things must be said, and first that: The rush of the river makes glad the city of God, and in another place: The river of God is filled with waters; you have prepared their food, for so is your preparation, and again in the plural: The rivers have lifted up, O Lord, the rivers have lifted up their voices. […]

47:8.t: And the guide who goes before, the teacher, teaches the prophet and says: These waters, which go out (or into Galilee of the nations according to the Seventy, or, as is more truly contained in the Hebrew:) to the mounds of sand of the east and go down to the plains of the desert (or to Arabia), will enter the sea (or to the outlets of the sea), and the waters will be healed; we said long ago that the waters signify either the grace of baptism or the teaching of the Gospel, which, if they go out from the threshold of the temple of the Lord and hold to the apostolic discipline, make the mounds of sand, previously sterile and unfruitful, to be fruit-bearing, and so water all the plains and deserts as to express among themselves too the mystery of the spring of Jericho — which Elisha healed with the evangelic and apostolic salt, to such a degree that where there had previously been sterility and death, there was fertility and life —; […]

Your way is in the sea. He came, the fountain of life, to sweeten the sea, the bitter sea, the Dead Sea. Therefore, according to Ezekiel, there goes forth from the temple of the Lord a fountain of living water, and it goes to the Dead Sea, which had nothing living. For no little fishes could be in the Dead Sea, nothing lived in the Dead Sea. From the temple of the Lord, that is, from his bosom, the Savior went forth, and sweetened the Dead Sea and the bitter waters.

47:9.t: Since, then, these waters have nothing of usefulness, as the plain account testifies, even if it should come about, as the foolish superstition of the Jews believes, according to the spiritual understanding, healed by the torrent of the Lord, they will have very many fish, and all things to which this torrent comes will live, so that fishermen stand over the banks from 'Engaddi' to 'Engallim' — of which the first means 'spring' or 'eye' 'of the kid', the next 'spring, or eye' 'of calves': En-eglaim is at the beginning of the Dead Sea, where the Jordan enters, and En-gedi where it ends and is consumed; and I think the Dead Sea is the one of which Zechariah speaks: On that day living water will go out from Jerusalem, and the middle of it into the first sea; […]

47:10.t: Over this sea — from 'Engaddi', 'the eye and spring of the kid', which is always offered for sins, up to 'Engallim', 'the spring of calves', which are slaughtered to the Lord and imitate the calf that puts forth horns and hoofs, which are slaughtered at the altar in type of the Savior — there will be fishermen, to whom Jesus speaks: Come to me and I will make you fishermen, of whom Jeremiah too: Behold, I, he says, will send fishermen; and very many species, or rather kinds, of fish will be in the sea once dead, which fish Peter drew out on the right-hand side at the Lord's command, and they were one hundred and fifty-three, so that the nets were breaking because of their multitude — and those who have written on the natures of animals, and especially those who have published ἁλιευτικά [works on fishing] in the Latin as well as the Greek tongue — of whom Opianicus the Cilician is a most learned poet —, say that there are one hundred and fifty-three kinds of fish; […]

47:11.t: But what follows: On its shores and in the marshy places (or in those which go out from the shore) the waters will not be healed, secretly shows that whoever was not in Noah's ark perishes while the flood reigns, and that those whom this river has not touched do not receive healing: But they will be given, he says, to salt-pits, according to that which is written: When the pestilent man is scourged, the fool will be wiser — for the examples of the worse instruct the good —, or: They will be given to salt-pits, according to that which is written in the Gospel: Salt is good; but if the salt has become foolish, it is useful for nothing, so that they may lack crops and greenness forever — which a city too, sprinkled with salt after its ruin, demonstrates —.

47:12.t: But over the torrent (or the river) there will rise on its banks on either side every fruit tree (or, as all have translated with one voice, βρώσιμον, 'that which provides food and nourishment' and 'that which can be eaten'; and in the Hebrew tongue it is called 'machal'). And: (nothing, according to the Seventy, will grow old in it, but its produce will be renewed daily, or:) its leaf will not fall from it, and its fruit will not fail, according to that which is written in Psalm 1: And he will be like the tree that is planted beside the runnings of waters, which will give its fruit in its season; and its leaf will not fall. Each month, he says, it will bring forth early fruits (or, as is written in the Seventy: its fruit in its renewal will give early fruits), so that all the fruits of believers may be firstfruits and the single months may be assigned to the single apostles; […]

The same prophet says in what follows that he saw trees on both banks of the stream, whose fruit was for food and whose leaves were for healing. The two banks signify the Two Testaments. Between them flows the great stream of Scripture, set forth by the holy Fathers. The trees represent the teachers of the Church, said to be planted on both banks, that is, in the teaching of the Old and New Testaments. Drawing waters of true knowledge, they produce both fruit and leaves: the fruit signifies good works, and the leaves, words of preaching. The fruit serves as food and the leaves as medicine, because a teacher gives the ailing soul the healing medicine of words only after first nourishing it with examples of good works.

47:13.t: Thus says the Lord God. This is the boundary by which you shall possess the land in the twelve tribes of Israel, because Joseph has a double cord; and you shall possess it — each one equally as his brother — the land which I lifted up my hand to give to your fathers; and this land shall fall to you as a possession. In place of what we said: Because Joseph has a double cord, the Seventy translated: Increase of the cord — for 'Ioseph' means 'increase —, understanding a thing in place of a name and confusing the mind of the reader: for when the Levitical tribe had been subtracted and assigned to the sacrifices of the temple, there remained eleven tribes, of which Joseph was divided into two, Ephraim and Manasseh, who said to Joshua son of Nun: Why have you given me a possession of one lot and one cord, though I am of so great a multitude and the Lord has blessed me?, to whom Joshua answered: If you are a numerous people, go up into the forest and cut down spaces for yourself in the land of the Perizzite and of Rephaim, […]

47:14.t: And the individual tribes receive equal spaces of land according to their multitude, by no means at the discretion of the one dividing but by lot, which rests in the power of the Lord. Finally Joshua himself too, who was the divider of the land, did not set apart his own land for himself, lest he should seem to have chosen the best, but received from the princes of all the tribes: Timnath-serah in mount Ephraim.

47:15.t: And this is the boundary of the land: toward the northern quarter, from the Great Sea, by the way of Ethalon, for those coming to Sadada, Hamath, Berotha, Sabarim, which is between the middle of Damascus and the border of Hamath, the court of Thicon, which is beside Hauran (or of Auranitis); and the boundary shall be from the sea up to 'the court of Enom' (or 'Aser-Enan'), the boundary of Damascus; and from north to north the boundary of Hamath, the northern quarter. Between the description of the holy land of the twelve tribes by Joshua son of Nun and the one which is now commanded to be made through Ezekiel there is this difference: that there the land is divided among the tribes by lot, here it is assigned by the discretion of the Lord who commands. […]

47:18.t: But the eastern quarter, from the midst of Hauran and from the midst of Damascus and from the midst of Gilead and from the midst of the land of Israel, the Jordan dividing, to the eastern sea; you shall measure the eastern quarter. For which in the book of Numbers I have found it written thus: Thence they shall measure the boundaries toward the eastern quarter from 'the village of Enan' (that is, 'Aser-Enon') as far as Sephama, and from Sephama the boundaries will go down to Rebla, opposite the spring; thence they will come toward the east to the sea of Chinnereth, and they will extend as far as the Jordan, and at the last they will be closed by the sea. […]

47:19.t: But the southern quarter, the meridional, from Tamar up to the waters of contradiction (or to the waters of 'Mariboth' — for these mean 'contradiction' or διαδίκασμοι, that is, 'disputes' —) of Kadesh too, and the torrent up to the Great Sea; this is the southern quarter toward the south. For which in the book of Numbers it is written thus: It will begin from the wilderness of Sin, which is beside Edom, and will have as boundaries toward the east the sea. And they will go around the southern quarter by the Ascent of the Scorpion, so that they pass Senna and come into the south as far as Kadesh-barnea, whence the borders will go out to a village named Addar, and will extend as far as Asemona. And the boundary will go around from Asemona as far as the torrent of Egypt, and will be ended by the shore of the Great Sea. […]

47:20.t: And the quarter of the sea, the Great Sea, from the border straight on until you come to Hamath; this is the quarter of the sea. Of which the book of Numbers writes more plainly and more briefly: But the western quarter will begin from the Great Sea, and will be closed by that same end, that is, from sea to sea: namely from the torrent of Rhinocorura, which flows into the sea, up to that place which is opposite Hamath, the city of Syria, of which we spoke above. But the west, according to the laws of tropology, is always in the sea, always in the brine and the waves, where every day shipwrecks are stirred up, and the deaths of the wretched, and the loss of riches and merchandise; and yet, when we have broken all these things by patience, we come straight on to 'Emath', that is, to the 'truth' of the Lord, who, once persecutions are overcome, has promised us eternal rewards.

47:21.t: And you shall divide this land for yourselves by the tribes of Israel; and you shall cast it as an inheritance, for yourselves and for the strangers who have come to you, who will have begotten sons in your midst, and they shall be to you as natives among the sons of Israel: with you they shall divide the possession in the midst of the tribes of Israel; and in whatever tribe the stranger shall be, there you shall give him a possession, says the Lord God. Through this passage we learn — and the haughtiness of the Jews is struck down — that nothing is divided between Israel and the people of the Gentiles: for if the land is divided to strangers and foreigners together with those who are of the people of Israel, that is, the natives, no one doubts that the inheritance is the same for the people of the Gentiles and for the people of the Jews, if only they have been converted to the worship of the God of Israel — which properly possesses the name Christian —, the Jews having the letter of the law and we the spirit, they […]

48:1.t: And these are the names of the tribes: from the borders of the north, beside the way of Ethalon, for those going to Hamath, Court Enon, the border of Damascus toward the north beside Hamath; and its eastern side shall be the sea, Dan one. And from the border of Dan, from the eastern side to the side of the sea, Asher one. And above the border of Asher, from the eastern side to the side of the sea, Naphtali one. And above the border of Naphtali, from the eastern side to the side of the sea, Manasseh one. And above the border of Manasseh, from the eastern side to the side of the sea, Ephraim one. And above the border of Ephraim, from the eastern side to the side of the sea, Reuben one. And above the border of Reuben, from the eastern side to the side of the sea, Judah one. […]

48:8.t: And above the border of Judah, from the eastern side to the side of the sea, shall be the firstfruits which you shall set apart, twenty-five thousand in breadth, and in length as each of the portions from the eastern side to the side of the sea; and the sanctuary shall be in the midst of it. The firstfruits which you shall set apart for the Lord: the length twenty-five thousand, and the breadth ten thousand. It is superfluous to discuss again what has been discussed, and to labor once more, as though they had not been said, over things on which we labored above. After the boundaries of the seven tribes, the firstfruits are described from the east to the west, whose breadth is to hold twenty-five thousand reeds, but the length as much as the individual tribes hold from the east to the sea; the number of this length is uncertain, for no measure was set down in the description of the individual tribes; […]

48:9.t: In the midst, moreover, the sanctuary is placed, beside the firstfruits which are set apart for the Lord, of a length of twenty-five thousand reeds and a breadth of ten thousand — reading which, we can say nothing else but that saying of the Apostle: O the depth of the riches and of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments, and untraceable his ways!, and in another place: That you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, to know also the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled unto all the fullness of God —. The number twenty-five, moreover, is referred to the senses — of which it was said: You shall possess a divine sense —, and that of ten thousand to perfect and consummate virtue — which by the decalogue of the old instrument reaches to the mystery of the Gospel; […]

48:10.t: These moreover shall be the firstfruits of the sanctuary of the priests: toward the north twenty-five thousand in length, and toward the sea ten thousand in breadth, and also toward the east ten thousand in breadth, and toward the south twenty-five thousand in length; and the sanctuary of the Lord shall be in the midst of it: the sanctuary for the priests, of the sons of Zadok, who kept my ceremonies and did not go astray when the children of Israel went astray, as the Levites went astray. And there shall be firstfruits from the firstfruits of the land, the Holy of Holies, beside the border of the Levites. The four sides of the firstfruits of the sanctuary are described — a portion which belongs not to the people or to the common crowd, nor to the Levites, a lower rank, but properly to the worship of the priests —: namely of the north and of the west and of the east and of the south; […]

The sanctuary, moreover (that is, the temple) of the Lord, shall be in the midst of the priestly firstfruits, and it will be walled about on every part with equal sides; and because he had said: These moreover shall be the firstfruits of the sanctuary of the priests, lest under the common term all priests should claim for themselves the possession of this place and the ceremonies to be observed, he sets it down specifically, adding: The sanctuary shall be for the priests, of the sons of 'Sadoc' — which means 'righteous', of whom it is said: The Lord is righteous and has loved righteousnesses; his face has seen equity; for 'Sadoc' the Seventy write 'Saduc'. This Sadoc speaks in the Gospel: For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, and of him, under the name of Solomon, the prophet mystically sings: O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king's son —. […]

48:12.t: For there shall be, he says, for 'them' firstfruits from the firstfruits of the land — that is, for the priests, and for those Who did not go astray when the children of Israel and the Levites went astray; and firstfruits from firstfruits, as tithes of tithes —, and the Holy of Holies beside the border of the Levites, so that the Levites indeed may have the borders adjoining the priests, but may not be able to hold the navel, that is, its middle, and the possession itself.

48:13.t: The possession of the Levites is also described, which is indeed neighboring to the borders of the priests, and has, for the multitude of the Levites, the same spaces in length and in breadth that the fewness of the priests has, but nevertheless uses its own boundaries and understands that it is separated from the priestly rank, to strike down the pride of the ministers who, ignorant of the humility of their station, swell up beyond the priests, that is, the presbyters: they reckon their dignity not by merit but by riches; certainly, whoever is first of the ministers, because he makes proclamation item by item among the people and yet does not depart from the side of the high priest, thinks it an injury if he is ordained a presbyter, and he does not remember, minister of tables and of widows, that he was appointed to the service not only of the priests but also of the widows and of the poor.

48:14.t: And they shall not sell, he says, of it, nor exchange, so that the possession of the Levitical allotment may remain eternal, and the merit of the dignity may not be overcome by price, nor be transferred from one to another: because the things that are sanctified to the Lord do not belong to those to whom they are given, but to him in whose name they are possessed.

And also for the Levites likewise, beside the borders of the priests, twenty-five thousand in length and ten thousand in breadth; the whole length twenty-five thousand and the breadth ten thousand; and they shall not sell of it, nor exchange (or measure), nor shall the firstfruits of the land be transferred (or taken away), because they are sanctified to the Lord. But the five thousand that remain in breadth by twenty-five thousand shall be profane, of the city, for dwelling and for suburbs; and the city shall be in the midst of it. What we have rendered as 'profane', for which Aquila translated βέβηλον, Symmachus and Theodotion λαικόν, the Seventy said προτείχισμα, which we can call 'outer wall'; but 'profane' and 'lay', that is, 'common', is what all the people may dwell in anywhere; and what they said: Nor shall it be measured nor taken away, for what we said: It shall not be exchanged nor transferred, plainly has no sense.

48:15.t: But the five thousand that remain in breadth by twenty-five thousand — 'of length' is understood —, shall be profane, of the city, so that all the Israelites and anyone of the common people may dwell there; not that they are unclean, or that anything in the dwelling of the holy land is thought defiled and filthy, but that, besides the priests, all are permitted to dwell in them; by which we understand that all the things we refer to the senses, that is, to the desires of the body — what we take in by sight and hearing, by touch, smell and taste — are profane and do not have the sanctity of the temple, and are not of priestly privilege but of lay cheapness. And the city shall be in the midst — of which it is written: The rush of the river gladdens the city of God, and: A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden —; of it we shall speak in what follows. Προτείχισμα, that is, 'outer wall', and διάστημα, that is, 'space', which the Seventy translated for 'suburbs': what sense it has in this place we do not know.

48:16.t: And these the measures of the same: toward the northern side four thousand five hundred, and toward the southern side four thousand five hundred, and toward the eastern side four thousand five hundred, and toward the western side four thousand five hundred. As to his saying: And these are its measures, 'of the city' is to be understood; for at the end of the preceding chapter it was set down: And the city shall be in the midst of it, that is, of the land. And first he begins from the northern side and sets the southern side opposite it, and again he matches like with like, so as to set over against the eastern side the western, that is, the sea; […]

48:17.t: And the suburbs of the city shall be toward the north two hundred fifty, and toward the south two hundred fifty, and toward the east two hundred fifty, and toward the sea two hundred fifty. For 'suburbs', which in Hebrew are called 'magras', the Seventy again translated διάστημα, that is, 'space'. As to its saying 'two hundred fifty' on each side, 'reeds' is understood, which have six cubits each and one handbreadth, and on each side they make a little less than six hundred and seventeen paces, and all together a thousand reeds, amounting to two thousand four hundred and sixty-eight paces: these spaces surround the walls of the city round about, so as to divide between the city and the things that remain. […]

48:18.t: And what remains in length alongside the firstfruits of the sanctuary, ten thousand to the east and ten thousand to the west, shall be as the firstfruits of the sanctuary, and its produce shall be for food (or for loaves) for those who serve (or work) in the works of the city. And those serving (or working) in the works of the city shall serve the city (or shall work) from all the tribes of Israel. All the firstfruits of twenty-five thousand, by twenty-five thousand foursquare, shall be set apart for the firstfruits of the sanctuary and the possession of the city. After the description of the holy city and its suburbs, he wishes the remaining part of the firstfruits of the sanctuary, ten thousand reeds stretching to the east and another ten thousand to the west, to be assigned to those who carry out the works of the city for various uses and for whatever the city needs: namely, that they be sown, and that the workers feed on the produce that grows in this space of land, those who either build the walls of the city […]

48:19.t: And the workers, he says (or those who serve in the works of the city), shall be from all the tribes of Israel, so that no one may think himself exempt from the works of the city, but all may vie with one another in building up the Church — which we read was done in the tabernacle too, so that, according to the variety of their means, one offered gold and silver, scarlet, fine linen and purple, and various and diverse woofs, others skins and goats' hair; and, though the gifts were diverse according to the measure of their substance, the reward of the givers was one, nay rather greater for those who offered small things indeed but greater in proportion to their means, after the example of the poor widow who put two mites into the gifts of the treasury and was praised by the judgment of the Lord, who said: Truly I say to you that this poor little widow has put in more than all; […]

48:20.t: As therefore we have spoken about the works of the city, so this must be touched on briefly: that all the firstfruits of the sanctuary and the possession of the city, reckoned together foursquare, contain two hundred and forty-six thousand and a third part — for if twenty-five thousand reeds — which have six cubits each and one handbreadth — make of our paces, that is, Roman paces, sixty-one thousand six hundred and sixty-seven, no one doubts that these, reckoned fourfold, produce the number above —; from which we perceive that all things are to be understood spiritually, and that the possession of the Church is much broader than it once was in Judea, where they did not even receive portions of the holy land, but from the individual tribes received, in forty-eight cities, not a full possession but a dwelling and lodgings; […]

48:21.t: And what remains shall be the prince's, on every side (or on this side and that) of the firstfruits of the sanctuary and of the possession of the city, over against (or before the face of) the twenty-five thousand of the firstfruits as far as the eastern border, and also from the sea over against (or before the face of) the twenty-five thousand as far as the border of the sea, likewise in the portions of the prince it shall be; and the firstfruits of the sanctuary and the sanctuary of the temple shall be in the midst of it. And of the possession of the Levites and of the possession of the city, in the midst of the portions of the prince, it shall be toward the border of Judah and toward the border of Benjamin, and shall belong to the prince. About this prince it was argued more fully above, and that he alone was to receive as much as one tribe; […]

48:22.t: But also whatever remains of the possession of the Levites and of the possession of the city will be allotted to the prince, and the furthest part of the seven tribes, neighboring the firstfruits and the city and the temple, will be in the tribe of Judah, and the furthest part of the five tribes, by the same right as above, in the tribe of Benjamin; and that furthest part itself will belong to the prince. Hence the mysteries of holy Scripture are to be marveled at, and pondered rather than set forth in speech. For in the earlier division of the lands beyond the Jordan, through Moses, the land was divided to the two tribes, Reuben and Gad, and to the half tribe of Manasseh; but within the Jordan, through Joshua son of Nun and Eleazar son of Aaron, Judah took possession on the south, and Ephraim and the half tribe of Manasseh on the north; […]

48:23.t: And for the remaining tribes: from the eastern side to the western side, Benjamin one. And over against the border of Benjamin, from the eastern side to the western side, Simeon one. And above the border of Simeon, from the eastern side to the side of the west, Issachar one. And above the border of Issachar, from the eastern side to the western side, Zebulun one. And above the border of Zebulun, from the eastern side to the side of the sea, Gad one. And above the border of Gad, toward the side of the south, toward the midday; and the boundary shall be from Tamar as far as the waters of Contradiction, Kadesh, and the inheritance over against the Great Sea. This is the land which you shall allot to the children of Israel, and these are their divisions, says the Lord God. […]

48:28.t: And this is briefly to be noted: that the tribe of Gad, the last of the five tribes — which in the earlier description was beyond the Jordan — is placed in that part which Judah held before, namely toward the side of the south, toward the midday, and that the boundary is from Thamar as far as the waters of Contradiction, Kadesh, the inheritance over against the Great Sea; Thamar is the very place of which we have already spoken, which they now call 'Palmyra', and which was once built by Solomon: for 'palm' in the Hebrew tongue is called 'Thamar', and some think it obtained this name from the fact that there are very many palm groves there. […]

48:30.t: But we do confess that a kingdom is promised to us upon the earth, although before heaven, only in another state of existence; inasmuch as it will be after the resurrection for a thousand years in the divinely-built city of Jerusalem, "let down from heaven," [Revelation 21:2] which the apostle also calls "our mother from above;" [Galatians 4:26] and, while declaring that our πολίτευμα, or citizenship, is in heaven, he predicates of it that it is really a city in heaven. This both Ezekiel had knowledge of [Ezekiel 48:30-35] and the Apostle John beheld. [Revelation 21:10-23] And the word of the new prophecy which is a part of our belief, attests how it foretold that there would be for a sign a picture of this very city exhibited to view previous to its manifestation. This prophecy, indeed, has been very lately fulfilled in an expedition to the East. For it is evident from the testimony of even heathen witnesses, that in Judæa there was suspended in the sky a city early every morning for forty days. […]

And these are the outgoings of the city: from the northern side you shall measure four thousand five hundred. And the gates of the city after the names of the tribes of Israel: three gates from the north, the gate of Reuben one, the gate of Judah one, the gate of Levi one. And toward the eastern side four thousand five hundred; and three gates: the gate of Joseph one, the gate of Benjamin one, the gate of Dan one. And toward the southern side you shall measure four thousand five hundred: the gate of Simeon one, the gate of Issachar one, the gate of Zebulun one. And toward the western side four thousand five hundred; their gates three: the gate of Gad one, the gate of Asher one, the gate of Naphtali one. Round about eighteen thousand; and the name of the city from that day: The Lord is there. Concerning the circuit of the city, that on each side, foursquare, it had four thousand five hundred reeds, the preceding discourse has told; […]

48:35.t: And it is necessary that such a city hold eighteen thousand reeds round about, under which number, in Psalm 18 (19) also, the natural law is set down, and the grace of the Gospel is described, by which the Church, that is, the city of the Savior, has been built. The name of the city itself, too, will by no means be, as before, 'Hierosolyma', which means 'vision of peace', but 'Adonai sam', which is rendered into the Latin tongue 'The Lord is there': who will never withdraw from her, as he departed before from the former people, saying to the disciples: Arise, let us go hence, and to the Jews: Your house shall be left to you desolate, but will have an eternal possession and himself be her possession, promising to the same disciples: Behold, I am with you even to the consummation of the age.
